data.value: turns back only below the air: lost

data.name: Aurora_Chart_Particles_Note
data.value: The field grows towards the poles. The particle turns back where it reaches the dashed level, 1/sin² of its pitch angle; if that lies past the air, it is lost.

data.name: Aurora_Chart_Shield_Caption
data.value: How far out the shield sits

data.name: Aurora_Chart_Shield_Note
data.value: Magnetopause distance against the solar wind's push (Shue et al. 1998); the dot is now. A southward field lets it in closer.

data.name: Aurora_Chart_Sky_Note
data.value: Where electrons of this energy stop (dashed) and which light survives there. Approximate: real aurorae mix many energies.

data.name: Aurora_Cycle_North
data.value: Northward field: the shield stays shut

data.name: Aurora_Energy_Tooltip
data.value: Its energy changes its real numbers below; the picture keeps the same scale.

data.name: Aurora_Hint_Particles
data.value: Drag to turn the view round Earth.

data.name: Aurora_Hint_Shield
data.value: Drag sideways to move through the cycle.

data.name: Aurora_Hint_Sky
data.value: Drag sideways to move through the night.

data.name: Aurora_Kp_Note
data.value: Kp (0–9) says how disturbed Earth's field is over three hours. It follows the solar wind in the first view, or set it here.

data.name: Aurora_Lesson_Particles_Choice1
data.value: The angle between its path and the field line

data.name: Aurora_Lesson_Particles_Choice3
data.value: How far it is from the Sun

data.name: Aurora_Particle_Note
data.value: Below the loss cone (a few degrees) the particle reaches the air and is lost.

data.name: Aurora_Particles_Fact1
data.value: The radiation belts were found in 1958 by James Van Allen's Geiger counters on Explorer 1 and Explorer 3, the first American satellites.

data.name: Aurora_Particles_Fact2
data.value: An outer-belt electron goes round its spiral tens of thousands of times a second, bounces pole to pole in under a second, and drifts round Earth in minutes to hours.

data.name: Aurora_Particles_Fact3
data.value: In a storm the ring current swells and weakens the field at the ground. Its strength is tracked by the Dst index, which falls by hundreds of nT in great storms.

data.name: Aurora_Particles_Fact4
data.value: Over the South Atlantic the inner belt dips closest to the ground, because Earth's field is weaker there. Satellites and the space station pick up extra radiation crossing it.

data.name: Aurora_Particles_Fact5
data.value: Waves in space keep nudging trapped particles into the loss cone. That steady drizzle lights the faint, diffuse aurora.

data.name: Aurora_Particles_Note
data.value: Earth's field as a dipole, the shell to scale. The spiral is drawn far wider and the drift far faster than real.

data.name: Aurora_Particles_Subtitle
data.value: Caught in Earth's field: spiral, bounce, drift

data.name: Aurora_See_Day_Text
data.value: Even with the aurora overhead, daylight or twilight drowns it out. Move the night on until the sky is dark.

data.name: Aurora_See_Hidden_Text
data.value: The oval is too far away: the curve of the Earth hides even the top of the curtain. It would take a stronger storm to bring it closer.

data.name: Aurora_See_High_Text
data.value: The curtain stands well above your horizon on the side of the magnetic pole. Look that way on a clear, dark night.

data.name: Aurora_See_Low_Text
data.value: Only the top of the curtain rises above your horizon, low and faint. A camera on a long exposure picks it up better than the eye.

data.name: Aurora_See_Overhead_Text
data.value: You are under the oval: on a clear, dark night the curtains can fill the sky and ripple right above you.

data.name: Aurora_Shield_Fact1
data.value: The solar wind blows at 300 to 800 km/s and takes two to four days to reach Earth; storm clouds can do it in less than a day.

data.name: Aurora_Shield_Fact2
data.value: On the day side the magnetopause is usually about 10 Earth radii out (some 64 000 km). The tail stretches hundreds of Earth radii, far past the Moon.

data.name: Aurora_Shield_Fact3
data.value: In the strongest storms the magnetopause is pushed inside geostationary orbit, 6.6 Earth radii out, and satellites there find themselves in the solar wind.

data.name: Aurora_Shield_Fact4
data.value: Mars lost its global magnetic field billions of years ago, and the solar wind has been stripping its upper atmosphere ever since.

data.name: Aurora_Shield_Fact5
data.value: James Dungey proposed in 1961 that the solar wind's field joins Earth's and drives the whole magnetosphere round: the Dungey cycle.

data.name: Aurora_Shield_Note
data.value: The noon–midnight slice; Earth and the magnetosphere to scale (the Sun is far off). Field lines simplified, solar wind sped up about 100×.

data.name: Aurora_Shield_Subtitle
data.value: The solar wind and Earth's magnetic shield

data.name: Aurora_Sky_Fact1
data.value: Atomic oxygen's green line at 557.7 nm is the commonest aurora colour. Its red line at 630 nm comes from above about 200 km.

data.name: Aurora_Sky_Fact2
data.value: The aurora is 100 to 400 km up, far above aircraft. The space station orbits at about 400 km, so astronauts often look down on it.

data.name: Aurora_Sky_Fact3
data.value: Northern and southern lights happen together: the same field lines end in both hemispheres, so the two ovals are near mirror images.

data.name: Aurora_Sky_Fact4
data.value: In the great storm of September 1859, the Carrington event, aurorae were seen as far south as the Caribbean.

data.name: Aurora_Sky_Fact5
data.value: In May 2024 the strongest geomagnetic storm in over twenty years brought aurorae far from the poles, and cameras caught them across northern China.

data.name: Aurora_Sky_Note
data.value: Real coastlines and night for your place, a rule-of-thumb oval by Kp, and Earth's curve to scale in the slice.

data.name: Aurora_Slice_Caption
data.value: Slice from you to the aurora (true scale)

data.name: Aurora_Slice_Hidden
data.value: {0} km away; its top is {1}° below the horizon

data.name: Aurora_Slice_Seen
data.value: {0} km away; {1}° to {2}° above the horizon

data.name: Aurora_Stage_Arrive_Text
data.value: The Sun's field, carried by the wind, meets the bow shock and drapes over the front of the magnetosphere. Here it points south, against Earth's northward field at the nose.

data.name: Aurora_Stage_Arrive_Title
data.value: A solar wind field line arrives

data.name: Aurora_Stage_NoField_Text
data.value: The solar wind flows straight onto the upper air. There is no magnetosphere to trap particles and no auroral oval, and over the ages the wind strips the air away.

data.name: Aurora_Stage_North_Text
data.value: The Sun's field points the same way as Earth's at the nose, so they cannot join there. The lines drape over the magnetosphere and slide past, and the aurora stays quiet.

data.name: Aurora_Stage_North_Title
data.value: Northward field: the shield stays shut

data.name: Aurora_Stage_Open_Text
data.value: At the nose the two fields join. The line is cut and rejoined: one end is now tied to Earth, the other is out in the solar wind, which drags it over the pole.

data.name: Aurora_Stage_Return_Text
data.value: The closed line drifts round the sides of Earth back to the day side, ready to be opened again. A real cycle takes about an hour.

data.name: Aurora_Stage_Return_Title
data.value: Back round to the day side

data.name: Aurora_Stage_Sink_Text
data.value: The open lines pile up in the tail lobes, storing energy, and sink towards the middle of the tail.

data.name: Aurora_Stage_Snap_Text
data.value: In the tail the lines from north and south rejoin. The closed line snaps back towards Earth and shoots electrons down into the auroral oval, and the aurora flares up.

data.name: Aurora_Stage_Snap_Title
data.value: Tail reconnection: the line snaps back

data.name: Aurora_Stage_Zero_Text
data.value: With no southward part there is hardly any reconnection at the nose. The shield is barely open and the aurora is faint.

data.name: Aurora_Stat_Needed
data.value: Kp for its top to clear your horizon

data.name: Aurora_Stat_Needed_Beyond
data.value: beyond 9: only the greatest storms on record

data.name: Aurora_Trap_Held_Electron
data.value: It spirals round its field line, bounces between the mirror points and drifts east round Earth. It can stay trapped for days or longer.

data.name: Aurora_Trap_Held_Proton
data.value: It spirals round its field line the other way, bounces between the mirror points and drifts west round Earth. Protons in the inner belt can stay for years.

data.name: Aurora_Trap_Lost_Text
data.value: Its pitch angle is inside the loss cone, so it would turn back only below the top of the atmosphere. It reaches the air near the pole and gives up its energy there: this is how the aurora is lit.

data.name: Aurora_View_Daylight
data.value: Too bright: the Sun is up or only just set

data.name: BackCover_Text
data.value: Look up, look around, and ask why.

data.name: Breeze_Cell_AloftFlow_Day_Description
data.value: Compare at one height: over the land the pressure surfaces have moved up, so at that height the pressure over the land is now higher than over the sea (a raised pressure surface means high pressure). Air aloft flows from the land toward the sea, from high to low.

data.name: Breeze_Cell_AloftFlow_Day_Title
data.value: Aloft the land's pressure is higher: air flows to the sea

data.name: Breeze_Cell_AloftFlow_Night_Description
data.value: Now the pressure surfaces are lower over the land, so at the same height the pressure over the sea is higher. Air aloft flows from the sea toward the land.

data.name: Breeze_Cell_AloftFlow_Night_Title
data.value: Aloft the sea's pressure is higher: air flows to the land

data.name: Breeze_Cell_Circulation_Day_Description
data.value: Over the warm land the air rises, aloft it flows out to sea, over the cool sea it sinks, and at the ground it comes back to the land: one closed loop driven only by a difference in temperature. The same loop turns between a city and its countryside, a valley and its mountain slopes, and a continent and its ocean (the monsoon).

data.name: Breeze_Cell_Circulation_Day_Title
data.value: The thermal circulation: up where it is warm, down where it is cool

data.name: Breeze_Cell_Circulation_Night_Description
data.value: Now the sea is the warm side: air rises over the sea, flows to the land aloft, sinks over the cold land and drains back out to sea along the ground. A smaller, weaker loop than by day.

data.name: Breeze_Cell_Circulation_Night_Title
data.value: The thermal circulation, turned round at night

data.name: Breeze_Cell_Even_Day_Description
data.value: Each pressure surface (a surface on which the air pressure is the same everywhere) lies flat: at any height the pressure over the land equals the pressure over the sea. Nothing pushes the air sideways, so there is no wind.

data.name: Breeze_Cell_Even_Night_Description
data.value: After a sunny day the land cools quickly once the Sun sets and soon matches the sea. For a moment the pressure surfaces lie flat and the air is calm.

data.name: Breeze_Cell_Even_Night_Title
data.value: Evening: land and sea equally warm

data.name: Breeze_Cell_Fact1
data.value: Warm air is thicker: the height between two pressure levels grows with the air's mean temperature (the hypsometric equation). Between 1000 and 900 hPa it is about 3 m more for every degree.

data.name: Breeze_Cell_Fact2
data.value: A pressure difference of 1 hPa over 20 km pushes air at about 4 mm per second every second: in twenty minutes it would reach 5 m/s if nothing held it back.

data.name: Breeze_Cell_Fact3
data.value: On a pressure surface, a bulge upward marks high pressure and a dip marks low pressure at that height. At the ground, high and low over the land are the opposite of those aloft.

data.name: Breeze_Cell_Fact4
data.value: Sideways, air moves from high to low pressure at the same height; up and down, warm air rises and cool air sinks. Together they make the thermal circulation, the simplest form of motion in the atmosphere.

data.name: Breeze_Cell_Fact5
data.value: The same loop drives the valley breeze up mountain slopes by day and the mountain breeze down them at night, the country breeze into a warm city, and on the largest scale the monsoon.

data.name: Breeze_Cell_Heating_Day_Description
data.value: The Sun shines on land and sea alike, but the land heats only a thin top layer and warms up fast, while the sea mixes its heat down tens of metres and hardly warms at all. The warmed air over the land expands upward: the column gets taller and lifts the pressure surfaces above it, the higher up the more.

data.name: Breeze_Cell_Heating_Day_Title
data.value: The land warms faster; its air expands

data.name: Breeze_Cell_Heating_Night_Description
data.value: At night the land radiates its heat away quickly while the sea stays warm. The cooled air over the land contracts: its column gets shorter and the pressure surfaces above it sink.

data.name: Breeze_Cell_Heating_Night_Title
data.value: The land cools faster; its air shrinks

data.name: Breeze_Cell_NoDifference_Description
data.value: With land and sea at the same temperature both columns of air weigh the same and stand equally tall: the pressure surfaces stay flat and nothing moves. Drag the two temperatures apart.

data.name: Breeze_Cell_Note
data.value: A schematic. The bending of the pressure surfaces is exaggerated hundreds of times: in real air they move by only some 10–20 m.

data.name: Breeze_Cell_Subtitle
data.value: How a difference in temperature becomes a wind

data.name: Breeze_Cell_SurfacePressure_Day_Description
data.value: Air has left the top of the land's column and piled up over the sea, so the land's column now holds less air in all: the pressure at the ground falls over the land (a heat low) and rises over the sea. Near the ground the pressure surfaces now dip over the land and bulge over the sea.

data.name: Breeze_Cell_SurfacePressure_Day_Title
data.value: At the ground: low over the land, high over the sea

data.name: Breeze_Cell_SurfacePressure_Night_Description
data.value: Air has flowed in aloft over the land and out of the sea's column, so the pressure at the ground rises over the land and falls over the sea.

data.name: Breeze_Cell_SurfacePressure_Night_Title
data.value: At the ground: high over the land, low over the sea

data.name: Breeze_Cell_SurfaceWind_Day_Description
data.value: At the ground the push now runs from the sea's high to the land's low, so cool sea air flows inland. The pressure difference is only about 1 hPa, a thousandth of the air pressure, yet over tens of kilometres it is enough to drive a breeze of 3–7 m/s.

data.name: Breeze_Cell_SurfaceWind_Day_Title
data.value: At the ground the wind blows from sea to land: the sea breeze

data.name: Breeze_Cell_SurfaceWind_Night_Description
data.value: At the ground the push runs from the land's high to the sea's low, so the cold land air drains out to sea. The land breeze is gentler than the sea breeze, usually 1–3 m/s.

data.name: Breeze_Cell_SurfaceWind_Night_Title
data.value: At the ground the wind blows from land to sea: the land breeze

data.name: Breeze_Chart_Day_Caption
data.value: Temperatures and the wind at the beach through the day

data.name: Breeze_Chart_Day_Note
data.value: The land's air swings by about 11 °C, the sea by less than 1 °C. The wind follows the difference less than an hour later, and only once the land is a degree or two warmer (or colder) than the sea. Shaded: night.

data.name: Breeze_Chart_Profile_Caption
data.value: Land minus sea pressure at each height

data.name: Breeze_Chart_Profile_Note
data.value: Worked out from the hydrostatic equation, with the land's extra warmth fading out 1 km up. Just after heating the difference is zero at the ground and grows upward; once air has flowed out aloft it is negative at the ground and positive aloft. That is why the wind blows one way at the ground and the other way aloft.

data.name: Breeze_Chart_Rain_Note
data.value: Typical (long-term average) rainfall, rounded. A monsoon climate has a wet summer and a dry winter; Darwin, south of the equator, has them the other way round.

data.name: Breeze_Coast_EveningCalm_Description
data.value: After sunset the land cools quickly and soon matches the sea: for an hour or two there is no breeze at all, the sticky, still time of a summer evening on the coast. As the land cools further the wind turns round into a land breeze.

data.name: Breeze_Coast_Fact1
data.value: Water needs about four to five times as much heat as dry sand or soil to warm by one degree (about 4.2 against 0.8–1 kJ per kilogram), and sunlight reaches metres into the sea while waves mix the heat down tens of metres. On land it stays in the top few centimetres.

data.name: Breeze_Coast_Fact2
data.value: Evaporation cools the sea's surface too: much of the sunshine falling on the sea goes into turning water into vapour rather than into warming it.

data.name: Breeze_Coast_Fact3
data.value: A typical sea breeze blows at 3–7 m/s (force 2–4), is a few hundred metres to about a kilometre deep, and its front travels 20–50 km inland, sometimes more than 100 km.

data.name: Breeze_Coast_Fact4
data.value: When the sea-breeze front passes, the air can cool by several degrees within minutes and the humidity jumps: welcome relief on a hot coast.

data.name: Breeze_Coast_Fact5
data.value: Clouds and showers often line up along the sea-breeze front. In Florida, where the sea breezes from both coasts meet over the peninsula, summer afternoon thunderstorms are more frequent than anywhere else in the United States.

data.name: Breeze_Coast_LandBreeze_Description
data.value: At night the land loses its heat to the sky much faster than the sea does. The air over the land is now the colder and denser, the pressure at the ground is higher over the land, and a gentle wind drifts out to sea. It is weaker and shallower than the sea breeze, because cold air lies still near the ground.

data.name: Breeze_Coast_MorningCalm_Description
data.value: The Sun has been up a few hours and the land has caught up with the sea, or just edged past it. A difference of a degree or two is not yet enough to push the air: the land breeze has died away and the smoke goes straight up.

data.name: Breeze_Coast_Note
data.value: A summer day, local solar time. Heights are drawn more than ten times taller than real: the breeze is about 1 km deep and reaches tens of kilometres inland.

data.name: Breeze_Coast_Overcast_Description
data.value: A cloud deck keeps the Sun off the land by day and holds its heat in at night, so land and sea stay within a degree or two of each other. Without a temperature difference there is no pressure difference, and the sea and land breezes hardly form. What wind there is comes from bigger weather systems.

data.name: Breeze_Coast_SeaBreezeBuilding_Description
data.value: The land is now a few degrees warmer than the sea. Its air expands and rises, the pressure at the ground drops over the land, and cooler air starts flowing in from the sea, first right at the coast. Its leading edge, the sea-breeze front, starts moving inland.

data.name: Breeze_Coast_SeaBreezeFading_Description
data.value: Late afternoon: the Sun is low and the land is cooling, so the difference with the sea shrinks and the sea breeze weakens. The front stops moving inland and its clouds fade.

data.name: Breeze_Coast_SeaBreeze_Description
data.value: Early afternoon, the land at its warmest: cool, moist air blows in from the sea, strongest at the beach. Over the land it rises, at a height of 1–2 km it flows back out to sea, and over the sea it sinks again. Where the front pushes the warm land air up, a line of cumulus clouds often forms.

data.name: Breeze_Coast_Subtitle
data.value: Sea breeze by day, land breeze by night

data.name: Breeze_Hint_Cell
data.value: Six steps play in turn: step through them with the arrows, or switch to night to see it all turn round.

data.name: Breeze_Hint_Coast
data.value: Watch the flag, the smoke and the sails turn round; drag the timeline to any time of day.

data.name: Breeze_Hint_Monsoon

data.value: From over the land toward the sea

data.name: Breeze_Lesson_Cell_Choice2
data.value: From over the sea toward the land

data.name: Breeze_Lesson_Monsoon_Choice1

data.name: Breeze_Monsoon_Autumn_Description
data.value: The land cools again and the heat low fills in. The monsoon withdraws southward, from north-west India in mid-September and from all of India by about mid-October, and the winter monsoon sets in. Northern China turns clear and dry, while the north-east winds bring south-east India its late-year rains.

data.name: Breeze_Monsoon_Fact1
data.value: "Monsoon" comes from the Arabic mawsim, "season": Arab sailors rode the south-west winds to India in summer and the north-east winds home in winter.

data.name: Breeze_Monsoon_Fact2
data.value: India gets about three quarters of its yearly rain from the summer monsoon, June to September; a weak monsoon means drought for hundreds of millions of farmers.

data.name: Breeze_Monsoon_Fact3
data.value: In June and July the plum rains (meiyu) soak the Yangtze valley, where warm, moist monsoon air from the south meets cooler air from the north along a front that stalls for weeks.

data.name: Breeze_Monsoon_Fact4
data.value: Where the monsoon runs into the Khasi Hills of north-east India, Mawsynram and Cherrapunji average around 11,000–12,000 mm of rain a year, among the wettest places on Earth.

data.name: Breeze_Monsoon_Fact5
data.value: The land-sea difference is not the whole story: the planet's pressure belts also follow the Sun north and south through the year, and the Tibetan Plateau, heating the air 4–5 km up, strengthens the Asian summer monsoon.

data.name: Breeze_Monsoon_Note
data.value: Sea-level pressure and surface winds from a simple model of the average January and July charts; rainfall is a long-term average and real years vary a lot.

data.name: Breeze_Monsoon_Spring_Description
data.value: The land warms quickly and the Siberian High weakens. Southern China gets its first heavy spring rains while India bakes before the monsoon (May is its hottest month). Over the Indian subcontinent a heat low deepens; the summer monsoon usually reaches Kerala, on India's south-west tip, around 1 June and spreads north from there.

data.name: Breeze_Monsoon_Subtitle
data.value: The monsoon: a sea breeze the size of a continent and a year

data.name: Breeze_Monsoon_Summer_Description
data.value: In summer the continent heats far above the ocean. A huge heat low forms over north-west India, Pakistan and Iran, and moist ocean air pours in: the south-west monsoon over India (the south-east trade winds of the southern Indian Ocean cross the equator and turn) and the south-east monsoon over eastern China, on the flank of the West Pacific subtropical high. It brings most of the year's rain: Mumbai gets about nine tenths of its rain from June to September.

data.name: Breeze_Monsoon_Winter_Description
data.value: In winter the continent cools far below the ocean. Cold, dense air piles up over Mongolia and Siberia: the Siberian High, the strongest high-pressure system on Earth, often above 1,035 hPa. Cold, dry winds blow out of it, from the north-west over northern China and from the north-east over southern China and India, so Beijing and Mumbai have dry, sunny winters. South of the equator it is summer, and northern Australia gets its own rainy north-west monsoon.

data.name: DayNight_Chart_Note
data.value: Clock time, so the band jumps by an hour where daylight saving starts and ends. The dot is now.

data.name: DayNight_Clocks_Note
data.value: +1 day: already the next day compared with {0}. Click a city to choose it.

data.name: DayNight_DragHint_Globe
data.value: Drag to turn the globe; click a place to choose it

data.name: DayNight_DragHint_Map
data.value: Click a place for its sunrise and sunset; drag sideways to move the Sun

data.name: DayNight_Globe_Fact1
data.value: Sunlight reaches Earth in parallel rays, so at any moment exactly half of Earth is lit. The edge of the lit half is a great circle: the circle of illumination.

data.name: DayNight_Globe_Fact2
data.value: The circle always stands at right angles to the sunlight. Because Earth's axis is tilted, it passes through the poles only at the equinoxes; at the solstices it leans 23.4° from the axis and just touches the polar circles.

data.name: DayNight_Globe_Fact3
data.value: Inside the polar circle tilted towards the Sun, Earth's turn never carries you out of the lit half: the Sun does not set (polar day). Inside the other one it does not rise (polar night).

data.name: DayNight_Globe_Fact4
data.value: On the flat map the same circle looks like a wave, because the map stretches the regions near the poles sideways.

data.name: DayNight_Globe_Fact5
data.value: Seen from above the North Pole, Earth turns anticlockwise, from west to east. That is why the Sun rises in the east, and places further east see it first.

data.name: DayNight_Globe_Note
data.value: Sunlight from the left; not to scale. City lights mark the night side.

data.name: DayNight_Globe_Subtitle
data.value: On the globe, the line between day and night is a circle

data.name: DayNight_Label_NewDay
data.value: Midnight: a new date to the east →

data.name: DayNight_Lesson_Zones_Choice1
data.value: Next to the international date line

data.name: DayNight_Map_Fact1
data.value: The edge of the lit half is the terminator. West of the Sun it is the sunrise line, where the day is beginning; east of it the sunset line, where it is ending.

data.name: DayNight_Map_Fact2
data.value: Earth turns once in 24 hours, 15° an hour, so the lit half sweeps west 15° every hour: at the equator that is about 1,670 km an hour.

data.name: DayNight_Map_Fact3
data.value: Dark does not come at sunset. Civil twilight lasts until the Sun is 6° below the horizon, and the sky is fully dark only once it is 18° below. Near the polar circles, summer nights never get fully dark.

data.name: DayNight_Map_Fact4
data.value: The line's shape follows the seasons: straight from pole to pole at the equinoxes, a wave that touches the polar circles at the solstices, with polar day on one side and polar night on the other.

data.name: DayNight_Map_Fact5
data.value: Sunrise and sunset are counted from the top edge of the Sun, and the air bends its light up by about half a degree, so even at an equinox the day is a few minutes longer than 12 hours.

data.name: DayNight_Map_Note
data.value: Equirectangular map. The shade deepens through civil, nautical and astronomical twilight into night. The Sun's real position at this moment.

data.name: DayNight_Map_Subtitle
data.value: Half of Earth is always in sunlight; the line between day and night sweeps west

data.name: DayNight_MiniMap_Caption
data.value: The same moment on a flat map

data.name: DayNight_MiniMap_Note
data.value: The circle on the globe becomes a wave on the map.

data.name: DayNight_Place_Hint
data.value: Or click anywhere on the map.

data.name: DayNight_ResetView_Hint
data.value: Drag the globe to look at it from another side.

data.name: DayNight_Stage_Astronomical_Description
data.value: The Sun is 12°–18° below the horizon. It looks dark, but a faint glow still hides the faintest stars.

data.name: DayNight_Stage_Dawn_Description
data.value: The Sun is still below the horizon, but the sky is already bright enough to see without lights.

data.name: DayNight_Stage_Day_Description
data.value: The Sun is up: this place is on the lit half of Earth.

data.name: DayNight_Stage_Dusk_Description
data.value: The Sun has set, but the sky still glows; it stays this light until the Sun is 6° below the horizon.

data.name: DayNight_Stage_Nautical_Description
data.value: The Sun is 6°–12° below the horizon: the brightest stars are out, and at sea the horizon can just be made out.

data.name: DayNight_Stage_Night_Description
data.value: The Sun is more than 18° below the horizon: full night on the dark half of Earth.

data.name: DayNight_Stage_PolarDay_Description
data.value: Inside the polar circle in summer: as Earth turns, this place never leaves the lit half, so the Sun circles the sky without setting.

data.name: DayNight_Stage_PolarNight_Description
data.value: Inside the polar circle in winter: this place never reaches the lit half, so the Sun does not rise all day; around noon there may still be twilight.

data.name: DayNight_Stage_Sunrise_Description
data.value: The Sun is low in the east. Earth's turn has just carried this place across the sunrise line into the light.

data.name: DayNight_Stage_Sunset_Description
data.value: The Sun is low in the west. This place is about to cross the sunset line into the night.

data.name: DayNight_Stat_Solar_ToolTip
data.value: What a sundial would show there: 12:00 when the Sun is highest.

data.name: DayNight_Stat_Sunrise_ToolTip
data.value: On today's date there, by the local clock.

data.name: DayNight_TimeZones_Fact1
data.value: Until the 19th century every town kept its own solar time. Railways and the telegraph needed one time: in 1884 the world agreed on Greenwich as 0°, and later on zones 15° (one hour) wide.

data.name: DayNight_TimeZones_Fact2
data.value: Real zones follow borders. China spans about 60° of longitude, five ideal zones, yet all of it keeps Beijing time (UTC+8): in Kashgar the Sun is highest close to 15:00.

data.name: DayNight_TimeZones_Fact3
data.value: Some zones are off by half or a quarter of an hour: India keeps UTC+5:30 and Nepal UTC+5:45.

data.name: DayNight_TimeZones_Fact4
data.value: At any moment two dates are in use, and for two hours each day even three. A new date begins at midnight and spreads west; it ends at the international date line, which runs roughly along 180°.

data.name: DayNight_TimeZones_Fact5
data.value: Kiritimati (UTC+14) and Honolulu (UTC−10) lie almost on the same meridian: their clocks show the same time, a whole day apart.

data.name: DayNight_TimeZones_Fact6
data.value: Daylight saving puts clocks an hour ahead in summer, as in London, New York and Sydney. China does not use it.

data.name: DayNight_TimeZones_Note
data.value: Ideal time zones 15° wide; real zones follow borders. Cities show the time on their real clocks, daylight saving included.

data.name: DayNight_TimeZones_Subtitle
data.value: Clocks follow the Sun: every 15° east, an hour later

data.name: Eclipse_Chart_Caption
data.value: The Moon's latitude: how far above or below the ecliptic (the Sun's path) it is

data.name: Eclipse_DragHint_Moon
data.value: Drag to move the Moon around its orbit

data.name: Eclipse_DragHint_Year
data.value: Drag sideways to move through the year

data.name: Eclipse_Lesson_Seasons_Choice1
data.value: The Moon passes just above or below the Sun

data.name: Eclipse_Lesson_Solar_Choice2
data.value: Only part of the Sun hidden

data.name: Eclipse_LunarPath
data.value: The Moon's path through Earth's shadow

data.name: Eclipse_LunarPath_Note
data.value: Where the Moon passes depends on how close to a node the full moon falls (see “Why not every month?”).

data.name: Eclipse_LunarSky_Caption
data.value: The Moon seen from Earth's night side

data.name: Eclipse_Lunar_Fact1
data.value: A lunar eclipse can only happen at full moon, when Earth is between the Sun and the Moon.

data.name: Eclipse_Lunar_Fact2
data.value: Everyone on Earth's night side sees it at the same time. It lasts hours, and totality alone can last up to about 1 hour 40 minutes.

data.name: Eclipse_Lunar_Fact3
data.value: The red is the light of all of Earth's sunrises and sunsets at once: Earth's atmosphere bends sunlight into the umbra and scatters the blue away.

data.name: Eclipse_Lunar_Fact4
data.value: A lunar eclipse is completely safe to watch with the naked eye.

data.name: Eclipse_Lunar_Subtitle
data.value: Lunar eclipse: at full moon, the Moon passes through Earth's shadow

data.name: Eclipse_ScaleNote
data.value: Sizes and distances are not to scale

data.name: Eclipse_Season_LastFullMoon
data.value: Last full moon: the Moon passed {0}° from the centre of Earth's shadow, {1}.

data.name: Eclipse_Season_LastNewMoon
data.value: Last new moon: the Moon passed {0}° from the Sun's path, {1}.

data.name: Eclipse_Season_YearCount
data.value: Past 12 months: {0} solar, {1} lunar and {2} penumbral lunar eclipses.

data.name: Eclipse_Seasons_Fact1
data.value: The Moon's orbit is tilted about 5.1° to the plane of Earth's orbit (the ecliptic); the picture exaggerates the tilt. The two planes cross along the line of nodes.

data.name: Eclipse_Seasons_Fact2
data.value: Most months the new moon passes a little above or below the Sun, and the full moon above or below Earth's shadow, so nothing happens.

data.name: Eclipse_Seasons_Fact3
data.value: Twice a year the line of nodes points at the Sun. These eclipse seasons last about 34 days, longer than a month (29.5 days), so each brings at least one solar eclipse: there are 2 to 5 a year.

data.name: Eclipse_Seasons_Fact4
data.value: The line of nodes slowly turns, once every 18.6 years, so the eclipse seasons come about 19 days earlier each year. The picture leaves this out.

data.name: Eclipse_Seasons_Subtitle
data.value: Why not every month? Because the Moon's orbit is tilted

data.name: Eclipse_Solar_Fact1
data.value: The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon and about 400 times farther away, so the two look almost the same size in the sky: just enough for the Moon to cover the Sun.

data.name: Eclipse_Solar_Fact2
data.value: A solar eclipse can only happen at new moon. The Moon's umbra is small, so totality is seen only along a narrow path, usually 100–200 km wide; on either side people see a partial eclipse.

data.name: Eclipse_Solar_Fact3
data.value: Totality lasts a few minutes at most, never more than about 7½. At any one place a total eclipse comes round only once every few hundred years on average.

data.name: Eclipse_Solar_Fact4
data.value: Never look at the Sun directly, or through a camera, binoculars or a telescope, without a proper solar filter, not even when most of it is covered. Only during totality is it safe to look.

data.name: Eclipse_Solar_Subtitle
data.value: Solar eclipse: at new moon, the Moon's shadow falls on Earth

data.name: Eclipse_Stage_InSeason_Description
data.value: The line of nodes points (nearly) at the Sun. For about five weeks the new and full moons fall close to the ecliptic, so eclipses happen.

data.name: Eclipse_Stage_LunarNone_Description
data.value: No eclipse right now. A lunar eclipse can only happen at full moon, when the Moon passes behind Earth into its shadow.

data.name: Eclipse_Stage_LunarPartial_Description
data.value: Part of the Moon is in Earth's umbra and looks as if a dark bite had been taken out of it.

data.name: Eclipse_Stage_LunarPenumbral_Description
data.value: The Moon is in Earth's penumbra, where only part of the Sun is hidden. It dims a little, which is easy to miss with the naked eye.

data.name: Eclipse_Stage_LunarTotal_Description
data.value: The whole Moon is in Earth's umbra. It does not go black: sunlight bent through Earth's atmosphere still reaches it, and as the blue is scattered away on the way, the Moon glows copper red.

data.name: Eclipse_Stage_OutOfSeason_Description
data.value: The line of nodes points away from the Sun. At new and full moon the Moon passes above or below the Sun or Earth's shadow, so there is no eclipse.

data.name: Eclipse_Stage_SolarAnnular_Description
data.value: The Moon is near its farthest point and looks a little smaller than the Sun, so its umbra ends before it reaches Earth. You are in the antumbra and see a ring of fire around the Moon.

data.name: Eclipse_Stage_SolarNone_Description
data.value: No eclipse right now. A solar eclipse can only happen at new moon, when the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth, and only where its shadow falls.

data.name: Eclipse_Stage_SolarPartial_Description
data.value: You are in the Moon's penumbra: from here the Moon covers only part of the Sun. Without eclipse glasses you would hardly notice the daylight fading.

data.name: Eclipse_Stage_SolarTotal_Description
data.value: You are in the Moon's umbra: the Sun is completely hidden. The sky turns dark, bright stars and planets appear, and the Sun's pearly corona shines around the black Moon.

data.name: Eclipse_Timeline_Moon
data.value: The Moon's position in its orbit

data.name: Eclipse_Track_Caption
data.value: Earth seen from the Sun: the Moon's shadow sweeps across

data.name: Eclipse_Track_Tooltip
data.value: Drag (or use the arrow keys) to move north or south of the eclipse path

data.name: Expand_Axis_Log
data.value: time, each step ten times longer →

data.name: Expand_Chart_History_Caption
data.value: Three universes, lined up on today

data.name: Expand_Chart_History_Note
data.value: Lined up on today (same size, same expansion rate), the universes differ in age and in future. Click a curve to pick that universe.

data.name: Expand_Chart_Hubble_Note
data.value: Every galaxy lies on one straight line: speed is proportional to distance. Its slope, the expansion rate, was steeper in the past (gold) than today (green, dashed).

data.name: Expand_Chart_Redshift_Caption
data.value: The universe's size during the light's journey

data.name: Expand_Chart_Redshift_Note
data.value: When the light leaves, the universe is the size at the dashed line; today it is 1. The light is stretched by 1 divided by that size. Drag along the curve to choose when it leaves.

data.name: Expand_Era_Contracting_Text
data.value: Gravity has stopped the expansion and pulls everything back together. Galaxies now come closer to each other, and their light is blueshifted.

data.name: Expand_Era_Crunch_Text
data.value: Everything is squeezed together, hotter and hotter: galaxies merge, and then even stars and atoms are torn apart.

data.name: Expand_Era_DarkAges_Text
data.value: Atoms have formed and light travels freely, but there are no stars yet. Gravity slowly gathers the gas into clumps.

data.name: Expand_Era_Dawn_Text
data.value: The first stars light up and the first small galaxies form. Their light is what the Webb telescope hunts for.

data.name: Expand_Era_Ended_Text
data.value: This universe has collapsed: after the crunch there is no time left to look at.

data.name: Expand_Era_FutureFast_Text
data.value: Dark energy keeps speeding up the expansion. Distant galaxies slip out of sight one by one, while our own group of galaxies stays together.

data.name: Expand_Era_FutureSlowing_Text
data.value: Without dark energy, gravity keeps braking the expansion. It goes on for ever, but ever more slowly.

data.name: Expand_Era_Galaxies_Text
data.value: Galaxies grow and merge and make stars. Gravity is slowing the expansion down.

data.name: Expand_Era_Now_Text
data.value: Every universe here is set to today's size and expansion rate. In ours, 13.8 billion years have passed since the Big Bang, and the expansion is speeding up.

data.name: Expand_Era_Plasma_Text
data.value: Nuclei and electrons fly about separately, and light keeps bumping into them, so it cannot travel far. The universe is opaque and glowing.

data.name: Expand_Era_Speeding_Text
data.value: Matter has thinned out, and dark energy now beats gravity: the expansion is getting faster.

data.name: Expand_Era_Start_Text
data.value: Too hot even for atomic nuclei to hold together: a soup of particles and light, expanding fast.

data.name: Expand_Hint_History
data.value: Drag along the horn to travel in time; click a moment to jump there.

data.name: Expand_Hint_Hubble
data.value: Click any galaxy to live there; drag sideways to run time back and forth.

data.name: Expand_Hint_Redshift
data.value: Drag along the strip of space to move the light; pick a galaxy on the left page.

data.name: Expand_History_Fact1
data.value: The universe is about 13.8 billion years old, measured from the microwave background by the Planck satellite.

data.name: Expand_History_Fact2
data.value: The Big Bang was not an explosion at one spot. It happened everywhere at once: every place in today's universe was once squeezed close together and very hot.

data.name: Expand_History_Fact3
data.value: Penzias and Wilson found the microwave background by accident in 1965, while chasing a hiss in their radio antenna. It earned them a Nobel Prize.

data.name: Expand_History_Fact4
data.value: In 1998 two teams measuring distant exploding stars found that the expansion is speeding up: the discovery of dark energy, Nobel Prize 2011.

data.name: Expand_History_Fact5
data.value: Today about 68% of the universe's energy is dark energy, 27% dark matter, and only 5% the ordinary atoms of stars, planets and us.

data.name: Expand_History_Note
data.value: The height of the horn is the size of the universe compared with today, from the real expansion model (ΛCDM, Planck 2018).

data.name: Expand_History_Panel_Note
data.value: All three universes have today's size and expansion rate now; they differ in what they are made of. Ours is 31% matter and 69% dark energy.

data.name: Expand_History_Subtitle
data.value: The size of the universe through time

data.name: Expand_Hubble_Fact1
data.value: In 1929 Edwin Hubble showed that the farther away a galaxy is, the faster it moves away. Georges Lemaître had worked it out two years earlier, so it is now also called the Hubble–Lemaître law.

data.name: Expand_Hubble_Fact2
data.value: Galaxies are not flying through space like pieces of a bomb. Space itself is stretching and carrying them apart; there is no edge and no centre.

data.name: Expand_Hubble_Fact3
data.value: Things held together — atoms, people, planets, the Solar System, the Milky Way — do not expand. Their own forces are far stronger than the gentle stretch.

data.name: Expand_Hubble_Fact4
data.value: Andromeda, our big neighbour, is actually coming towards us at about 110 km/s: close by, gravity beats the expansion.

data.name: Expand_Hubble_Fact5
data.value: Measurements of the expansion rate disagree a little: about 67 km/s per Mpc from the early universe's light, about 73 from nearby stars and supernovae. Nobody knows why yet; it is called the Hubble tension.

data.name: Expand_Hubble_Home_Text
data.value: As space stretches, every galaxy moves away from us, and a galaxy twice as far away moves twice as fast. The galaxies themselves stay the same size.

data.name: Expand_Hubble_Law
data.value: v = H × d H = {0} km/s per Mpc

data.name: Expand_Hubble_NewHome_Text
data.value: From this galaxy too, every other galaxy is moving away, faster the farther it is. Every galaxy sees the same, so none of them is the centre.

data.name: Expand_Hubble_Note
data.value: A patch of the universe about 2 billion light-years across, seen from home in the middle. Each dot stands for a cluster of galaxies.

data.name: Expand_Hubble_Overlay_Text
data.value: The blue circles are where the galaxies were about six billion years ago. Lined up on home, every galaxy has moved straight outwards, the far ones farthest.

data.name: Expand_Hubble_Overlay_Title
data.value: Two photos, one on top of the other

data.name: Expand_Hubble_Panel_Note
data.value: Each dot stands for a cluster of galaxies, drawn far bigger than it is. The distances and speeds follow our universe's real expansion.

data.name: Expand_Hubble_Subtitle
data.value: Why every galaxy is moving away from us

data.name: Expand_Label_Drift
data.value: space grows faster than the light crosses it

data.name: Expand_Lesson_History_Choice1
data.value: One with much more matter and no dark energy

data.name: Expand_Obj_Travel
data.value: How far the light has come

data.name: Expand_Redshift_Deep_Text
data.value: This light left when the universe was less than a billion years old, and it is stretched more than seven times. Only infrared telescopes such as Webb can see these galaxies.

data.name: Expand_Redshift_Fact1
data.value: Redshift z tells you how much the universe has grown since the light left: the light is stretched by 1 + z, and the universe was 1/(1 + z) of today's size.

data.name: Expand_Redshift_Fact2
data.value: Beyond about z = 1.5, a galaxy is moving away from us faster than light today. That breaks no rule: nothing races through space; space itself is growing.

data.name: Expand_Redshift_Fact3
data.value: The most distant galaxies we see sent their light when the universe was less than 300 million years old. It is stretched about fifteen times, from ultraviolet into infrared.

data.name: Expand_Redshift_Fact4
data.value: Vesto Slipher measured the first galaxy redshifts between 1912 and 1917, before anyone knew that galaxies lie far beyond the Milky Way.

data.name: Expand_Redshift_Fact5
data.value: The oldest light of all, the microwave background, is stretched about 1,100 times: it left as the glow of gas at about 3,000 K and arrives as microwaves at 2.7 K.

data.name: Expand_Redshift_Infrared_Text
data.value: The waves are now too long for our eyes. Telescopes that see infrared are needed to catch this light.

data.name: Expand_Redshift_Nearby_Text
data.value: Light from nearby galaxies is stretched only a tiny bit, because space grew very little while it travelled. Close by, a galaxy's own motion can matter more.

data.name: Expand_Redshift_Note
data.value: Distances are drawn to one scale, so you can see space stretch; the galaxies and the waves are drawn far bigger than they are.

data.name: Expand_Redshift_Panel_Note
data.value: Redshifts are from published spectra, rounded. The light shown is hydrogen's Hβ line; the slider picks any redshift by hand.

data.name: Expand_Redshift_Subtitle
data.value: Light stretched on its way across space

data.name: Expand_Redshift_Visible_Text
data.value: The light is stretched enough to change colour: blue-green light arrives yellow, orange or red.

data.name: Expand_Value_Falling
data.value: falling back at {0} km/s per Mpc

data.name: Expand_Value_HomeElsewhere
data.value: another galaxy, {0} from the Milky Way

data.name: Explore_ClickHint
data.value: Click anything in the picture to hear what it is

data.name: Green_Chart_Co2_Note
data.value: Ice cores (Law Dome, rounded) before 1959, Mauna Loa yearly means after (NOAA). The gold line is the amount on the slider.

data.name: Green_Chart_Day_Note
data.value: The model runs three days and shows the last, so the day ends as it began. The pale hill is the sunlight. Hours are local solar time (the Sun highest at 12:00).

data.name: Green_Chart_Glow_Note
data.value: Each curve scaled to its own peak, on a log axis. The Sun (about 5500 °C) shines mostly at 0.3–3 µm, the ground (15 °C) at 4–50 µm; grey is what the air catches.

data.name: Green_Chart_Share_Note
data.value: Shares of the whole effect (Schmidt et al. 2010). Water vapour and clouds come and go with the temperature; CO₂ and the other long-lived gases set it.

data.name: Green_Chart_Worlds_Caption
data.value: Neighbours, without and with their air

data.name: Green_Chart_Worlds_Note
data.value: Circle: the temperature with no greenhouse gases (from the sunlight and how much is reflected); dot: the real average (NASA). Venus' thick CO₂ air makes it hotter than Mercury; Mars' thin air adds only a few degrees.

data.name: Green_Gas_Ar_Description
data.value: A noble gas of single atoms, with no bonds to stretch or bend: it cannot catch infrared at all.

data.name: Green_Gas_CH4_Description
data.value: Four hydrogens round a carbon at the corners of a tetrahedron, symmetric at rest. Its lopsided stretch and bend shift the charge (3.3 and 7.7 µm); its even ones do not.

data.name: Green_Gas_CH4_Lifetime
data.value: about 12 years, then it becomes CO₂ and water

data.name: Green_Gas_CH4_Shape
data.value: a carbon and four hydrogens, a tetrahedron

data.name: Green_Gas_CO2_Description
data.value: Straight and symmetric, O=C=O, so it has no dipole at rest. But its bend and its lopsided stretch push the charge off-centre and back, at 15 µm and 4.3 µm: those wiggles catch infrared. Its even stretch does not.

data.name: Green_Gas_CO2_Lifetime
data.value: centuries to millennia (a share far longer)

data.name: Green_Gas_CO2_Shape
data.value: three atoms in a line, O=C=O

data.name: Green_Gas_H2O_Description
data.value: Bent at 104.5°, with the oxygen pulling the electrons, it is always a small dipole. Every wiggle, and even spinning, shakes that dipole, so water catches infrared over a wide range: the main greenhouse gas.

data.name: Green_Gas_H2O_Lifetime
data.value: about 9 days, then it rains out

data.name: Green_Gas_N2_Description
data.value: Two nitrogen atoms with a triple bond. When they stretch, both ends move alike about the middle: the charge stays even and the light has nothing to push on.

data.name: Green_Gas_O2_Description
data.value: Two oxygen atoms with a double bond. As with nitrogen, stretching keeps it symmetric, so it lets the ground's infrared through.

data.name: Green_GlassHouse_Fact1
data.value: A greenhouse warms mostly because the glass stops the warm air from rising away; holding in the infrared adds a few degrees more. Opening the vents cools it far more than a roof that lets infrared out (rock salt, as R. W. Wood tried in 1909).

data.name: Green_GlassHouse_Fact2
data.value: So the atmosphere's "greenhouse effect" is named after the smaller half of how a greenhouse works: the air has no lid, it catches the infrared itself.

data.name: Green_GlassHouse_Fact3
data.value: Glass lets through about 85–90% of visible light but almost no infrared beyond about 5 µm: it soaks it up, warms, and glows half of it back in.

data.name: Green_GlassHouse_Fact4
data.value: A car in the sun warms by about 20 °C within an hour, most of it in the first half hour, even on a mild day; opening a window a crack hardly helps. Never leave a child or a pet in a parked car.

data.name: Green_GlassHouse_Fact5
data.value: At night a shut glass greenhouse stays a little warmer than outside because the glass keeps the floor's infrared in. Under a clear sky a roof that lets infrared out can make it colder than the air outside: that is how frost forms on clear nights.

data.name: Green_GlassHouse_Note
data.value: Temperatures from a simple heat-balance model of a small glass greenhouse and a parked car on a clear day; real ones vary with size, wind and shade.

data.name: Green_GlassHouse_Subtitle
data.value: A greenhouse and a car in the sun

data.name: Green_Glass_AfternoonVents_Description
data.value: Warm air leaves through the vents and cooler air sinks in, so the greenhouse stays only a few degrees above the outside air. The shut car is still far hotter.

data.name: Green_Glass_Afternoon_Description
data.value: The greenhouse and the car are far warmer than the air outside: the sunlight keeps coming in, but the warm air cannot get out. Open the vents to let it go.

data.name: Green_Glass_Evening_Description
data.value: With the Sun low, less light gets in. The greenhouse is still warmer than outside but cooling; the car cools fastest.

data.name: Green_Glass_LocationNote
data.value: The Sun's path is for {0} ({1}° {2}); the outside air is a typical clear day of the season, {3}–{4} °C.

data.name: Green_Glass_Morning_Description
data.value: Sunlight passes the glass and warms the floor and the plants; they warm the air, which rises and gathers under the roof. Temperatures climb fast.

data.name: Green_Glass_Night_Description
data.value: No sunlight. The floor gives back the heat it stored by day and glows in the infrared; the glass sends half of it back in, so the shut greenhouse cools more slowly than the air outside.

data.name: Green_Glass_Pane
data.value: glass: lets sunlight in, stops infrared

data.name: Green_Glass_SaltPane
data.value: rock salt: lets sunlight and infrared through

data.name: Green_Glass_WindowOpen
data.value: window open a crack (click to shut)

data.name: Green_Glass_WindowShut
data.value: windows shut (click to open a crack)

data.name: Green_Hint_GlassHouse
data.value: Drag sideways to turn the day; click the roof vents or the car's window to open them.

data.name: Green_Hint_Molecules
data.value: Pick a gas and one of its wiggles; every ray crossing it is labelled with its wavelength.

data.name: Green_Hint_Planet
data.value: Move the CO₂ slider or take the greenhouse gases away and watch the ground settle; turn on the energy flows for the numbers.

data.name: Green_Lesson_Glass_Choice1
data.value: The glass stops the warm air rising away

data.name: Green_Lesson_Molecules_Choice1
data.value: The molecule catches it and wiggles harder

data.name: Green_Lesson_Planet_Choice1
data.value: It's sent out again in any direction, as often down as up

data.name: Green_Lesson_Planet_Choice2
data.value: It goes straight up into space

data.name: Green_Lesson_Planet_Choice3
data.value: It stays in the molecule for good

data.name: Green_Mol_Dipole
data.value: gold arrow: the dipole, where the charge leans

data.name: Green_Mol_Holding
data.value: caught a {0} µm ray: wiggling harder, about to send it out again

data.name: Green_Mol_NoModes
data.value: a single atom: nothing to wiggle

data.name: Green_Molecules_Fact1
data.value: Nitrogen and oxygen, 99% of the air, are pairs of identical atoms: stretching them keeps the charge perfectly even, so infrared passes straight through. Argon is a single atom with nothing to wiggle at all.

data.name: Green_Molecules_Fact2
data.value: CO₂'s bend, at 15 µm, sits close to the peak of the ground's glow (about 10 µm). That is why so little CO₂, 0.04% of the air, matters so much.

data.name: Green_Molecules_Fact3
data.value: A caught ray does not stay caught: within a split second the molecule bumps into its neighbours (warming the air) or sends a ray out again in a random direction, as likely back down as on up.

data.name: Green_Molecules_Fact4
data.value: Water vapour is the strongest greenhouse gas, but how much the air holds is set by its temperature: it rains out within about 9 days. CO₂ sets the temperature; water vapour follows and roughly doubles the effect.

data.name: Green_Molecules_Fact5
data.value: Kilogram for kilogram, methane warms about 30 times as much as CO₂ over 100 years (IPCC AR6: 27–30), but it is broken down in about 12 years; CO₂ stays for centuries.

data.name: Green_Molecules_Note
data.value: A molecule catches infrared when one of its wiggles shifts its charge back and forth at the light's frequency. Wiggles about 10¹³ times slower and the atoms' movements enlarged; the bands are simplified.

data.name: Green_Molecules_Subtitle
data.value: Why only some gases catch the ground's heat

data.name: Green_Planet_Air_NoGases
data.value: air of nitrogen and oxygen only

data.name: Green_Planet_Bare_Description
data.value: Every ray of heat from the ground goes straight to space. To send out as much as the sunlight it keeps, the ground needs only about −18 °C: the seas freeze.

data.name: Green_Planet_Bare_Title
data.value: No greenhouse gases: a frozen world

data.name: Green_Planet_Emission
data.value: heat leaves for space from about {0} km up, where the air is {1} °C

data.name: Green_Planet_Fact1
data.value: Without greenhouse gases Earth would average about −18 °C, the temperature at which it sends out as much heat as the sunlight it keeps. The real average is about 15 °C: the greenhouse effect adds some 33 °C and makes Earth liveable.

data.name: Green_Planet_Fact2
data.value: The air lets most sunlight through but catches most of the ground's infrared: only about a tenth goes straight out to space, through the "window" between 8 and 13 µm.

data.name: Green_Planet_Fact3
data.value: The ground gets 333 W/m² back from the air, twice the sunlight it takes in (161 W/m²). That is why it is so much warmer than sunlight alone could make it.

data.name: Green_Planet_Fact4
data.value: More CO₂ hardly catches "more" rays: the middle of its band is black already. It raises the height the heat finally leaves from, where the air is colder and glows less, so the whole column must warm until the balance is back.

data.name: Green_Planet_Fact5
data.value: Doubling CO₂ pushes about 3.7 W/m² more; with the feedbacks (more water vapour, less ice) the world settles about 3 °C warmer (IPCC: likely 2.5–4 °C). The temperatures here are such settled values; the oceans take decades to catch up.

data.name: Green_Planet_IceAge_Description
data.value: About 180 ppm, as at the depth of the last ice age 20,000 years ago. CO₂ alone makes it about 2 °C colder; the ice sheets reflecting sunlight did most of the rest (the real ice age was about 5–6 °C colder).

data.name: Green_Planet_More_Description
data.value: Each doubling adds about the same warming, about 3 °C once settled: 560 ppm is about 3 °C over before industry, 1120 ppm about 6 °C.

data.name: Green_Planet_Note
data.value: Not to scale: a strip of ground with 12 km of air over it. Each dash of sunlight or wiggle of infrared stands for a share of Earth's average energy flows (Trenberth et al. 2009).

data.name: Green_Planet_Preindustrial_Description
data.value: About 280 ppm, as for thousands of years before 1750. Water vapour and CO₂ hold the ground at about 14 °C.

data.name: Green_Planet_Subtitle
data.value: Sunlight gets in, the ground's heat is held back

data.name: Green_Planet_Today_Description
data.value: About 425 ppm in 2024, half as much again as before industry, mostly from burning coal, oil and gas. Once everything has caught up that is worth about 1.8 °C; the world had warmed about 1.1 °C by 2011–2020.

data.name: Green_Spectrum_Axis
data.value: wavelength, µm (false colours: infrared is invisible)

data.name: Green_Spectrum_Caught
data.value: shaded: what {0} alone catches, {1}% of it

data.name: Green_Vib_Note
data.value: Each wiggle has its own frequency; light of that frequency can drive it only if it shifts the charge.

data.name: Hole_Chart_Lensing_Caption
data.value: How much brighter the source looks

data.name: Hole_Chart_Lensing_Note
data.value: As the hole drifts along its track, the light from the source's middle is focused and it brightens, then fades again. Click or drag the chart to move the hole.

data.name: Hole_Chart_Orbits_Caption
data.value: The probe's energy and the hill it must climb

data.name: Hole_Chart_Orbits_Note
data.value: The curves are the effective potential for the probe's spin round the hole. The blue line is its energy: where the line is above the curve, it can go. Einstein's curve has a top near the hole that Newton's lacks; above it, the probe falls in.

data.name: Hole_Chart_Shadow_Note
data.value: The closer light passes, the more it is turned. Below 5.2 M it is caught: that is the edge of the shadow. The dashed line is Einstein's rule for light passing far away, 4M/b.

data.name: Hole_Hint_Lensing
data.value: Drag the black hole across the sky, or click anywhere to put it there.

data.name: Hole_Hint_Orbits
data.value: Drag the probe to move its start, or drag its green arrow to launch it your own way.

data.name: Hole_Hint_Shadow
data.value: Drag up or down on the picture to tilt the view.

data.name: Hole_Label_Hat
data.value: Far side of the disk, bent over the top

data.name: Hole_Lens_Far_Text
data.value: Far from the line to the source, the hole bends its light only a little: the picture is nudged outwards round the hole, like looking through the foot of a wine glass.

data.name: Hole_Lens_Inside_Text
data.value: The source is now within one Einstein radius of the line: both images sit close to the ring and the light is strongly focused.

data.name: Hole_Lens_Near_Text
data.value: The source is stretched round the hole into an arc, and a second, smaller image appears on the other side. Together they are brighter than the source alone.

data.name: Hole_Lens_Off_Text
data.value: This is the sky as it really is. Switch the bending back on to see what the black hole does to it.

data.name: Hole_Lens_Ring_Text
data.value: Lined up exactly, the light comes round every side alike, and the source becomes a complete ring round the hole.

data.name: Hole_Lensing_Fact1
data.value: In 1919, during a total eclipse, Arthur Eddington measured stars near the Sun shifted by 1.75 arcseconds, as Einstein predicted, twice what Newton's ideas gave. It made Einstein famous overnight.

data.name: Hole_Lensing_Fact2
data.value: The first lensed quasar, found in 1979, appeared as two identical 'twins' side by side: one quasar seen twice through a galaxy in front of it.

data.name: Hole_Lensing_Fact3
data.value: Galaxy clusters bend the light of galaxies far behind them into long arcs. How much they bend shows how much mass they hold: far more than their stars, most of it dark matter.

data.name: Hole_Lensing_Fact4
data.value: In 2022 astronomers announced the first lone black hole found by lensing: about 7 Suns, 5000 light years away, seen when it made a background star brighten for months.

data.name: Hole_Lensing_Fact5
data.value: A supernova seen through a lensing cluster in 2014 appeared four times at once. Astronomers predicted it would appear once more, by a longer path, and it did, in 2015.

data.name: Hole_Lensing_Note
data.value: Not to scale: the black hole itself is far too small to see, and the bending is hugely enlarged.

data.name: Hole_Lensing_Panel_Note
data.value: The real ring's size depends on the lens: about a thousandth of an arcsecond for a star-sized hole, arcseconds for a galaxy.

data.name: Hole_Lensing_Subtitle
data.value: A black hole far away bends the light behind it

data.name: Hole_Lesson_Orbits_Choice3
data.value: They run at the same pace

data.name: Hole_Lesson_Shadow_Choice1
data.value: The gas there is moving towards us

data.name: Hole_Lesson_Shadow_Choice3
data.value: That side is closer to us

data.name: Hole_Obj_Hat
data.value: The far side, bent over the top

data.name: Hole_Obj_Inner
data.value: The inner edge of the disk

data.name: Hole_Orbit_Circle_Text
data.value: At 10 M the probe circles steadily, as a planet circles a star. Newton's probe, started the same way, swings out on an ellipse: this close in, gravity pulls harder than Newton's law says. Far out, the two agree.

data.name: Hole_Orbit_Custom_Text
data.value: Watch the chart: if the blue energy line is below the hill near the hole, the probe is held in orbit; above it, the probe falls in, unless it is fast enough to escape.

data.name: Hole_Orbit_Escape_Text
data.value: With more energy than it needs, the probe flies off and never comes back, bent a little as it leaves.

data.name: Hole_Orbit_Escaped_Text
data.value: The probe is heading out for good. Far from the hole, gravity is weak and its clock runs almost at the far clock's pace again.

data.name: Hole_Orbit_Isco_Text
data.value: At 6 M, three times the horizon's radius, is the last circle a probe can keep to. A tiny nudge inwards and it spirals in. Newton's probe, given the same start, never would.

data.name: Hole_Orbit_Lost_Text
data.value: The probe has crossed the event horizon and can never send anything out again. Its own clock kept ticking, but seen from far away it would seem to slow, redden and freeze at the edge.

data.name: Hole_Orbit_Plunge_Text
data.value: Newton's probe swings close and comes back out. The real one has too little spin to get over the top of the potential near the hole, so it plunges in.

data.name: Hole_Orbit_Rosette_Text
data.value: Newton's probe goes round the same ellipse every time. The real one swings round further at each close pass, so its ellipse turns and traces a rosette.

data.name: Hole_Orbits_Fact1
data.value: Far from a black hole, it pulls just like a star of the same mass. If the Sun became a black hole, the Earth would keep going round it exactly as before (in the dark).

data.name: Hole_Orbits_Fact2
data.value: Mercury's orbit turns a little more each century than Newton predicts, 43 arcseconds. Einstein's theory explained this in 1915: the same turning as the rosette here, only much smaller.

data.name: Hole_Orbits_Fact3
data.value: Closer in than three times the horizon's radius, there is no steady circular orbit. Gas reaching that line spirals in, so disks round black holes have a sharp inner edge.

data.name: Hole_Orbits_Fact4
data.value: Gravity slows time even on Earth. GPS satellites higher up gain about 45 microseconds a day from weaker gravity (and lose 7 from their speed); without correcting for it, GPS would drift by kilometres a day.

data.name: Hole_Orbits_Fact5
data.value: Falling into a small black hole, the pull on your feet would be so much stronger than on your head that you would be stretched like spaghetti. At a giant one you would cross the horizon without feeling anything.

data.name: Hole_Orbits_Note
data.value: Seen from above, in units of the hole's mass M (for 10 Suns, 1 M is 15 km). Gold follows Einstein's gravity, grey follows Newton's.

data.name: Hole_Orbits_Panel_Note
data.value: Both probes start the same way. Speeds are fractions of the speed of light.

data.name: Hole_Orbits_Subtitle
data.value: How a black hole bends light and steers orbits

data.name: Hole_Shadow_Above_Text
data.value: Looking down on the disk, it is a glowing ring with the shadow in the middle. Its inner edge is the innermost stable orbit; closer than that, gas falls straight in.

data.name: Hole_Shadow_Edge_Text
data.value: The disk crosses in front of the hole as a thin band, yet you also see its far side, bent up over the top, and its underside, bent round below. The side coming towards you is brighter.

data.name: Hole_Shadow_Fact1
data.value: A black hole is mass packed so tightly that not even light can climb out. Its boundary, the event horizon, is not a surface: just the point of no return.

data.name: Hole_Shadow_Fact2
data.value: Squeeze the Earth into a ball about 18 mm across, smaller than a marble, and it becomes a black hole. The Sun would need to be just 6 km across.

data.name: Hole_Shadow_Fact3
data.value: The Event Horizon Telescope linked radio dishes across the Earth into one Earth-sized telescope. It showed the shadow of M87* in 2019 and of Sagittarius A* in 2022.

data.name: Hole_Shadow_Fact4
data.value: The shadow is about 2.6 times as wide as the horizon. Light bent round the hole makes it look much bigger than it is.

data.name: Hole_Shadow_Fact5
data.value: The black hole in the film Interstellar was worked out the same way, by tracing light rays. The film left out the Doppler effect, so both sides of its disk look equally bright.

data.name: Hole_Shadow_Flat_Text
data.value: Now both sides glow alike, as in the film Interstellar. Only gravity's own redshift is left: light climbing out from near the hole loses energy and looks redder and dimmer.

data.name: Hole_Shadow_NoDisk_Text
data.value: Without gas, a black hole is a black patch on the sky. Round its edge the stars behind it are bent and stretched into a warped mirror of the whole sky.

data.name: Hole_Shadow_NoDisk_Title
data.value: Just the hole and the stars

data.name: Hole_Shadow_Note
data.value: Ray traced: each pixel's light is followed back along its real, bent path. The disk's colours are shifted into visible light.

data.name: Hole_Shadow_Panel_Note
data.value: The picture is the same for any black hole that does not spin; only its size changes. Pick one to see its real size.

data.name: Hole_Shadow_Straight_Text
data.value: Without bending, you would see a flat disk and a small black ball, the horizon at its real size. The arch, the rings and the big shadow are all made by gravity bending light.

data.name: Hole_Shadow_Subtitle
data.value: What a black hole looks like up close

data.name: Hole_Shadow_Tilted_Text
data.value: The disk looks like a tilted ring, but the far side is lifted up and bent towards you, so the hole is framed by light all the way round.

data.name: Hole_Side_Title
data.value: Seen from the side (not to scale)

data.name: Hole_Value_RingBright
data.value: spread into a ring, hugely brighter

data.name: HowTo_Contents
data.value: Lost your place? The Contents button takes you back to the table of contents.

data.name: HowTo_Explore
data.value: Each chapter is one spread: read on the left, explore on the right. Click anything in a picture to find out what it is.

data.name: HowTo_Listen
data.value: Every lesson can be read aloud. Switch between English and Chinese at the top at any time.

data.name: HowTo_Turn
data.value: Turn a page: drag the outer edge of a page, click it, or press the left and right arrow keys.

data.name: Kepler_Areas_Fact1
data.value: Kepler actually found this law first, in 1609, before he knew the orbit was an ellipse.

data.name: Kepler_Areas_Fact2
data.value: Equal areas means the planet's angular momentum stays the same: at half the distance it goes twice as fast sideways. A spinning skater who pulls in their arms speeds up for the same reason.

data.name: Kepler_Areas_Fact3
data.value: Earth is fastest in early January (30.3 km/s) and slowest in early July (29.3 km/s).

data.name: Kepler_Areas_Fact4
data.value: So the northern summer half of the year, from the March to the September equinox, is about 7 days longer than the winter half.

data.name: Kepler_Areas_Fact5
data.value: Halley's comet races past the Sun at about 55 km/s, and crawls at under 1 km/s far out, where it spends most of its 75 years.

data.name: Kepler_Areas_Note
data.value: Each coloured slice takes the same time. Near the Sun they are short and wide, far out long and thin, but all have the same area. Not to scale.

data.name: Kepler_Areas_Subtitle
data.value: Second law: the line from the Sun to the planet sweeps equal areas in equal times

data.name: Kepler_DragHint_Orbit
data.value: Drag to move the planet along its orbit

data.name: Kepler_DragHint_You
data.value: Drag to move your planet nearer to or farther from the Sun

data.name: Kepler_Earth_Note
data.value: From Earth's orbit, to within a day or two. Earth is closest to the Sun in the northern winter: the seasons come from the tilt of its axis, not from the distance.

data.name: Kepler_Ecc_Note
data.value: c is how far the Sun is from the centre, a half the long axis. The planets are all near 0: their orbits are almost circles, just with the Sun a little off centre. Moving the slider shapes the example orbit.

data.name: Kepler_Ellipse_Fact1
data.value: Kepler found the ellipse in 1609 from Tycho Brahe's measurements of Mars: a circle missed them by 8 arcminutes, a quarter of the Moon's width, and he would not ignore it.

data.name: Kepler_Ellipse_Fact2
data.value: Earth's orbit is nearly a circle (e = 0.017): its distance from the Sun only goes from 147.1 to 152.1 million km.

data.name: Kepler_Ellipse_Fact3
data.value: The Sun sits at one focus; the other is just an empty point in space. The centre of the ellipse is empty too.

data.name: Kepler_Ellipse_Fact4
data.value: Newton showed in 1687 why: a pull that weakens with the square of the distance gives ellipses, or for anything fast enough to escape, open curves that never come back.

data.name: Kepler_Ellipse_Fact5
data.value: Halley's comet (e = 0.967) goes from inside Venus's orbit to beyond Neptune's. It was last near the Sun in 1986 and comes back in 2061.

data.name: Kepler_Ellipse_Note
data.value: Like drawing with two pins and a loop of string: the two parts of the string always add up to the same length. Not to scale: the Sun and the planet are drawn far too big.

data.name: Kepler_Ellipse_Subtitle
data.value: First law: a planet goes round the Sun on an ellipse, with the Sun at one focus

data.name: Kepler_Label_EqualAreas
data.value: {0} slices of {1} each: all the same area

data.name: Kepler_OpenSolarSystem
data.value: See the planets in the Solar System

data.name: Kepler_PeriodChart_Caption
data.value: Year against distance, on log scales

data.name: Kepler_PeriodChart_Note
data.value: On logarithmic scales T² = a³ is a straight line, rising 3 for every 2 across. Every planet, the dwarf planets and Halley's comet sit on it: one rule for everything going round the Sun.

data.name: Kepler_Periods_Fact1
data.value: Kepler published the third law in 1619, ten years after the first two, in his book Harmonices Mundi (The Harmony of the World).

data.name: Kepler_Periods_Fact2
data.value: Twice as far means 2.8 times as long a year: the path is twice as long and the planet goes 1.4 times slower.

data.name: Kepler_Periods_Fact3
data.value: Neptune takes 165 years: discovered in 1846, it finished its first round since then only in 2011.

data.name: Kepler_Periods_Fact4
data.value: Newton's version includes the mass in the middle, so a moon's orbit weighs its planet: that is how we know Jupiter's mass.

data.name: Kepler_Periods_Fact5
data.value: It works for satellites too: 42,164 km from Earth's centre one round takes 23 h 56 min, just as long as Earth takes to turn, so a geostationary satellite stays over one spot.

data.name: Kepler_Periods_Note
data.value: Distances to scale: the planets at their real places today, seen from above the Sun's north pole. The view zooms out to keep your planet in sight; the planets are drawn far too big.

data.name: Kepler_Periods_Subtitle
data.value: Third law: the square of a planet's year goes with the cube of its distance

data.name: Kepler_Speed_Caption
data.value: Speed and distance through one round

data.name: Kepler_Speed_Note
data.value: Where the distance is smallest the speed is greatest, and the other way round: distance times sideways speed stays the same all the way.

data.name: Kepler_Stage_Aphelion_Description
data.value: Farthest from the Sun and slowest. It does not stop: still moving sideways, it begins to fall back towards the Sun.

data.name: Kepler_Stage_Approaching_Description
data.value: Falling back towards the Sun, the pull now speeds it up, all the way to perihelion.

data.name: Kepler_Stage_Circle
data.value: A circle: the same speed all the way

data.name: Kepler_Stage_Circle_Description
data.value: On a circle the distance never changes, so neither does the speed: equal areas then simply means equal arcs.

data.name: Kepler_Stage_Perihelion_Description
data.value: The Sun's pull is strongest here and the planet is moving fastest. It swings round the Sun and starts to climb away again.

data.name: Kepler_Stage_Receding_Description
data.value: The Sun pulls back on it as it climbs outward, so it slows down, like a ball thrown upward.

data.name: Kepler_Stat_Swept_Value
data.value: {0:0}% of the area in {0:0}% of the time

data.name: Kepler_Table_Caption
data.value: Measured: T² ÷ a³ is 1 for all of them

data.name: Kepler_Timeline_Orbit
data.value: Time since perihelion: one round of the orbit

data.name: Kepler_You_Earth
data.value: At Earth's distance its year is Earth's year: the two go round side by side.

data.name: Kepler_You_Inner
data.value: Closer than Earth: the Sun pulls harder, so it goes faster round a shorter path. Its year is shorter than ours and it laps Earth.

data.name: Kepler_You_Outer
data.value: Farther than Earth: a longer path at a slower speed, so its year is longer than ours and it falls behind Earth.

data.name: Kepler_YourAxis_Caption
data.value: Your planet's distance from the Sun

data.name: Kepler_YourAxis_Like
data.value: Put it where a real one is:

data.name: Lesson_Done_Text
data.value: That's the end of this walkthrough. Keep dragging and clicking things in the picture to explore, or switch to another view and listen again.

data.name: Lesson_Start_Tooltip
data.value: A spoken walkthrough of this view, with subtitles

data.name: Lightning_Chart_Charge_Note
data.value: Rubbing builds it up toward a limit (beyond it the air at the surface breaks down); a spark takes a bite out of it; damp air drains it away.

data.name: Lightning_Chart_Current_Note
data.value: It peaks within about a microsecond and halves in about 200 µs; later strokes are smaller and quicker (IEC 62305 shapes). Half of all first strokes stay under 30 kA.

data.name: Lightning_Chart_Field_Caption
data.value: The field at the ground, last minute

data.name: Lightning_Chart_Field_Note
data.value: Fair weather gives about 0.13 kV/m pointing down. Under a storm it turns over and climbs; each flash knocks it back: the saw-tooth meteorologists' field mills record.

data.name: Lightning_Chart_Rate_Note
data.value: Flashes a minute grow as the fifth power of the storm's height (Price and Rind 1992): a storm twice as tall flashes about 30 times as often.

data.name: Lightning_Chart_Reach_Caption
data.value: Striking distance and the rolling sphere

data.name: Lightning_Chart_Reach_Note
data.value: Weaker strokes come closer before anything reaches up, so they can slip past a rod: protection standards roll spheres of 20 to 60 m (classes I to IV) over a building to find where it needs rods.

data.name: Lightning_Chart_Series_Note
data.value: Rub two materials together and the higher one gives electrons to the lower one: it ends up positive, the lower one negative. The further apart, the more charge. The order is the usual one; the bar lengths are only illustrative.

data.name: Lightning_CloudTop_Note
data.value: Taller storms have stronger updrafts and more ice and graupel colliding in the cold part of the cloud, so they charge much faster.

data.name: Lightning_Cloud_Charging_Description
data.value: The updraft carries small ice crystals up past falling graupel. Each knock moves a little charge: the light crystals take positive charge up to the top, the heavy graupel keeps negative charge in the middle. The field at the ground grows.

data.name: Lightning_Cloud_CloudToGround_Description
data.value: A flash carried the middle's negative charge down into the ground. The field drops at once, then the cloud charges up again: the meter draws a saw-tooth.

data.name: Lightning_Cloud_Danger_Description
data.value: The ground under the storm is strongly positive and the field is over 5 kV/m: points such as treetops and hair start to leak charge (corona). A flash could come down at any moment.

data.name: Lightning_Cloud_Fact1
data.value: Lightning is one enormous static spark: the ice in the cloud pulls tens of coulombs of charge apart, building up some hundred million volts.

data.name: Lightning_Cloud_Fact2
data.value: About −15 °C is where the charging turns over: colder, graupel hit by ice crystals goes negative; warmer, it goes positive (Takahashi's 1978 experiments).

data.name: Lightning_Cloud_Fact3
data.value: Satellites count about 44 flashes a second over the whole Earth, most of them over land, where the afternoon sun drives strong updrafts.

data.name: Lightning_Cloud_Fact4
data.value: Most flashes never reach the ground: about six stay in the cloud for each one to the ground in the tropics, about three in middle latitudes (Prentice and Mackerras 1977).

data.name: Lightning_Cloud_Fact5
data.value: Hair standing on end, a tingling skin or a buzzing from metal means the field at the ground is already strong: a strike may be seconds away. Get off high ground at once.

data.name: Lightning_Cloud_Intracloud_Description
data.value: The air broke down inside the cloud, between the negative middle and the positive top. Most flashes are like this: from the ground you only see the cloud light up.

data.name: Lightning_Cloud_Note
data.value: A storm in slice, 36 km across and 16.5 km high, to scale. The tripole of charges is a sketch; flash rate from Price and Rind (1992); the clock runs in real time, the grains move faster than real.

data.name: Lightning_Current
data.value: Peak current of the first stroke

data.name: Lightning_Hint_Cloud
