data.value: Click the ground to move the field meter (and the person); grow the storm taller and watch how much more often it flashes.

data.name: Lightning_Hint_Static
data.value: Drag the rod (or balloon) yourself: rub it on the cloth, then take it to the paper, the water and the metal ball. Try other materials, or damper air.

data.name: Lightning_Hint_Strike
data.value: Drag the picture sideways to go back and forth in time; take the rod away or change the current and see what gets hit.

data.name: Lightning_Lesson_Cloud_Choice1
data.value: It turns positive, pulled up by the cloud's negative middle

data.name: Lightning_Lesson_Cloud_Choice2
data.value: It turns negative, like the bottom of the cloud

data.name: Lightning_Lesson_Cloud_Choice3
data.value: Nothing: the ground can't hold charge

data.name: Lightning_Lesson_Static_Choice1
data.value: The balloon holds on to electrons more strongly

data.name: Lightning_Lesson_Static_Choice3
data.value: The hair is warmer than the balloon

data.name: Lightning_Lesson_Strike_Choice1
data.value: When the leader comes within about a hundred metres

data.name: Lightning_Lesson_Strike_Choice2
data.value: Only when the leader touches it

data.name: Lightning_Lesson_Strike_Choice3
data.value: As soon as the leader leaves the cloud

data.name: Lightning_Stat_Hit_House
data.value: {0}: the current goes through roof and walls

data.name: Lightning_Stat_Hit_Person
data.value: {0}: in the open you may be the highest point!

data.name: Lightning_Stat_Share
data.value: In the cloud : to the ground

data.name: Lightning_Stat_Thunder_Value
data.value: {0} s after the flash, from {1} km

data.name: Lightning_Static_Bending_Description
data.value: The stream bends toward the rod whichever charge it has: the side of the water nearest the rod takes the opposite charge, and opposites attract.

data.name: Lightning_Static_Charged_Description
data.value: The rod is an insulator, so its charge stays on the part that was rubbed. It only leaks away slowly, through the thin film of water damp air leaves on its surface.

data.name: Lightning_Static_Fact1
data.value: Rubbing does not make charge, it moves it: electrons pass from one material to the other, so one ends up exactly as negative as the other is positive.

data.name: Lightning_Static_Fact2
data.value: Shuffling across a carpet can charge you to about 35 000 V in dry winter air (10–20% humidity), but only about 1500 V when the air is damp (65–90%).

data.name: Lightning_Static_Fact3
data.value: The volts are high but the charge is tiny: a balloon's spark carries only a few millijoules, which is why it stings but does no harm.

data.name: Lightning_Static_Fact4
data.value: You only feel a discharge above about 3000 V, yet the chips in a phone can be damaged by a few hundred volts or less, so electronics factories ground their workers with wrist straps.

data.name: Lightning_Static_Fact5
data.value: Petrol vapour can be lit by a spark of about 0.2 millijoules, less than a static shock: that is why pumps have a metal plate to touch first, to discharge yourself.

data.name: Lightning_Static_Lifting_Description
data.value: The paper has no charge, but the rod pulls its charges a little apart (polarises it): the near side takes the opposite charge and is pulled up. Once it touches, it shares the rod's charge and is pushed off again.

data.name: Lightning_Static_Neutral_Description
data.value: The rod holds as many positive charges as negative ones, so it is neutral. Rub it to and fro on the cloth.

data.name: Lightning_Static_Note
data.value: A bench a metre wide, from the front. Charges from the triboelectric series and the air's breakdown limit; spark gaps from Paschen's law; the number of + and − signs only shows how much.

data.name: Lightning_Static_Rubbing_Description
data.value: Where two materials touch and part, the one that holds electrons more tightly pulls some away from the other. Rubbing just makes more of them touch.

data.name: Lightning_Static_Spark_Description
data.value: The voltage was high enough to break down the air in the gap: the air turned into a glowing, conducting path and the charge rushed across. A lightning bolt in miniature. Only the charge near the tip goes: the rod is an insulator.

data.name: Lightning_Static_Subtitle
data.value: Charging by rubbing: electrons hop from one thing to another

data.name: Lightning_Static_Touched_Description
data.value: Too few volts for a spark you could see: the charge simply flowed into the earthed ball where they touched.

data.name: Lightning_Strike_Attach_Description
data.value: When the leader's tip comes within striking distance of something, the field there is strong enough to send a streamer up. Whatever's streamer meets the leader first gets the strike: that is the rolling sphere.

data.name: Lightning_Strike_Dart_Description
data.value: The next discharge does not feel its way or branch: it darts straight down the still-warm channel in a millisecond or two.

data.name: Lightning_Strike_Fact1
data.value: The channel is only a few centimetres wide, but within microseconds it is heated to about 30 000 °C, five times hotter than the surface of the Sun.

data.name: Lightning_Strike_Fact2
data.value: A flash usually has 3 or 4 return strokes, tens of milliseconds apart, down the same channel: that is why lightning flickers.

data.name: Lightning_Strike_Fact3
data.value: Thunder is the shock wave of air heated and expanding all at once. Count the seconds from the flash and divide by 3: that is roughly how many kilometres away it was.

data.name: Lightning_Strike_Fact4
data.value: A lightning rod does not attract lightning from afar: when a leader comes near, it sends up its streamer first, and leads the current down its conductor into the earth. Benjamin Franklin proposed it around 1750.

data.name: Lightning_Strike_Fact5
data.value: Never shelter under a lone tree: the current can jump from its trunk to you, or spread through the ground (step voltage). A building with protection, or a car with its doors shut (a metal cage), is safe.

data.name: Lightning_Strike_Glow_Description
data.value: After a stroke the channel glows on for a while as it cools, while charge elsewhere in the cloud gathers at its top, ready to go again.

data.name: Lightning_Strike_Heard_Description
data.value: Sound from every part of the long channel arrives one after another, so thunder rumbles instead of banging once. The seconds divided by 3 are about the kilometres to the strike.

data.name: Lightning_Strike_Later_Description
data.value: The same channel is used again: the current is smaller but rises faster. These repeated strokes are why lightning flickers.

data.name: Lightning_Strike_Leader_Description
data.value: Negative charge from the cloud's base feels its way down along an ionised channel, jumping about 50 m at a time, pausing tens of microseconds, branching as it goes. It is faint: you would hardly see it.

data.name: Lightning_Strike_Note
data.value: The lowest 100-odd metres are to scale, the rest up to the cloud (2 km) squeezed. Each part of the flash is slowed by a different amount; after the last stroke time runs at its real pace and the thunder travels at 343 m/s.

data.name: Lightning_Strike_Strip_Wait
data.value: The light reaches you at once; the sound will take {0} s

data.name: Lightning_Strike_Stroke_Description
data.value: The moment the channel connects, a huge current (typically 30 000 amps) surges up from the ground at about a third of the speed of light, heating the channel to some 30 000 °C: the flash you see.

data.name: Lightning_Strike_Subtitle
data.value: One strike in slow motion, and its thunder

data.name: Lightning_Strike_Thunder_Description
data.value: The light reached you almost at once; the sound covers only 343 m a second. Count the seconds since the flash.

data.name: Lightning_Strike_Thunder_Title
data.value: The thunder is on its way

data.name: Location_Chip_Tooltip
data.value: The place the chapters of the book are seen from. Shared by all of them and saved.

data.name: Location_Custom_Hint
data.value: Latitude north positive, longitude east positive, in degrees. Its clock is the ideal time zone of its meridian.

data.name: Location_Description
data.value: Used by every chapter that depends on where you are: day and night, the tides and more to come. Saved for next time.

data.name: Location_Gravity_Note
data.value: "Earth" uses the pull of gravity at {0}: g = {1} m/s². It is 9.780 at the equator and 9.832 at the poles, because Earth spins and bulges.

data.name: MoonPhases_Chart_Caption
data.value: How much is lit through the month

data.name: MoonPhases_Disc_Caption
data.value: The Moon as seen from Earth

data.name: MoonPhases_DragHint_Month
data.value: Drag left or right to move through the month

data.name: MoonPhases_DragHint_Orbit
data.value: Drag to move the Moon along its orbit

data.name: MoonPhases_DragHint_Sky
data.value: Drag left or right to change the time of day

data.name: MoonPhases_Hemisphere_Hint
data.value: Everyone sees the same phase on the same night, but from the southern hemisphere the Moon looks upside down.

data.name: MoonPhases_Label_DailyPath
data.value: Path of the Sun and the Moon across the sky

data.name: MoonPhases_Legend_Note
data.value: We see only the part of the Moon that is both lit and facing us: that is the phase.

data.name: MoonPhases_Lesson_Month_Choice1
data.value: Earth has moved on around the Sun

data.name: MoonPhases_Lesson_Sky_Choice1
data.value: In the daytime, with the Sun

data.name: MoonPhases_Moment_Sidereal
data.value: Once round against the stars, but not yet new moon

data.name: MoonPhases_Moment_Synodic
data.value: Between Earth and the Sun: new moon

data.name: MoonPhases_Month_Fact1
data.value: Sidereal month, 27.32 days: once round Earth, back in line with the same distant star.

data.name: MoonPhases_Month_Fact2
data.value: Synodic month, 29.53 days: from new moon to new moon. Earth moves about 29° round the Sun in a month, and the Moon needs about 2.2 more days to catch up.

data.name: MoonPhases_Month_Fact3
data.value: Days work the same way: Earth turns once against the stars in 23 h 56 min, but the Sun returns to the same place in the sky after 24 hours.

data.name: MoonPhases_Month_Fact4
data.value: The months of the Chinese calendar follow the phases: 29 or 30 days, starting at new moon. Twelve of them make only 354 days, so a leap month is added about every three years.

data.name: MoonPhases_Month_Note
data.value: Not to scale: the Moon's orbit is drawn far too large for Earth's

data.name: MoonPhases_Month_Subtitle
data.value: The Moon goes round Earth in 27.3 days, so why do the phases take 29.5?

data.name: MoonPhases_Month_Text
data.value: Day {0:0.0}: the Moon has gone {1:0}° round Earth against the stars, but only {2:0}° against the Sun, because Earth has moved {3:0.0}° round the Sun meanwhile.

data.name: MoonPhases_Obj_EarthOrbit
data.value: Earth on its way round the Sun

data.name: MoonPhases_Obj_Moon
data.value: The Moon and its two halves

data.name: MoonPhases_Observer_Caption
data.value: Where you are on the turning Earth (seen from above the North Pole)

data.name: MoonPhases_Observer_Note
data.value: The shaded half is your sky. When the Moon is in it (ringed), the Moon is above your horizon.

data.name: MoonPhases_Phase_FirstQuarter_Description
data.value: A quarter of the way round: we see half of the lit half. It is due south at sunset and sets around midnight.

data.name: MoonPhases_Phase_Full_Description
data.value: Earth is between the Sun and the Moon: the whole lit half faces us. It rises at sunset and is up all night.

data.name: MoonPhases_Phase_LastQuarter_Description
data.value: Three quarters of the way round: half lit again, the other half. It rises around midnight and is due south at sunrise.

data.name: MoonPhases_Phase_New_Description
data.value: The Moon is between Earth and the Sun: its lit half faces away from us. It crosses the sky with the Sun, lost in its glare.

data.name: MoonPhases_Phase_WaningCrescent_Description
data.value: Only a sliver of the lit half still faces us. Look low in the east just before sunrise.

data.name: MoonPhases_Phase_WaningGibbous_Description
data.value: The lit part shrinks, now from the other side. It rises in the evening and is still up after sunrise.

data.name: MoonPhases_Phase_WaxingCrescent_Description
data.value: A thin sliver of the lit half turns towards us. Look low in the west just after sunset.

data.name: MoonPhases_Phase_WaxingGibbous_Description
data.value: More than half the disc is lit and growing. It rises in the afternoon and is up most of the evening.

data.name: MoonPhases_Phases_Fact1
data.value: The Moon makes no light of its own. Like Earth, it is always half lit by the Sun; the phase is how much of that lit half faces us.

data.name: MoonPhases_Phases_Fact2
data.value: The phases are not Earth's shadow: at a crescent, Earth's shadow points far away from the Moon. Earth's shadow only falls on the Moon in a lunar eclipse.

data.name: MoonPhases_Phases_Fact3
data.value: Eclipses can only happen at new moon (solar) and full moon (lunar), yet most months there is none: the Moon's orbit is tilted 5°, so it usually passes above or below.

data.name: MoonPhases_Phases_Fact4
data.value: The Moon turns once on its axis each time it goes round Earth, so it always shows us the same face. The far side is not dark: it is fully lit at new moon.

data.name: MoonPhases_Phases_Fact5
data.value: Waxing (growing) phases are lit on the right, waning ones on the left, as seen from the northern hemisphere; from the southern hemisphere it is the other way round.

data.name: MoonPhases_Phases_Note
data.value: Seen from far above the North Pole; not to scale. Outer ring: the Moon as seen from Earth ({0})

data.name: MoonPhases_Phases_Subtitle
data.value: Why does the Moon change shape? It is always half lit by the Sun

data.name: MoonPhases_SkyNow_Down
data.value: {0}: the Moon is below the horizon. {1}

data.name: MoonPhases_SkyNow_Up
data.value: {0}: the Moon is {1:0}° up in the {2}. {3}

data.name: MoonPhases_Sky_Fact1
data.value: The Moon moves about 12° east against the stars each day, so it rises about 50 minutes later each day.

data.name: MoonPhases_Sky_Fact2
data.value: The full moon is opposite the Sun: it rises as the Sun sets and sets as the Sun rises.

data.name: MoonPhases_Sky_Fact3
data.value: A crescent is always close to the Sun in the sky: in the west after sunset while waxing, in the east before sunrise while waning.

data.name: MoonPhases_Sky_Fact4
data.value: For about half of the month the Moon is up in daylight too. Around first quarter it is easy to see in the afternoon.

data.name: MoonPhases_Sky_Note
data.value: Simplified: the Sun and the Moon follow the celestial equator, as at an equinox. Local solar time; the Moon is drawn larger

data.name: MoonPhases_Sky_Subtitle
data.value: When can you see the Moon? It rises about 50 minutes later each day

data.name: MoonPhases_Stat_RiseSet_ToolTip
data.value: Local solar time at an equinox. Through the year real times shift by up to a few hours.

data.name: MoonPhases_Today_Text
data.value: Today: {0}, {1:P0} lit, {2:0.0} days after new moon.

data.name: MoonPhases_Upcoming_Note
data.value: In your time zone. Calculated, to within a few minutes.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Obj_Aurora
data.value: The aurora: a ring of light around each magnetic pole, where electrons from the magnetosphere crash into the upper air. It glows brighter when the solar wind is fast and its field points south.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Obj_Belts
data.value: The Van Allen radiation belts: energetic particles trapped in Earth's field, in an inner and an outer belt. Spacecraft cross them quickly to keep the radiation dose down.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Obj_BowShock
data.value: The bow shock: where the supersonic solar wind suddenly slows down in front of Earth's field, like the wave piled up in front of a ship's bow.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Obj_ClosedLine
data.value: A closed field line: both ends are tied to Earth. After reconnecting in the tail it snaps back like a rubber band, and throws particles down into the auroral oval.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Obj_Curtain
data.value: The aurora curtain: a thin sheet of light, often hundreds of kilometres tall but only about a kilometre thick, standing along the field lines.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Obj_Cusp
data.value: The cusp: the funnel above each pole where the solar wind can reach right down into the upper air. It gives a faint red aurora around noon.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Obj_DayX
data.value: Reconnection at the nose: the southward field of the solar wind meets Earth's northward field. The lines break and rejoin, opening Earth's field to the solar wind.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Obj_Earth
data.value: Earth. Electric currents in its molten iron outer core make a magnetic field much like a giant bar magnet's, tilted about ten degrees from the spin axis.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Obj_Foot
data.value: Where the field line meets the air, about a hundred kilometres up. A particle in the loss cone ends up here and gives its energy to the air, which glows.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Obj_Green
data.value: Oxygen green, at 557.7 nanometres: the commonest aurora colour, from about one hundred to two hundred kilometres up. Lower down, collisions take the energy before it can shine.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Obj_Horizon
data.value: Your horizon. Anything below this line is hidden by the curve of the Earth, however bright it is.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Obj_Imf
data.value: The interplanetary magnetic field: the Sun's field, carried out by the solar wind. Whether it points north or south decides whether it can join Earth's field and open the shield.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Obj_Inner
data.value: The inner Van Allen belt, around one and a half Earth radii from the centre: mostly very energetic protons, made indirectly by cosmic rays striking the upper air.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Obj_Line
data.value: The particle's field line. The centre of its spiral slides along this line, from one mirror point to the other.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Obj_Lobe
data.value: The tail lobes: bundles of open field lines, tied to Earth at one end and to the solar wind at the other. They store the energy that a substorm later lets go.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Obj_LossCone
data.value: The loss cone. A particle whose pitch angle at the equator is smaller than this would only turn back below a hundred kilometres, so it hits the air instead. Out here the cone is just a few degrees wide.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Obj_Magnetopause
data.value: The magnetopause: the edge of Earth's magnetic field, where its pressure balances the solar wind's. The stronger the wind, the closer it comes.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Obj_Meridian
data.value: The magnetic meridian from you to the magnetic pole. The slice on the right is cut along this line.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Obj_Mirror
data.value: A mirror point: where the field becomes strong enough to turn the particle back. Its spiral is tightest here, and for a moment it only goes round, not along.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Obj_Night
data.value: The midnight side of the oval. Substorms usually break out here, a little before magnetic midnight, when the aurora suddenly brightens and starts to dance.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Obj_OpenLine
data.value: An open field line: one end is tied to Earth near the pole, the other is out in the solar wind. The wind drags it over the pole and into the tail.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Obj_Outer
data.value: The outer Van Allen belt, about three to six Earth radii out: mostly energetic electrons. It swells and shrinks with every storm.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Obj_Oval
data.value: The auroral oval: the ring around each magnetic pole where the aurora usually is. It keeps its place towards the Sun, is wider on the night side, and grows towards the equator in storms.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Obj_Particle
data.value: A trapped particle. A real one is far too small to see, and much faster: an electron like this goes round its spiral tens of thousands of times a second.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Obj_PlasmaSheet
data.value: The plasma sheet: a layer of hot plasma in the middle of the tail. When the tail reconnects, particles from here are shot towards Earth and feed the aurora.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Obj_Pole
data.value: The geomagnetic pole, where the axis of Earth's magnetic field comes out. It's about a thousand kilometres from the geographic pole, so two places at the same latitude can be very different distances from the aurora.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Obj_Red
data.value: Oxygen red, at 630 nanometres: from above about two hundred kilometres, where the air is thin enough for an excited atom to wait nearly two minutes and still shine.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Obj_Ring
data.value: The ring current: protons drift west and electrons east, so together they carry a current westward round Earth. In a storm it grows, and weakens the field at the ground.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Obj_Seen
data.value: How far from the oval the top of the aurora can still peek over your horizon. The higher it glows, and slower electrons make it glow higher, the farther away it can be seen.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Obj_Sheath
data.value: The magnetosheath: the slowed, hot, squeezed solar wind between the bow shock and the magnetopause. It flows around the magnetosphere, with the Sun's field draped over it.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Obj_Shell
data.value: The drift shell. As it bounces, the particle also drifts slowly round Earth on this shell, because the field is stronger nearer Earth and bends its circles a little more on that side.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Obj_Sight
data.value: Your lines of sight to the bottom and the top of the curtain. Their angles above the horizon are how high the aurora stands in your sky.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Obj_Spiral
data.value: The spiral: the magnetic force always pushes sideways, so the particle circles the field line while gliding along it. Electrons and protons circle in opposite directions.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Obj_Stripped
data.value: Without a magnetic field, the solar wind reaches the upper air directly and slowly strips it away. Mars has lost much of its atmosphere like this over billions of years.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Obj_Sun
data.value: The Sun, drawn far too close: it's about twenty-three thousand Earth radii away. As well as light, it blows out the solar wind, and now and then it hurls out huge clouds of plasma that set off storms.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Obj_Tail
data.value: The magnetotail: the night side of the magnetosphere, stretched by the solar wind to hundreds of Earth radii, far beyond the Moon's orbit.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Obj_TailX
data.value: Reconnection in the tail: the stretched open lines from north and south rejoin in the middle of the tail. The closed part snaps back towards Earth, and the rest flies off with the wind.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Obj_View
data.value: Your sky, facing the aurora. The curtain is drawn where the slice puts it, folding and rippling the way real ones do.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Obj_Violet
data.value: Nitrogen violet and blue, around 428 nanometres: a fringe along the bottom edge, where the fastest electrons reach deepest.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Obj_Wind
data.value: The solar wind: charged particles, mostly protons and electrons, streaming off the Sun at three hundred to eight hundred kilometres a second. It takes two to four days to reach Earth.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Obj_You
data.value: This is you, at the observing place chosen on the left-hand page. Change it to see how far from the aurora other places are.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Particles_01
data.value: Some particles don't just flow past. They get trapped inside Earth's magnetic field. Follow this bright dot: it's a single electron.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Particles_02
data.value: A magnetic field pushes a moving charge sideways, so the electron can't cross the field line. Instead it circles around it while sliding along it. That makes a spiral.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Particles_03
data.value: Near the poles, the field lines crowd together and the field gets stronger. That squeezes the spiral tighter and tighter, until the electron stops and turns back. This turning point is called a mirror point.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Particles_04
data.value: So the electron bounces from north to south and back, again and again. And slowly, its whole path creeps around Earth. Electrons drift east, and protons drift west.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Particles_05
data.value: Here's a question. What decides how close to the pole the electron gets before it turns back?

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Particles_06
data.value: It's the angle between its path and the field, called the pitch angle. The more steeply it runs along the field, the farther it gets. Below a few degrees, inside what's called the loss cone, it never turns back at all.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Particles_07
data.value: Instead, it reaches the air near the pole and stops there, and its energy makes the air glow. Every aurora is made of particles like this one, falling out of the loss cone.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Particles_08
data.value: The particles that do stay trapped fill two huge doughnuts around Earth, the Van Allen belts. The inner one holds mostly protons, and the outer one mostly electrons.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Particles_09
data.value: Your turn. Try a proton instead of an electron, and watch which way it drifts. Or change the pitch angle, and see where it turns back.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Shield_01
data.value: Here is Earth seen side on, with the Sun far away to the left. The Sun blows out a thin wind of charged particles, the solar wind, at around four hundred kilometres a second. Those are the streaks coming in from the left.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Shield_02
data.value: The wind is faster than any wave can travel through it. So in front of Earth it piles up into a shock wave, the bow shock, a bit like the wave in front of a boat. Behind it, the wind slows down and heats up.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Shield_03
data.value: Inside is Earth's own magnetic field. Its edge, the magnetopause, is where the field pushes back as hard as the wind pushes in. On the day side that's about ten Earth radii out. On the night side, the wind drags the field out into a long tail.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Shield_04
data.value: So here's a question. If the solar wind blows harder, what happens to the magnetopause?

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Shield_05
data.value: It gets pushed closer. Here is a storm: a cloud thrown off the Sun, arriving at over eight hundred kilometres a second. Look how much the magnetopause shrinks. In the biggest storms, satellites in geostationary orbit end up outside it, right in the solar wind.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Shield_06
data.value: The solar wind also carries the Sun's magnetic field along with it. When that field points south, as it does here, it points the opposite way to Earth's field at the front of the magnetosphere. Then something remarkable happens.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Shield_07
data.value: The two fields join up. The lines break and reconnect, so this field line from the Sun is now tied to Earth at one end. The wind keeps pulling at the other end, dragging it over the poles and back into the tail.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Shield_08
data.value: Deep in the tail, the stretched lines from north and south meet in the middle and reconnect a second time. The new closed line snaps back towards Earth like a released rubber band, and flings electrons down along it.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Shield_09
data.value: Those electrons rain down into the air in a ring around each pole and make it glow. That's the aurora. This whole loop is called the Dungey cycle, and a real one takes about an hour.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Shield_10
data.value: Your turn. Use the slider to turn the Sun's field northward, or switch off Earth's field altogether, and see what happens to the shield.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Sky_01
data.value: Here is Earth seen from above the magnetic pole nearest you. The green ring is the auroral oval, where falling electrons reach the air. Notice it's centred on the magnetic pole, not the geographic one.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Sky_02
data.value: The oval stays turned away from the Sun, while Earth spins underneath it. It's brightest a little before magnetic midnight, so that's the best time to look.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Sky_03
data.value: The gold dot is you, at the observing place chosen on the left-hand page. The dashed blue line runs from you towards the magnetic pole, and the slice on the right is taken along it.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Sky_04
data.value: A question. When the Sun is stormy, which way does the oval move?

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Sky_05
data.value: It grows, and slides towards the equator. The dashed gold line shows how far away you can still glimpse it, low over the horizon. That's possible because the aurora is so high up, from about one hundred to four hundred kilometres.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Sky_06
data.value: On the right is a slice from you to the aurora, drawn with Earth's real curve. The curtain stands upright. If it's too far away, the curve of the Earth hides it below your horizon.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Sky_07
data.value: The colours come from the air itself. Low down, oxygen atoms glow green. Higher up, where the air is thin, oxygen glows red, because up there an excited atom can wait almost two minutes to shine without bumping into anything. At the very bottom, nitrogen adds a violet fringe.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Sky_08
data.value: Slower electrons stop higher up, so the aurora they make is mostly red. In great storms, people far from the poles often see only this red glow.

data.name: Narr_Aurora_Sky_09
data.value: Your turn. Drag the Kp slider up and down, or change the electrons' energy, and watch how the curtain, its colours, and your sky change.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Cell_01
data.value: Let's build that loop step by step. Sea on the left, land on the right. These white lines are surfaces of equal pressure. While the land and the sea are equally warm, they lie flat.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Cell_02
data.value: Now the Sun heats the land, and the air over it warms from twenty-four to thirty-two degrees. Warm air expands, so the column over the land grows taller. The pressure surfaces bulge upward, more and more the higher you go.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Cell_03
data.value: Look at one height, high up. Over the land the pressure surfaces have been pushed above it, so the pressure there is now higher than over the sea. Which way will the air move up there?

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Cell_04
data.value: Up high, air flows from higher pressure to lower: from over the land, out over the sea. Watch the white arrow at the top.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Cell_05
data.value: Now the land's column has lost some air, so it presses less on the ground: low pressure at the surface. The sea's column has gained air: high pressure. Look at the two marks near the ground.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Cell_06
data.value: Near the ground, the air now flows from the sea's high to the land's low. That's the sea breeze.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Cell_07
data.value: Put it all together. Air rises over the warm land, flows out to sea up high, sinks over the cool sea, and comes back along the ground. A closed loop, driven only by a difference in temperature: we call it a thermal circulation.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Cell_08
data.value: At night the land cools to about eighteen degrees, below the sea's twenty-four. Every step happens the other way round: the air sinks over the land, rises over the sea, and near the ground the land breeze blows out to sea.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Cell_09
data.value: Your turn. Drag the land or the sea temperature slider. The bigger the difference, the stronger the circulation. Make them equal, and the loop stops.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Coast_01
data.value: Here's a coast on a sunny summer afternoon: the sea on the left, the land on the right. Look at the two thermometers. The air over the land is about thirty-one degrees, but over the sea it's only about twenty-four.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Coast_02
data.value: Why such a difference, under the same Sun? Water warms slowly. Sunlight reaches metres down, waves mix the heat even deeper, and water needs a lot of energy to warm up. The ground only heats a thin top layer, so it gets hot fast.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Coast_03
data.value: The hot ground warms the air above it. Warm air expands, becomes lighter, and rises. See the orange arrow going up over the land.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Coast_04
data.value: So the air over the land is rising, and something has to take its place near the ground. Which way do you think the wind blows along the beach?

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Coast_05
data.value: It blows from the sea. Cooler sea air slides in along the ground: this is the sea breeze. Look at the beach: the flag, the chimney smoke and the sails all point inland.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Coast_06
data.value: Now let's turn on the pressure lines. Near the ground, the warm land has low pressure and the cool sea has high pressure, and air always flows from high to low. Higher up it's the other way round, so the air flows back out to sea. One closed loop.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Coast_07
data.value: The leading edge of the sea breeze is called the sea-breeze front. Through the afternoon it pushes inland, here about seventeen kilometres, lifting the warm air ahead of it. That's why a line of puffy clouds often forms along it.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Coast_08
data.value: Now jump to three in the morning. On a clear night the land loses its heat to the sky fast, and ends up cooler than the sea. So everything turns round: a gentle land breeze blows out to sea. It's weaker, and much shallower, than the sea breeze.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Coast_09
data.value: What about a cloudy day? Under thick cloud the land hardly warms up, so it's barely warmer than the sea. With almost no temperature difference, there's almost no wind. See: calm.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Coast_10
data.value: Your turn. It's half past eight in the morning. Drag the time slider through the day, and find out when the sea breeze starts, and when it turns into a land breeze.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Monsoon_01
data.value: The same idea works on a much bigger scale: a whole continent, and a whole year. It's January. The heart of Asia is bitterly cold, and the cold, dense air piles up into a huge high-pressure system: the Siberian High.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Monsoon_02
data.value: Air spreads out of it toward the warmer ocean. Over northern China it arrives as the cold, dry north-west winter monsoon, and over India as the north-east monsoon. So winter here is the dry season.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Monsoon_03
data.value: Now think about summer. The land heats up far more than the ocean. What happens to the pressure over the continent?

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Monsoon_04
data.value: Low pressure forms over the land. Jump to July: the Siberian High is gone, and a deep heat low sits over north-west India instead.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Monsoon_05
data.value: Moist air from the ocean is pulled in: the south-west monsoon over India. Watch the winds south of the equator. They start as south-east trade winds, and as they cross the equator, Earth's spin bends them into south-westerlies.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Monsoon_06
data.value: This dashed line is the equatorial trough, where the winds from both hemispheres meet and rain clouds build up. In July it has moved far to the north; in January it lies south of the equator.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Monsoon_07
data.value: Look at Mumbai. In July alone it gets about eight hundred and forty millimetres of rain, yet from December to April it hardly rains at all. A wet summer and a dry winter: that's a monsoon climate.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Monsoon_08
data.value: South of the equator, the seasons are the other way round. Back in January it's summer in Darwin, in northern Australia, and the rain pours down; in July it's almost dry.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Monsoon_09
data.value: Your turn. Click a city on the map, then drag the month slider through the year, and watch how its rain comes and goes.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Obj_AsianLow
data.value: The Asian heat low forms in summer over north-west India, Pakistan and Iran, where the land gets scorching hot. It pulls in moist air from the Indian Ocean: the south-west monsoon.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Obj_Australia
data.value: Over Australia, the pressure swings with the seasons: a heat low in the southern summer, which draws the north-west monsoon onto northern Australia, and a high in the southern winter.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Obj_Beijing
data.value: Beijing has a strongly monsoonal climate. Most of its rain falls in July and August, while its winters, under the cold north-west monsoon, are very dry, with only a few millimetres a month.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Obj_Boat
data.value: Sailors have used these breezes for thousands of years. Fishing boats went out on the land breeze before dawn, and came home on the sea breeze in the afternoon.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Obj_Calm
data.value: Calm. Around sunrise and sunset, and on cloudy days, the land and the sea are almost equally warm. With no temperature difference there's nothing to push the air, so the wind dies away.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Obj_Changsha
data.value: Changsha lies inland, in central China. Its rain comes early, with the spring rains and the June plum rains; then late summer turns hot and drier, under the subtropical high.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Obj_Cooling
data.value: At night the land gives off its heat to the sky, as invisible infrared radiation. With no Sun to warm it again, the ground and the air just above it cool quickly, and end up colder than the sea.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Obj_Darwin
data.value: Darwin, in northern Australia, lies south of the equator, so its wet season runs from December to March, the southern summer. From June to August it hardly rains at all.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Obj_Equator
data.value: At the equator, Earth's spin doesn't bend the wind. North of it, winds are bent to the right; south of it, to the left. That's why the south-east trades turn into the south-west monsoon as they cross into the north.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Obj_Flag
data.value: A flag is a simple wind vane: it streams out with the wind. In the afternoon it points inland, at night it points out to sea, and in a calm it hangs limp.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Obj_Front
data.value: The sea-breeze front is where cool sea air meets the hot air over the land. It creeps inland through the afternoon and lifts the warm air ahead of it, so a line of cumulus clouds, sometimes even a thunderstorm, can grow along it.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Obj_Guangzhou
data.value: Guangzhou, in southern China, has rain for much of the year, but most of it falls from April to September, brought by moist summer winds from the South China Sea, and by typhoons.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Obj_High
data.value: High pressure. At this height, the pressure here is higher than at the same height nearby. Air flows out of a high, toward lower pressure.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Obj_Isobars
data.value: Surfaces of equal pressure. Where a surface bulges up, the pressure at that height is higher than around it; where it dips, it's lower. The bends are hugely exaggerated here: in real air they move only ten or twenty metres.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Obj_Land
data.value: The land heats fast, and cools fast. Only a thin layer of ground takes the Sun's heat, and soil and rock need far less heat than water to warm up. On a clear summer day, the air over it can swing by more than ten degrees.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Obj_LandBreeze
data.value: The land breeze blows from the land out to sea at night, once the land has become cooler than the water. It's gentle and shallow, only a few hundred metres deep, because cold air lies heavy and still near the ground.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Obj_Low
data.value: Low pressure. At this height, the pressure here is lower than at the same height nearby. Air flows in toward a low from around it, and near the ground, the air that gathers there has to rise.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Obj_Mascarene
data.value: The Mascarene High sits over the southern Indian Ocean. In the northern summer it strengthens, and the trade winds flowing out of it cross the equator to feed the Indian monsoon.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Obj_MonsoonAustralia
data.value: Northern Australia's monsoon. In the southern summer, winds from the Asian side cross the equator and turn into north-westerlies, bringing the wet season to Darwin.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Obj_MonsoonNE
data.value: The north-east monsoon is India's winter wind, blowing from the cold continent toward the ocean. It keeps most of India dry, but it picks up moisture over the Bay of Bengal and brings winter rain to the south-east coast.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Obj_MonsoonNW
data.value: The north-west monsoon blows out of the Siberian High in winter, over northern China, Korea and Japan. It's cold and dry, and sometimes it surges south as a cold wave.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Obj_MonsoonSE
data.value: The south-east monsoon blows from the Pacific onto eastern China in summer, bringing warm, moist air and the rainy season.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Obj_MonsoonSW
data.value: The south-west monsoon blows from the Indian Ocean onto India and South-east Asia in summer. It carries huge amounts of moisture, and its arrival, usually in June, starts the rainy season.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Obj_Mumbai
data.value: Mumbai, on India's west coast, has a classic monsoon climate: about two thousand four hundred millimetres of rain a year, almost all of it from June to September, when the south-west monsoon arrives from the Arabian Sea.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Obj_PacificRidge
data.value: The western Pacific subtropical high shapes East Asia's summer. Moist air flowing round its western edge brings the south-east monsoon to China, and where it meets cooler air from the north, the plum-rain front forms.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Obj_Return
data.value: The return flow, higher up. The air that rose drifts back the other way, from higher pressure to lower. You can't feel it on the beach, but without it the loop couldn't close.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Obj_Rising
data.value: Rising air. Wherever it's warmest, the air expands, becomes lighter, and rises: over the land by day, over the sea at night. As it rises it cools, so clouds can form.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Obj_Scale
data.value: This picture is stretched upward. The sea breeze is only about a kilometre deep, but it reaches tens of kilometres inland. Drawn to true scale, the whole circulation would be a thin sliver.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Obj_Sea
data.value: The sea warms and cools slowly. Sunlight reaches metres into the water, waves mix the heat downward, and water needs a lot of heat to change its temperature. So day and night, its surface changes by only about a degree.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Obj_SeaBreeze
data.value: The sea breeze blows from the sea onto the land on sunny days, strongest in the early afternoon. It's cool and moist, a welcome relief on a hot coast, and it can reach tens of kilometres inland.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Obj_Shanghai
data.value: Shanghai's rain peaks in June with the plum rains, the Meiyu, when the summer monsoon stalls over the Yangtze for weeks. Its winters are cool and fairly dry.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Obj_Shower
data.value: At night, the land breeze meets the warmer sea air offshore and pushes it up. So clouds and showers can form out at sea before dawn, while the coast stays clear.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Obj_Siberian
data.value: The Mongolian-Siberian High forms in winter, when the interior of Asia gets extremely cold. It's the strongest high-pressure system on Earth, and its cold air spills out as the winter monsoon. In summer it all but disappears.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Obj_Sinking
data.value: Sinking air. Over the cooler side, air comes down to close the loop. Sinking air is squeezed and warms up, so clouds dry out: skies here are usually clear.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Obj_Smoke
data.value: Smoke from the chimney shows the wind near the ground. In the sea breeze it's carried inland, in the land breeze it drifts out to sea, and in a calm it rises almost straight up.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Obj_Sun
data.value: The Sun shines on the land and the sea alike. The difference is how they take its heat: the land warms up fast, while the sea hardly changes. That difference is what drives the wind.

data.name: Narr_Breeze_Obj_Trough
data.value: The equatorial trough, also called the ITCZ, is a belt of low pressure where the trade winds of the two hemispheres meet. The air there rises, so it's full of rain clouds. It follows the Sun: north in July, south in January.

data.name: Narr_Common_MoveOn
data.value: Let's keep going. You can try it again later.

data.name: Narr_Common_Reveal
data.value: Time's up! Here's the right answer.

data.name: Narr_Common_Wrong
data.value: Not quite. Let's look at the answer.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Globe_01
data.value: Now let's look at a globe. Sunlight comes in from the left, and it can only ever light up half of Earth at a time.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Globe_02
data.value: The edge between the lit half and the dark half is a great circle. As Earth spins once a day, every place passes through it twice, once at sunrise and once at sunset.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Globe_03
data.value: Earth's axis is tilted. So, except at the equinoxes, this circle doesn't pass through the poles. It's turned away from the axis by an angle.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Globe_04
data.value: Let's jump to June. Now that angle is at its largest, about twenty-three and a half degrees, the same as the tilt of the axis.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Globe_05
data.value: Look near the North Pole. However Earth turns, it stays in the lit half all day long. That's polar day, the midnight sun. Near the South Pole it stays dark all day: polar night.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Globe_06
data.value: Quick question. In December, where is there polar day?

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Globe_07
data.value: It's near the South Pole. In December the southern half leans towards the Sun, so the South Pole has polar day, and the North Pole has its long polar night. Drag the globe to look at it from another angle.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Map_01
data.value: This is a map of the whole world. The bright part is in daylight and the dark part is in night. The curved gold line between them is where day meets night.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Map_02
data.value: Right here the Sun is straight overhead. Earth spins from west to east, so the Sun seems to slide west, fifteen degrees every hour, all the way round in a day.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Map_03
data.value: On this half of the line, the Sun is rising right now. It's called the sunrise line. On the other half, the sunset line, the Sun is going down.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Map_04
data.value: Everywhere on the gold vertical line it's noon, and everywhere on the blue one it's midnight. Both lines slide west along with the Sun.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Map_05
data.value: Think about it. If you lived further east, would you see sunrise earlier or later?

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Map_06
data.value: The answer is earlier: the sunrise line reaches the east first. Now let's run through a whole year, stopping at the same moment each day. Watch the line change shape. Around June the north has the long days, around December the south does, and only at the equinoxes does the line run straight from pole to pole.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Map_07
data.value: Now you try. Click a city on the map, and the left page shows what time it is there and how high the Sun is.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Map_08
data.value: Wherever you are, sunrise, noon and sunset all come from the same thing: Earth turning you towards the Sun and away again.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Obj_Angle
data.value: The angle between the axis and the edge of the lit half. It's the same as how far north or south of the equator the Sun is overhead: zero at the equinoxes, about twenty-three and a half degrees at the solstices.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Obj_Axis
data.value: Earth's axis, through the North and South Poles. It's tilted about twenty-three and a half degrees, which is why day length changes through the year.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Obj_DateLine
data.value: The international date line, mostly along one hundred and eighty degrees. Going east across it, you set your calendar back a day; going west, forward a day.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Obj_Equator
data.value: The equator. On it, day and night are about twelve hours each, all year round.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Obj_Midnight
data.value: Everywhere under this line it's midnight by the Sun, halfway between sunset and sunrise.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Obj_NewDay
data.value: This is where it's midnight. East of it, the date has already changed. The new day spreads west by one zone every hour.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Obj_Noon
data.value: Everywhere under this line it's noon by the Sun: the Sun is at its highest point of the day.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Obj_PolarCircle
data.value: The polar circles, about sixty-six and a half degrees north and south. Inside them there's at least one day a year without sunset, and one without sunrise.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Obj_PolarDay
data.value: Polar day. Here the whole circle of latitude stays in the lit half as Earth turns, so the Sun never sets.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Obj_PolarNight
data.value: Polar night. Here the whole circle of latitude stays in the dark half, so the Sun never rises.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Obj_Sun
data.value: This is where the Sun is straight overhead. It moves west fifteen degrees every hour, and over the year it wanders between the two tropics.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Obj_Sunlight
data.value: Sunlight from far away arrives as parallel rays, so it lights exactly half of Earth at any moment.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Obj_SunriseLine
data.value: The sunrise line. Everywhere along it, the Sun is just coming up. It sweeps west across the world as Earth turns.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Obj_SunsetLine
data.value: The sunset line. Everywhere along it, the Sun is just going down, and evening is beginning.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Obj_Tropics
data.value: The tropics, about twenty-three and a half degrees north and south. They're as far from the equator as the Sun is ever overhead.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Obj_Utc
data.value: UTC is world time, kept by atomic clocks and almost exactly the time at Greenwich in London. Every time zone is a whole number of hours ahead of it or behind it, with a few exceptions.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Obj_Zone
data.value: This is the time zone of the place you've picked. Each zone is about fifteen degrees of longitude, one hour of the Sun's journey.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Zones_01
data.value: If every town set its clocks by its own Sun, even neighbouring towns would be a few minutes apart. So the world is divided by longitude into twenty-four time zones, each about fifteen degrees wide.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Zones_02
data.value: The numbers along the top show how many hours each zone is ahead of or behind world time, called UTC. Along the bottom is the time on clocks there right now.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Zones_03
data.value: Look at this blue line. It's where midnight is right now. East of it, a new day has already begun, and the new date spreads west by one time zone every hour.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Zones_04
data.value: Think about it. Where does each new date begin first?

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Zones_05
data.value: A new date begins first just west of the international date line, out in the middle of the Pacific. Cross the line going east and you go back a day. Cross it going west and you jump forward a day.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Zones_06
data.value: Time zones follow borders, not just longitude. China spans about five zones but uses Beijing time everywhere, so in the far west the Sun rises very late by the clock.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Lunar_01
data.value: Now it's Earth's turn to cast a shadow. Like the Moon's, it points straight away from the Sun, out into space.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Lunar_02
data.value: When the Moon is on the far side of Earth from the Sun, it's full moon. That's the only time it can pass through Earth's shadow.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Lunar_03
data.value: Earth's umbra is much wider than the Moon, so the whole Moon fits inside it. That's why a total lunar eclipse can last for more than an hour.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Lunar_04
data.value: Now the Moon is deep in Earth's umbra. Think about it: what colour does it turn?

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Lunar_05
data.value: Copper red. Earth's air bends a little sunlight into the shadow, and on the way the blue light is scattered away, just like at sunset. In a way, the Moon is lit by all the sunrises and sunsets on Earth at once.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Lunar_06
data.value: And unlike a solar eclipse, everyone on the night side of Earth can see a lunar eclipse, all at the same time.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Lunar_07
data.value: Now you try. On the left page, choose a different path for the Moon through Earth's shadow, and watch how the eclipse changes.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Lunar_08
data.value: If the Moon only passes through the penumbra, it just dims a little. It's so faint that most people never notice.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Obj_Antumbra
data.value: The antumbra, beyond the tip of the umbra. From here, the Moon looks a little smaller than the Sun, so you see a ring of sunlight around it. That's an annular eclipse.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Obj_Earth
data.value: Earth. The side facing the Sun is in daytime. Its shadow points away from the Sun, and at full moon the Moon can pass through it.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Obj_Ecliptic
data.value: The plane of Earth's orbit, called the plane of the ecliptic. Seen from Earth, the Sun always moves along it.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Obj_FullMoon
data.value: Full moon. Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, and we see the Moon's whole lit side. Only now can a lunar eclipse happen.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Obj_Moon
data.value: The Moon. At new moon its shadow can fall on Earth, and at full moon it can move into Earth's shadow. In the side views you can drag it around its orbit.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Obj_MoonOrbit
data.value: The Moon's orbit, tilted by about five degrees, drawn steeper here. The solid half is above the plane of Earth's orbit, and the dashed half is below.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Obj_NewMoon
data.value: New moon. The Moon is between the Sun and Earth, and its lit side faces away from us. Only now can a solar eclipse happen.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Obj_NodeLine
data.value: The line of nodes, joining the two points where the Moon crosses the plane of Earth's orbit. When it points at the Sun, it's eclipse season.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Obj_Observer
data.value: This is you, on Earth's day side, where it's around noon. On the left page, you can move north or south and see how the eclipse looks from there.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Obj_Penumbra
data.value: The penumbra, the lighter shadow around the umbra. From here, only part of the Sun is hidden.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Obj_Season
data.value: An eclipse season. While Earth is on this stretch of its orbit, the line of nodes points close to the Sun, and eclipses can happen.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Obj_Sun
data.value: The Sun. It's about four hundred times wider than the Moon, and about four hundred times farther away. That's why the two look almost the same size in our sky.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Obj_Umbra
data.value: The umbra, the darkest part of a shadow. From inside it, the Sun is completely hidden.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Seasons_01
data.value: If there's a new moon every month, why isn't there a solar eclipse every month? Here's Earth going round the Sun over a year, with the Moon going round Earth.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Seasons_02
data.value: Look at the Moon's orbit. It's tilted, really by about five degrees, drawn steeper here so you can see it. The solid blue half is above the plane of Earth's orbit, and the dashed orange half is below it.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Seasons_03
data.value: The Moon crosses the plane of Earth's orbit at two points, called nodes. The line joining them is the line of nodes.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Seasons_04
data.value: Think about it. In most months, what happens at new moon?

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Seasons_05
data.value: Most of the time, the Moon passes just above or below the Sun, so its shadow misses Earth. For an eclipse, the new or full moon has to fall close to a node.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Seasons_06
data.value: That only happens when the line of nodes points towards the Sun: twice a year, for about five weeks each time. These are the eclipse seasons.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Seasons_07
data.value: Every eclipse season brings at least one solar eclipse somewhere on Earth, and often a lunar eclipse too. That's why there are between four and seven eclipses every year.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Seasons_08
data.value: Now you try. Drag across the picture to move through the year, and find the next eclipse season.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Seasons_09
data.value: The line of nodes slowly turns, so the eclipse seasons come about nineteen days earlier each year.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Solar_01
data.value: This is a view from far above. The Sun is on the left, Earth on the right, and the Moon goes round Earth. The sizes and distances aren't to scale, or the Sun would be far off the screen.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Solar_02
data.value: The Moon goes round Earth about once a month. When it passes between the Sun and Earth, we call it new moon.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Solar_03
data.value: Like everything in sunlight, the Moon casts a shadow. The darkest part is called the umbra. Inside it, the Sun is completely hidden.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Solar_04
data.value: Around it is a lighter shadow, the penumbra. From there, the Moon covers only part of the Sun.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Solar_05
data.value: Now the Moon's shadow falls on Earth. Think about it: if you stood right inside the umbra, what would you see?

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Solar_06
data.value: A total solar eclipse. The sky goes dark, bright stars come out, and the Sun's pearly corona glows around the black Moon. The umbra only covers a narrow strip of Earth, so most people see a partial eclipse instead.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Solar_07
data.value: The Moon's distance from Earth changes a little. When it's farther away, its umbra is too short to reach Earth. Then we see an annular eclipse: a ring of fire around the Moon.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Solar_08
data.value: Now you try. Drag the Moon around its orbit, and watch its shadow sweep across Earth.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Solar_09
data.value: So a solar eclipse can only happen at new moon. At full moon, it's the Moon's turn to move into Earth's shadow. That's a lunar eclipse.

data.name: Narr_Expand_History_01
data.value: This horn tells the story of our universe. Its height shows how big the universe was at each moment. The green ring is today.

data.name: Narr_Expand_History_02
data.value: At the far left is the Big Bang, thirteen point eight billion years ago. Everything we can see was squeezed together, unbelievably hot and dense.

data.name: Narr_Expand_History_03
data.value: The first moments were so busy that we need a different clock, where each step is ten times longer than the one before. Within about three minutes, the first atomic nuclei formed: hydrogen and helium.

data.name: Narr_Expand_History_04
data.value: Look through the window. For hundreds of thousands of years, the universe was a glowing fog. Light kept bumping into particles and couldn't get anywhere.

data.name: Narr_Expand_History_05
data.value: Then, about three hundred and eighty thousand years after the Big Bang, it cooled enough for atoms to form, and suddenly light could travel freely. We still see that light today, stretched into microwaves.

data.name: Narr_Expand_History_06
data.value: After a long dark age, the first stars switched on, a couple of hundred million years after the Big Bang. Soon, galaxies began to grow.

data.name: Narr_Expand_History_07
data.value: For billions of years, gravity slowed the expansion down. But about six billion years ago, it started to speed up again. See how the horn begins to flare? We call the cause dark energy.

data.name: Narr_Expand_History_08
data.value: What do you think? Which universe would end in a big crunch?

data.name: Narr_Expand_History_09
data.value: With much more matter, gravity would win. The universe would stop growing, fall back, and end hot and crushed together. That's a big crunch.

data.name: Narr_Expand_History_10
data.value: Our universe, though, will keep expanding faster and faster. Distant galaxies will slip out of sight, and the sky beyond our neighbourhood will slowly go dark.

data.name: Narr_Expand_History_11
data.value: Your turn. Drag along the horn to travel through time, or pick another universe to compare.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Hubble_01
data.value: Here's a patch of the universe, about two billion light-years across. Each dot is a whole cluster of galaxies, and the golden one in the middle is our home, the Milky Way. Watch what happens as time runs forward.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Hubble_02
data.value: Everything is moving away from us. But look closely at the galaxies themselves. Are they getting bigger? No! They stay the same size. Only the space between them grows.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Hubble_03
data.value: These tape measures show how far away three galaxies are, and how fast each one is moving away. Compare them. A galaxy twice as far away is moving twice as fast.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Hubble_04
data.value: This is Hubble's law: speed equals the expansion rate times distance. In 1929, Edwin Hubble showed it with real galaxies, and Georges Lemaître had worked it out two years before.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Hubble_05
data.value: Quick question. One galaxy is three times farther away than another. How fast is it moving away from us?

data.name: Narr_Expand_Hubble_06
data.value: Now let's lay an older photo underneath, from about six billion years ago, lined up on the Milky Way. See the blue circles? Every galaxy has moved straight away from us, and the farther ones have moved the most.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Hubble_07
data.value: So, are we at the centre of the universe? Let's move house to another galaxy and find out. From here, everything is moving away too! Every galaxy sees exactly the same thing. There is no centre.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Hubble_08
data.value: Here's a better way to picture it. Imagine a grid drawn on space itself, like the lines on a rubber sheet. The galaxies sit still in their squares. It's the squares that grow.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Hubble_09
data.value: The label up here shows how long ago this is, and how big the universe was compared with today. In six billion years, every distance has grown by about two thirds.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Hubble_10
data.value: Your turn. Click any galaxy to live there, or drag left and right to run time backwards and forwards.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Obj_Andromeda
data.value: In about four and a half billion years, the Andromeda galaxy will merge with the Milky Way. Close by, gravity beats the expansion.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Obj_Arriving
data.value: The same lines as they arrive from the galaxy. Every one has slid to longer wavelengths by the same factor. That's the redshift.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Obj_Arrow
data.value: Each arrow shows how fast a galaxy is moving away from home. A galaxy twice as far away has an arrow twice as long.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Obj_Axis
data.value: The time axis. When it's even, the first million years hide in the tip of the horn. In powers of ten, each step is ten times longer than the last, so even the first minutes get some room.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Obj_BigBang
data.value: The Big Bang wasn't an explosion at one spot. It was the moment when everything, everywhere, was squeezed together, hot and dense, and began to expand.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Obj_Clock
data.value: How long ago this moment is, and how big the universe was then compared with today. About six billion years ago, it was six tenths of today's size.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Obj_Cmb
data.value: About three hundred and eighty thousand years in, the universe cooled to about three thousand degrees, atoms formed, and light was set free. That light is the cosmic microwave background.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Obj_Crunch
data.value: The Big Crunch: everything falls back together, hotter and hotter, like the Big Bang running backwards.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Obj_Cursor
data.value: The moment you're looking at. Drag along the horn to move it, and the window below shows what space looked like then.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Obj_DistNow
data.value: How far away the galaxy is at this moment. This distance keeps growing the whole time the light is travelling.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Obj_DistThen
data.value: Where the galaxy was when the light set off. Back then, it was much closer to us than it is today.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Obj_Drift
data.value: Here, the space between the light and us grows faster than the light can cross it, so for a while the light is actually carried away from us. Later, the light catches up and starts to gain.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Obj_FirstStars
data.value: A couple of hundred million years in, clouds of gas collapsed and lit up the first stars, ending the dark ages.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Obj_Galaxy
data.value: Clicking a galaxy makes it your new home. Galaxies don't stretch: their own gravity holds them together, so only the space between them grows.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Obj_Ghost
data.value: The blue circles show where the galaxies were at the start, lined up on home. Every galaxy has moved straight outwards, and the far ones have moved the most.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Obj_Grid
data.value: A grid drawn on space itself. As space stretches, the squares grow, and the galaxies ride along in their own squares.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Obj_Home
data.value: This is home, the galaxy we look out from. From any home, every other galaxy seems to rush away, and the farther it is, the faster it goes.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Obj_Infrared
data.value: Infrared is light with waves too long for our eyes. We feel it as warmth. Light from distant galaxies ends up here.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Obj_Jades
data.value: The galaxy JADES-GS-z14-0, seen by the James Webb telescope as it was about three hundred million years after the Big Bang. It's one of the most distant galaxies ever confirmed.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Obj_Jwst
data.value: The James Webb Space Telescope sees infrared, from just past red out to much longer waves. That's where the light of the first galaxies arrives.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Obj_Lab
data.value: These are the lines this kind of gas gives off in a laboratory here on Earth, standing still. They're the ruler we compare with.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Obj_Law
data.value: Hubble's law: speed equals the expansion rate H, times distance. H was bigger in the past. Today it's close to seventy kilometres a second for every megaparsec, which is about three point three million light-years.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Obj_Light
data.value: The light, drawn as a short train of waves. The waves stretch along with the space they travel through, so the longer the trip, the longer the waves.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Obj_Line
data.value: Hydrogen's blue-green line, called H-beta. Where it lands on arrival tells us how much the universe has grown since the light set off.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Obj_Noon
data.value: About ten billion years ago, galaxies were making stars faster than ever before or since. Astronomers call it cosmic noon.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Obj_Now
data.value: Today, thirteen point eight billion years after the Big Bang. Every universe here is set to today's size and today's expansion rate.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Obj_Nuclei
data.value: About three minutes in, protons and neutrons fused into the first nuclei, mostly hydrogen and helium. Stars are still made mostly of them today.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Obj_Patch
data.value: A window into a small patch of space at this moment. Earlier on, the galaxies were packed closer together. Later, they're spread farther apart.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Obj_Protons
data.value: In the first ten-thousandth of a second, at about a trillion degrees, tiny quarks clumped together into protons and neutrons.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Obj_RedshiftClock
data.value: How old and how big the universe is while the light travels. It keeps growing the whole way.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Obj_Ruler
data.value: A tape measure from home to a galaxy, with its distance and its speed away from us. Divide the speed by the distance, and every galaxy gives the same number: the expansion rate.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Obj_Size
data.value: The height of the horn is the size of the universe compared with today. Any two galaxies are that much farther apart, or closer together.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Obj_Source
data.value: This is the galaxy the light comes from. It keeps moving away from us the whole time its light is on the way.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Obj_Space
data.value: These lines cut the space between the galaxy and us into equal pieces. Watch them spread apart. That's space itself stretching.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Obj_Speedup
data.value: About six billion years ago, dark energy took over from gravity, and the expansion began to speed up.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Obj_Sun
data.value: Four point six billion years ago, our Sun and Earth formed from a cloud of gas and dust.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Obj_Travel
data.value: How far the light has come so far, and how much it has been stretched. In one year of travel, light covers one light-year.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Obj_Turnaround
data.value: In a universe with too much matter, gravity stops the expansion right here. This is as big as it will ever get.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Obj_Us
data.value: The Milky Way, where we are. This is where the light finally arrives and goes into our telescopes.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Obj_Visible
data.value: The colours our eyes can see, from violet to red. Redshift pushes light from here towards the red end, and beyond.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Redshift_01
data.value: Far away on the left is a galaxy. When this light set off, the universe was only half the size it is today. Let's follow the light all the way to us.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Redshift_02
data.value: Here's the light, drawn as a wave. Keep an eye on the gap between its crests as it travels.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Redshift_03
data.value: These lines mark out the space between the galaxy and us. Space keeps stretching while the light is on its way, and the waves stretch right along with it.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Redshift_04
data.value: Meanwhile, the galaxy keeps getting farther away. By the time the light reaches us, the galaxy is much farther away than when the light left.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Redshift_05
data.value: Now the light has arrived. Every wave is twice as long as when it set off. Longer waves look redder, so we call this redshift.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Redshift_06
data.value: Astronomers measure redshift with lines in the spectrum. Look: hydrogen's blue-green line has slid all the way past red, into the infrared.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Redshift_07
data.value: Try this one. Light from a galaxy arrives stretched to three times its length. How big was the universe when the light set off?

data.name: Narr_Expand_Redshift_08
data.value: Now a galaxy near the edge of what we can see. Its light set off when the universe was less than three hundred million years old, and it's stretched about fifteen times. Even its ultraviolet light arrives as infrared. That's why the James Webb telescope looks in infrared.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Redshift_09
data.value: This light has been travelling for more than thirteen billion years. But the galaxy is now over thirty billion light-years away, because space kept stretching behind the light.

data.name: Narr_Expand_Redshift_10
data.value: Your turn. Pick another galaxy, or drag along the chart to choose when the light set off.

data.name: Narr_Green_Glass_01
data.value: Here's a small glass greenhouse and a car, parked in the summer sun. Look at the readings: inside both, it's far warmer than the air outside.

data.name: Narr_Green_Glass_02
data.value: Sunlight passes through the glass easily, and warms the floor and the plants inside.

data.name: Narr_Green_Glass_03
data.value: The warm floor glows in the infrared. Glass doesn't let those rays through: it soaks them up, warms, and glows half of that heat back inside.

data.name: Narr_Green_Glass_04
data.value: So what do you think keeps a greenhouse warm, most of all?

data.name: Narr_Green_Glass_05
data.value: Mostly, it's the lid. Warm air rises off the floor and gathers under the roof. With nowhere to go, the heat builds up. Trapping the infrared adds only a few degrees more.

data.name: Narr_Green_Glass_06
data.value: Open the roof vents. The warm air escapes through the top, cooler air sinks in, and the greenhouse cools down a lot.

data.name: Narr_Green_Glass_07
data.value: In 1909, Robert Wood tried a roof of rock salt, which lets infrared out. It cooled the greenhouse far less than opening the vents. The air has no lid at all: its greenhouse effect comes only from catching the infrared.

data.name: Narr_Green_Glass_08
data.value: A parked car is a greenhouse too. In the sun it can be twenty degrees warmer inside within an hour, even on a mild day, and opening a window a crack hardly helps. Never leave a child or a pet in a parked car.

data.name: Narr_Green_Glass_09
data.value: Your turn. Drag across the picture to turn the day, or click the roof vents or the car's window, and watch the temperatures change.

data.name: Narr_Green_Molecules_01
data.value: Why do only some gases catch heat rays? Start with nitrogen, most of the air. It's two identical atoms. When they stretch, the charge stays perfectly even, so light has nothing to push on, and every ray passes straight through.

data.name: Narr_Green_Molecules_02
data.value: Carbon dioxide is different. Its oxygen atoms pull the electrons a little, so they're slightly negative, and the carbon slightly positive. But when it stretches evenly, the charges stay balanced. Still no catch.

data.name: Narr_Green_Molecules_03
data.value: Now watch it bend. The charge swings up and down: see the gold arrow. Light with the same rhythm can push on that swinging charge.

data.name: Narr_Green_Molecules_04
data.value: The bend wiggles in step with infrared of about fifteen micrometres. What happens when a ray like that comes by?

data.name: Narr_Green_Molecules_05
data.value: It's caught, and the molecule wiggles harder. A moment later, it either bumps into its neighbours, warming the air, or sends a ray out again in a random direction.

data.name: Narr_Green_Molecules_06
data.value: Below is the ground's glow by wavelength. Carbon dioxide's band at fifteen micrometres sits close to its peak. That's why so little carbon dioxide, about four hundredths of a percent of the air, matters so much.

data.name: Narr_Green_Molecules_07
data.value: Between eight and thirteen micrometres, little is caught by anything: this is the atmospheric window. Through it, about a tenth of the ground's glow escapes straight to space.

data.name: Narr_Green_Molecules_08
data.value: Water is bent even at rest, so every one of its wiggles catches light, and it can spin as well. Water vapour is the strongest greenhouse gas of all, but how much the air holds depends on its temperature.

data.name: Narr_Green_Molecules_09
data.value: Your turn. Pick another gas or another wiggle; you can also click a line on the spectrum. Watch which rays get caught.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_Air
data.value: The air is about seventy-eight percent nitrogen and twenty-one percent oxygen, and both let heat rays through. A tiny share of greenhouse gases does all the catching.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_BudgetAirSun
data.value: Sunlight taken in by the air itself, mostly by water vapour, ozone and clouds: seventy-eight watts per square metre.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_BudgetBack
data.value: Back radiation: three hundred and thirty-three watts per square metre of infrared, sent down by the greenhouse gases and the clouds. This is the greenhouse effect at work.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_BudgetFromAir
data.value: Infrared sent to space from high in the air and from the tops of clouds: about a hundred and ninety-nine watts per square metre. With the window, it balances the sunlight kept.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_BudgetGlow
data.value: The ground's glow: about three hundred and ninety-six watts per square metre of infrared, more than twice the sunlight it takes in. It can glow that much only because the air sends heat back.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_BudgetIn
data.value: Sunlight coming in: three hundred and forty-one watts per square metre, averaged over the whole globe, day and night.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_BudgetReflected
data.value: Sunlight reflected straight back to space by clouds, air, ice and the ground: about thirty percent of it.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_BudgetRising
data.value: Heat carried up by rising warm air, and by evaporating water, which gives its heat back when it condenses into clouds: about ninety-seven watts per square metre.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_BudgetSurface
data.value: Sunlight taken in by the ground: a hundred and sixty-one watts per square metre, less than half of what arrives.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_BudgetWindow
data.value: Infrared that goes straight from the ground out to space, through the atmospheric window: about forty watts per square metre, a tenth of the ground's glow.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_Car
data.value: A car shut in the sun heats up like a greenhouse: sunlight gets in through the windows, and the hot air is trapped inside. Never leave a child or a pet in a parked car.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_CarWindow
data.value: A window open a crack lets very little air through, so the car hardly cools. Click it to open or shut it.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_Clouds
data.value: Clouds work both ways. Their white tops reflect sunlight back to space, cooling the planet, while their undersides send heat back down, warming it. Overall, today's clouds cool Earth a little.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_Dipole
data.value: The gold arrow is the dipole: which way the molecule's charge leans. Light can only push on a molecule whose dipole swings back and forth as it wiggles.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_Emission
data.value: This is roughly the height the heat finally leaves from on its way to space. The air there is about minus eighteen degrees, the temperature a planet with no greenhouse gases would have. More carbon dioxide lifts this height.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_Floor
