data.name: Rain_Chart_DarkBand
data.value: dark band: no light comes out

data.name: Rain_Chart_Deviation_Caption
data.value: Where the light comes out, by where it went in

data.name: Rain_Chart_Deviation_Note
data.value: Across: where the ray enters, from the centre (0) to the edge (1). Up: its angle from the point opposite the Sun. The primary curve tops out at 42° and turns back, so many rays pile up there; the secondary bottoms out at 51°. Nothing comes out in between.

data.name: Rain_Chart_Prism_Caption
data.value: How far the prism turns each colour

data.name: Rain_Chart_Prism_Note
data.value: Across: the angle the beam meets the first face at. Each colour has an angle of least turn (circle), where it crosses the prism symmetrically. Violet is always turned more than red; too flat a beam cannot get out of the second face.

data.name: Rain_Chart_Profile_Caption
data.value: Brightness by angle from the point opposite the Sun

data.name: Rain_Chart_Profile_Note
data.value: Worked out from rays through drops of this size, in the colours they make: the sky glows inside the primary, the bow peaks at 42°, then the dark band, then the fainter secondary at 51° (square-root scale, so the faint parts show).

data.name: Rain_Chart_Side_Caption
data.value: From the side: which drops send you which colour

data.name: Rain_Chart_Side_Note
data.value: Every drop sends red out at about 42° and violet at about 40.6°. So the red you see comes from drops a little higher up and the violet from drops a little lower: red is on the outside of the bow. In the secondary bow it is the other way round.

data.name: Rain_Chart_Surface_Caption
data.value: Bent angle and reflection, by the beam's angle

data.name: Rain_Chart_Surface_Note
data.value: The dashed line would be no bending at all. Going in, the bent ray is always nearer the normal; coming out it leaves further from it, until past the critical angle nothing leaves. Straight on only a few percent is reflected; toward grazing it climbs steeply.

data.name: Rain_Chart_ToAntisolar
data.value: to the point opposite the Sun

data.name: Rain_Diagram_Antisolar
data.value: Opposite the Sun: your head's shadow

data.name: Rain_Diagram_Out
data.value: {0} of the light comes out here

data.name: Rain_DragHint_Drop
data.value: Drag up or down to pick where the ray enters.

data.name: Rain_DragHint_Refraction_Prism
data.value: Drag to aim the lamp at the prism.

data.name: Rain_DragHint_Refraction_Surface
data.value: Drag anywhere to aim the lamp, or let it sweep.

data.name: Rain_DragHint_Sky
data.value: Drag the bow up or down: a lower bow means a higher Sun.

data.name: Rain_Drop_Edge_Primary
data.value: Past the rainbow ray the angle turns back and gets smaller again. So no light from a single reflection comes out wider than 42°: outside the bow the sky is darker.

data.name: Rain_Drop_Edge_Secondary
data.value: Past its rainbow ray the angle grows again. No twice-reflected light comes out at less than 51°, which leaves a dark band between the two bows.

data.name: Rain_Drop_Fact1
data.value: René Descartes worked out the 42° in 1637 by following rays through a drop one by one, much as this chapter does.

data.name: Rain_Drop_Fact2
data.value: Each drop sends just one colour to your eye. The bow you see is made of millions of drops, a different set for each colour, and the person next to you sees a different bow.

data.name: Rain_Drop_Fact3
data.value: Light that reflects three or four times inside makes bows near the Sun, very faint and drowned in its glare; they were only photographed in 2011.

data.name: Rain_Drop_Fact4
data.value: Rainbow light is strongly polarised along the bow: through polarising sunglasses, parts of a rainbow can vanish as you tilt your head.

data.name: Rain_Drop_Fact5
data.value: Faint extra pink and green bands just inside a bright bow (supernumerary bows) cannot be explained by rays at all: they come from light waves interfering, which helped prove light is a wave.

data.name: Rain_Drop_Middle_Primary
data.value: A ray through the middle comes almost straight back. Further out it comes back at a wider and wider angle, but not past about 42°.

data.name: Rain_Drop_Middle_Secondary
data.value: With two reflections a ray near the middle carries on almost forward. Further out it comes back nearer and nearer the Sun's direction, down to about 51°.

data.name: Rain_Drop_Note
data.value: Sunlight from the left through one drop. A ray bends going in, reflects off the back and bends again coming out, heading back toward someone with the Sun behind them.

data.name: Rain_Drop_Rainbow_Primary
data.value: About 0.86 of the way out, the ray comes back at its widest, 42°. Here moving the ray in or out hardly changes where it goes, so the light from a wide band of the drop piles up at this one angle: that bright pile-up is the rainbow.

data.name: Rain_Drop_Rainbow_Secondary
data.value: About 0.95 of the way out, the twice-reflected ray turns back least, at 51°. Light piles up here too: the secondary bow. Two reflections lose more light, so it is fainter.

data.name: Rain_Drop_Secondary_Note
data.value: Sunlight from the left through one drop. A ray entering low bends going in, reflects off the back twice and bends again coming out of the top, heading back toward someone with the Sun behind them.

data.name: Rain_Drop_Secondary_Subtitle
data.value: In, reflected twice, and out at 51°

data.name: Rain_Home_AllDay
data.value: {0} today: the Sun stays below {1}° all day, so a rainbow can show at any hour when rain falls opposite the Sun.

data.name: Rain_Home_Never
data.value: {0} today: the Sun never gets below {1}° while it is up.

data.name: Rain_Home_Window
data.value: {0} today: the Sun is higher than {1}° from {2} to {3}, too high for a rainbow. Look for one earlier or later in the day.

data.name: Rain_Lesson_Refraction_Choice1
data.value: It all reflects back into the water

data.name: Rain_Lesson_Refraction_Choice2
data.value: It goes straight out without bending

data.name: Rain_Prism_Bent_Description
data.value: One colour gives one spot on the screen. Going in it bends toward the face's normal, coming out away from the other face's normal: both turn it down toward the prism's base.

data.name: Rain_Prism_Least_Description
data.value: The ray crosses the prism parallel to its base, symmetrically. Turning the prism either way only turns the light more. Measuring this angle is how the index of glass is found.

data.name: Rain_Prism_Split_Description
data.value: Each colour has its own index: violet is slowed most and bent most, red least. The second face bends them the same way again, so the colours fan out into a spectrum.

data.name: Rain_Prism_Trapped_Description
data.value: The beam meets the second face past the critical angle and is all reflected; it leaves through the base instead. Binoculars use prisms this way as mirrors.

data.name: Rain_Refraction_Prism_Fact1
data.value: Newton split sunlight with a prism in 1666, then put the colours back together with a second prism, showing that white light is a mix of all colours.

data.name: Rain_Refraction_Prism_Fact2
data.value: Dispersion (each colour bent differently) is why cheap lenses give coloured fringes; camera lenses pair two glasses to cancel it.

data.name: Rain_Refraction_Prism_Fact3
data.value: A diamond spreads colours about three times more than window glass: the flashes of colour it throws are called its fire.

data.name: Rain_Refraction_Prism_Fact4
data.value: Violet light slows down more in glass than red, which is why it is bent more. In empty space every colour travels at the same speed.

data.name: Rain_Refraction_Prism_Fact5
data.value: Binoculars and periscopes use prisms as mirrors: past the critical angle a glass face reflects all the light, better than a silvered mirror.

data.name: Rain_Refraction_Prism_Note
data.value: Bent once going in and again coming out, both times the same way. Violet slows a little more than red, so it is bent a little more.

data.name: Rain_Refraction_Prism_Subtitle
data.value: A prism splits white light into its colours

data.name: Rain_Refraction_Surface_Fact1
data.value: Snell's law: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂. It was found by Ibn Sahl in Baghdad in 984, and again by Willebrord Snellius in 1621.

data.name: Rain_Refraction_Surface_Fact2
data.value: A straw in a glass of water looks broken, and a pool looks shallower than it is (about three quarters as deep), because light bends as it leaves the water.

data.name: Rain_Refraction_Surface_Fact3
data.value: A diamond's index of 2.42 gives it a critical angle of only 24°, so light that enters is reflected round inside many times before it gets out: that is its sparkle.

data.name: Rain_Refraction_Surface_Fact4
data.value: Optical fibres carry the internet as light kept inside thin glass by total internal reflection, round bends and under oceans.

data.name: Rain_Refraction_Surface_Fact5
data.value: Light's colour is set by its frequency, which never changes: in water the waves are only closer together. A fish sees the same colours you do.

data.name: Rain_Refraction_Surface_Note
data.value: Light is slower in water (by 1.33 times), glass (1.5) and diamond (2.4). The crests are drawn more than 10 000 times further apart than real light's.

data.name: Rain_Refraction_Surface_Subtitle
data.value: Light bends where it changes speed

data.name: Rain_Sky_Fact1
data.value: A rainbow is not in any one place: it is a direction, 42° from the point opposite the Sun. Walk toward it and it moves with you.

data.name: Rain_Sky_Fact2
data.value: From a plane or a mountain top, where there is rain below you as well, you can see the whole circle.

data.name: Rain_Sky_Fact3
data.value: The sky inside a rainbow is brighter than outside, and between the two bows is a darker band, named after Alexander of Aphrodisias, who described it around 200 AD.

data.name: Rain_Sky_Fact4
data.value: Fog and cloud droplets are so small that the colours smear together into a white fog bow; moonlight makes a faint moonbow that looks white to the eye.

data.name: Rain_Sky_Fact5
data.value: Because the bow's centre is as far below the horizon as the Sun is above it, from the ground you only see rainbows when the Sun is less than about 42° high (51° for the secondary).

data.name: Rain_Sky_Low_Description
data.value: The point opposite the Sun is on the horizon too, so half of each circle is in the sky: the tallest bows come early in the morning and late in the afternoon. Low sunlight is red, and so is the bow.

data.name: Rain_Sky_Low_Title
data.value: Sun on the horizon: a half circle

data.name: Rain_Sky_Note
data.value: Looking at falling rain with the Sun behind you. Colours and brightness are worked out from rays through the drops, coloured by the sunlight reaching them.

data.name: Rain_Sky_SecondaryOnly_Description
data.value: With the Sun more than 42° up, the primary bow is below the horizon. The secondary, 51° round, still peeks over it for a few more degrees.

data.name: Rain_Sky_Sinking_Description
data.value: The bow is always centred on the point opposite the Sun, as far below the horizon as the Sun is above it. The higher the Sun, the less of the circle is left above the ground.

data.name: Rain_Sky_Sinking_Title
data.value: The bow sinks as the Sun climbs

data.name: Rain_Sky_Subtitle
data.value: A circle of light 42° round your shadow's head

data.name: Rain_Sky_TooHigh_Description
data.value: Both circles are below the horizon. Around midday in summer you will not see a rainbow from the ground, but you can from a plane, or in the spray of a garden hose looking down.

data.name: Rain_Spread_Note
data.value: The colours are drawn spread five times wider than they really are, so they can be seen; the numbers are real.

data.name: Rain_Stat_Antisolar_Value
data.value: {0}° (as far down as the Sun is up)

data.name: Rain_Stat_Polarised_Value
data.value: {0}% of the bow's light, along the bow

data.name: Rain_Stat_Top_Value
data.value: {0}° up · {1}% of its circle in the sky

data.name: Rain_Surface_Away_Description
data.value: Coming out into air the light speeds up, so the side that leaves first runs ahead and the beam swings away from the normal. The steeper it comes, the more it bends.

data.name: Rain_Surface_Grazing_Description
data.value: Close to the critical angle the light that gets out barely leaves the surface, and more and more of it is reflected back inside.

data.name: Rain_Surface_Straight_Description
data.value: Along the normal the whole wavefront slows down at the same moment, so nothing turns it. It only slows down, and its waves close up.

data.name: Rain_Surface_Total_Description
data.value: Past the critical angle the light would have to leave at more than 90°, so none gets out: the surface becomes a perfect mirror. Optical fibres and the sparkle of diamonds work this way.

data.name: Rain_Surface_Toward_Description
data.value: One side of each wavefront reaches the surface first and slows down first, while the other side is still fast. The front swings round, like a row of marchers stepping from road onto mud: the beam turns toward the normal.

data.name: Retro_Above_Fact1
data.value: Average orbital speeds: Mercury 47 km/s, Venus 35, Earth 30, Mars 24, Jupiter 13, Saturn 10. The inner planet always overtakes.

data.name: Retro_Above_Fact2
data.value: When you overtake a slower car on the motorway, it seems to slide backwards against faraway hills, though both cars keep driving forwards.

data.name: Retro_Above_Fact3
data.value: Seen from above Earth's north pole, every planet goes round the Sun anticlockwise. That is why their usual drift among the stars is eastward.

data.name: Retro_Above_Fact4
data.value: The farther away the planet, the smaller its backward step: Mars backs up some 10 to 20 degrees, Jupiter about 10, Saturn about 7.

data.name: Retro_Above_Fact5
data.value: Mercury and Venus go backwards as they pass between Earth and the Sun, just when they move from the evening sky to the morning sky.

data.name: Retro_Above_Note
data.value: Seen from above the Sun's north; orbits and distances to scale (the stars are really far, far farther away).

data.name: Retro_Chart_Note
data.value: The planet's ecliptic longitude through the loop: rising means moving east; the orange dip is the retrograde stretch, the circles the two stations.

data.name: Retro_Epicycle_Earth_Inner
data.value: With Earth held still, the planet circles the Sun while the Sun circles Earth: the deferent carries the Sun, and the epicycle is the planet's own orbit.

data.name: Retro_Epicycle_Earth_Outer
data.value: With Earth held still, the planet's path is its own orbit plus a copy of Earth's orbit: a circle carried round on a circle, just as Ptolemy drew it.

data.name: Retro_Epicycle_Fact1
data.value: Ptolemy's Almagest, written in Alexandria around AD 150, predicted the planets with deferents, epicycles and the equant. It was used for some 1,400 years.

data.name: Retro_Epicycle_Fact2
data.value: Copernicus's book of 1543 put the Sun in the middle and explained the loops as Earth's own motion showing up in the sky.

data.name: Retro_Epicycle_Fact3
data.value: In Ptolemy's model the epicycles of Mars, Jupiter and Saturn all turned once a year, in step with the Sun: a clue nobody could explain until the Sun went in the middle.

data.name: Retro_Epicycle_Fact4
data.value: 13 Venus years are almost exactly 8 Earth years, so the pattern Venus draws as seen from Earth repeats every eight years.

data.name: Retro_Epicycle_Fact5
data.value: Kepler swapped circles for ellipses in 1609, and the planets finally matched Tycho Brahe's careful measurements.

data.name: Retro_Epicycle_Note
data.value: The planet's real positions with Earth or the Sun held still in the middle; distances to scale.

data.name: Retro_Epicycle_Subtitle
data.value: {0} with Earth or the Sun at the centre

data.name: Retro_Epicycle_Sun_Inner
data.value: With the Sun held still, the planet simply goes round inside Earth's orbit. The loops came from watching it from a moving Earth.

data.name: Retro_Epicycle_Sun_Outer
data.value: With the Sun held still, each planet simply goes round its own orbit. The loops were Earth's own motion showing up in what we see.

data.name: Retro_Epicycle_Sun_Title
data.value: Sun held still: {0} just goes round

data.name: Retro_Hint_Above
data.value: Drag Earth round its orbit to move through the days.

data.name: Retro_Hint_Epicycle
data.value: Drag sideways to run time forwards or back.

data.name: Retro_Hint_Sky
data.value: Drag across the sky to move through the days.

data.name: Retro_Lesson_Above_Choice1
data.value: Earth overtakes it on the inside lane

data.name: Retro_Lesson_Epicycle_Choice1
data.value: The loops untangle into plain orbits

data.name: Retro_Lesson_Sky_Choice1
data.value: It turns back west for a while

data.name: Retro_Loops_Note
data.value: The dates are when the planet stops and turns, worked out from the planets' orbits (good to a day or two).

data.name: Retro_Obj_Marks
data.value: Lines of sight, step by step

data.name: Retro_Obj_StationDirect
data.value: Second station: it turns east again

data.name: Retro_Orientation_North
data.value: In the sky strip east is on the left, as you see it facing the planet from {0} (northern hemisphere).

data.name: Retro_Orientation_South
data.value: In the sky strip east is on the right, as you see it facing the planet from {0} (southern hemisphere).

data.name: Retro_Pattern_Jupiter
data.value: 11 loops in 12 years, about one in each zodiac constellation

data.name: Retro_Pattern_Venus
data.value: 5 loops in 8 years: a five-petalled flower

data.name: Retro_Phase_Pro_Inner
data.value: Its usual way among the stars: east, as it goes round the Sun, though it never strays far from the Sun in our sky.

data.name: Retro_Phase_Pro_Outer
data.value: Its usual way: it goes round the Sun more slowly than Earth, and night after night it moves a little east against the stars.

data.name: Retro_Phase_Retro_Inner
data.value: It is passing between Earth and the Sun, overtaking us on the inside lane, so it seems to slide back west against the stars.

data.name: Retro_Phase_Retro_Outer
data.value: Earth is overtaking it on the inside lane, so it seems to slide back west against the far stars, though it is still going round the Sun as always.

data.name: Retro_Phase_Station_Inner
data.value: Seen from Earth, its sideways motion cancels out for a few days, so it seems to stand still among the stars before it turns.

data.name: Retro_Phase_Station_Outer
data.value: Earth is catching up with it on the inside lane. For these days the two motions cancel out and it hardly moves against the stars.

data.name: Retro_Sky_Fact1
data.value: Mars goes backwards about every 26 months, for two to three months. Jupiter does it every 13 months and Saturn every 12½, each for four to five months.

data.name: Retro_Sky_Fact2
data.value: Mercury goes retrograde three or four times a year, for about three weeks; Venus only every 19 months, for about six weeks.

data.name: Retro_Sky_Fact3
data.value: An outer planet is in the middle of its loop at opposition, opposite the Sun: up all night, at its closest and brightest. That is the best time to look.

data.name: Retro_Sky_Fact4
data.value: Whether the path makes a loop or a zigzag depends on the planet's tilted orbit: if it crosses the plane of Earth's orbit during the loop, the path folds into a Z.

data.name: Retro_Sky_Fact5
data.value: Retrograde motion changes nothing about the planet, or about us. It is only how its path looks from a moving Earth.

data.name: Retro_Sky_Note
data.value: A strip of sky along the ecliptic, longitude and latitude to the same scale; real planet positions and real stars.

data.name: Retro_Today_Next
data.value: {0} isn't retrograde today; its next loop starts {1} (in {2} days).

data.name: Seasons_Beam_Caption
data.value: The same beam of sunlight on the ground

data.name: Seasons_Beam_None
data.value: Today the Sun does not rise here, so no sunlight reaches the ground.

data.name: Seasons_Beam_Text
data.value: The lower the Sun, the larger the patch the same sunlight spreads over. Today at noon each patch of ground gets {0:P0} of the light it would get with the Sun straight overhead.

data.name: Seasons_DayLength_Caption
data.value: Hours of daylight through the year

data.name: Seasons_DistanceChart_Caption
data.value: Distance to the Sun (million km), and daily sunlight in the north and the south

data.name: Seasons_DistanceChart_Note
data.value: Earth is closest to the Sun in January, yet the north has winter then: the tilt matters far more than the distance.

data.name: Seasons_Distance_Fact1
data.value: Many people think summer comes when Earth is closest to the Sun. In fact Earth is closest in early January, in the middle of the northern winter.

data.name: Seasons_Distance_Fact2
data.value: Earth's orbit is almost a circle: the distance changes by only about 3%, from 147.1 to 152.1 million km. That changes the sunlight by about 7%, far less than the tilt does.

data.name: Seasons_Distance_Fact3
data.value: If the distance caused the seasons, both hemispheres would have summer at the same time. Instead they always have opposite seasons.

data.name: Seasons_Distance_Fact4
data.value: The distance does matter a little: southern summers get about 7% more sunlight than northern ones, but the southern hemisphere's large oceans even this out.

data.name: Seasons_Distance_Note
data.value: The orbit is drawn in its true shape: almost a perfect circle

data.name: Seasons_Distance_Subtitle
data.value: Myth: is it summer when Earth is closer to the Sun?

data.name: Seasons_DragHint_Orbit
data.value: Drag to move Earth along its orbit

data.name: Seasons_DragHint_Sky
data.value: Drag left or right to move the Sun through the day

data.name: Seasons_Lesson_SunPath_Choice1
data.value: The Sun is higher and the days are longer

data.name: Seasons_Lesson_SunPath_Choice2
data.value: Earth is closer to the Sun

data.name: Seasons_Noon_Caption
data.value: Noon sunlight where you are (Earth cut in half)

data.name: Seasons_Stage_Autumn_Description
data.value: The axis is side-on to the Sun, and your hemisphere is turning away from it: every day the noon Sun is a little lower and the days grow shorter.

data.name: Seasons_Stage_Equator_Description
data.value: The day is always about 12 hours long and the noon Sun is high all year. Instead of four seasons, many tropical places have a wet and a dry season.

data.name: Seasons_Stage_NoTilt_Description
data.value: Without a tilt the Sun is over the equator every day of the year: every place has the same noon Sun and 12-hour days all year round.

data.name: Seasons_Stage_Spring_Description
data.value: The axis is side-on to the Sun, but your hemisphere is turning towards it: every day the noon Sun climbs a little higher and the days grow longer.

data.name: Seasons_Stage_Summer_Description
data.value: Your hemisphere leans towards the Sun. The Sun climbs high at noon and stays up longer, so the ground gets much more sunlight every day.

data.name: Seasons_Stage_Winter_Description
data.value: Your hemisphere leans away from the Sun. The Sun stays low and the days are short: sunlight comes in at a slant, and for fewer hours.

data.name: Seasons_Stat_PolarDay
data.value: The Sun does not set (polar day)

data.name: Seasons_Stat_PolarNight
data.value: The Sun does not rise (polar night)

data.name: Seasons_Stat_Sunlight_ToolTip
data.value: Sunlight reaching a level patch of ground over the whole day, above the atmosphere; 100% is the equator at an equinox

data.name: Seasons_SunNow_Down
data.value: {0}: the Sun is below the horizon.

data.name: Seasons_SunNow_Up
data.value: {0}: the Sun is {1:0}° above the horizon.

data.name: Seasons_SunPath_Fact1
data.value: At the equinoxes the Sun rises due east and sets due west everywhere on Earth, and day and night are each about 12 hours.

data.name: Seasons_SunPath_Fact2
data.value: In summer the Sun rises north of east and sets north of west (south of them in the southern hemisphere). Its path is longer and higher, so the day is longer.

data.name: Seasons_SunPath_Fact3
data.value: Beyond the Arctic and Antarctic Circles (66.6°) the Sun can stay up all day in summer (polar day) and not rise at all in winter (polar night). Try Tromsø.

data.name: Seasons_SunPath_Fact4
data.value: Times here are local solar time. Clock time differs because of time zones and daylight saving, and the atmosphere bends sunlight so that real days are a few minutes longer than shown.

data.name: Seasons_SunPath_Note
data.value: Times are local solar time: the Sun is highest at 12:00

data.name: Seasons_SunPath_Subtitle
data.value: The Sun's path across your sky, through the day and the year

data.name: Seasons_Tilt_Fact1
data.value: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.4° and keeps pointing the same way in space, towards the North Star, all year. So for half the year the north leans towards the Sun, and for the other half the south does.

data.name: Seasons_Tilt_Fact2
data.value: When your hemisphere leans towards the Sun you get two things at once: a higher noon Sun, so the light is more concentrated, and longer days, so it shines for more hours.

data.name: Seasons_Tilt_Fact3
data.value: The two hemispheres always have opposite seasons: when it is summer in Beijing it is winter in Sydney.

data.name: Seasons_Tilt_Fact4
data.value: The hottest weeks come about a month after the June solstice, and the coldest a month after the December one: land and sea take time to warm up and to cool down.

data.name: Seasons_Tilt_Fact5
data.value: Here the seasons start at the equinoxes and solstices (astronomical seasons). Weather services often use whole months instead, and the traditional Chinese solar terms start them about six weeks earlier, at Lichun, Lixia, Liqiu and Lidong.

data.name: Seasons_Tilt_Note
data.value: Sizes and distances are not to scale

data.name: Seasons_Tilt_Subtitle
data.value: Why are there seasons? Because Earth's axis is tilted

data.value: Off: pages change at once, for readers who prefer less motion.

data.value: Read out what you click in a picture

data.name: Settings_Tip
data.value: Language, theme, observer location, narration and page turning

data.name: Sky_AirMass_Caption
data.value: How much air the sunlight crosses

data.name: Sky_AirMass_Note
data.value: In times the air straight overhead, against the Sun's altitude (log scale). It hardly changes while the Sun is high, then shoots up in the last few degrees.

data.name: Sky_DragHint_Path
data.value: Drag round the observer to move the Sun

data.name: Sky_DragHint_Scattering
data.value: Change the time of day to change how much air the light crosses

data.name: Sky_DragHint_Sky
data.value: Drag up or down in the sky to move the Sun

data.name: Sky_Haze_Caption
data.value: Haze and dust in the air

data.name: Sky_LookAway
data.value: Turn your back to the Sun

data.name: Sky_Path_Fact1
data.value: With the Sun overhead its light crosses the air once; at 30° up, twice as much; on the horizon, about 38 times as much.

data.name: Sky_Path_Fact2
data.value: Squeezed to the density at sea level, all the air above you would be a layer only about 8 km thick.

data.name: Sky_Path_Fact3
data.value: The blue taken out of your sunset is not lost: it lights the sky for people further west, where the Sun is still higher.

data.name: Sky_Path_Fact4
data.value: Near the horizon the air bends sunlight up by about half a degree, the Sun's own width: when it seems to touch the horizon, it has already set. This chapter leaves the bending out.

data.name: Sky_Path_Fact5
data.value: In a total lunar eclipse the Moon turns red: the only sunlight reaching it is bent through the Earth's air, as if through every sunrise and sunset at once.

data.name: Sky_Path_Grazing
data.value: Sunlight skims over you and lights the air above

data.name: Sky_Path_Note
data.value: A slice through the Earth, its air drawn many times too thick (only the lowest 50 km, where nearly all of it is). The colours show the sunlight that reaches each point.

data.name: Sky_Path_Overhead
data.value: Sun overhead: only this much air

data.name: Sky_Path_Subtitle
data.value: At sunset the light crosses far more air, and loses its blue on the way

data.name: Sky_Phase_Day_Description
data.value: Sunlight crosses little air on its way down, so the Sun looks white. The air bounces a share of it aside, blue far more than red, and that light reaches you from every direction: the blue sky.

data.name: Sky_Phase_GoldenHour_Description
data.value: The Sun is low and its light comes a long way through the air. Much of its blue is scattered out on the way, so the light left is yellow and warm, and shadows are long.

data.name: Sky_Phase_NauticalTwilight_Description
data.value: Only the highest air is still in sunlight. The sky turns deep blue and the brightest stars come out; once the Sun is 12° down it is dark enough to call it night.

data.name: Sky_Phase_Night_Description
data.value: The Sun is more than 12° below the horizon and hardly any sunlight is scattered towards you. The last glow (astronomical twilight) fades by 18°.

data.name: Sky_Phase_Sunrise_Description
data.value: The Sun's light skims along the ground through about 38 times as much air as straight overhead. Nearly all its blue and green is scattered out; orange and red get through, so the rising Sun is red.

data.name: Sky_Phase_Sunset_Description
data.value: The Sun's light skims along the ground through about 38 times as much air as straight overhead. Nearly all its blue and green is scattered out; orange and red get through, so the setting Sun is red.

data.name: Sky_Phase_Twilight_Description
data.value: The Sun is below the horizon but still lights the air high above you, so the sky stays bright: blue overhead, orange and red low on the Sun's side. Opposite it, the Earth's shadow lies on the air.

data.name: Sky_Scatter_Box_Down
data.value: Air: the Sun has set; about 38× the air overhead along the horizon

data.name: Sky_Scatter_Caption
data.value: How strongly each colour is scattered

data.name: Sky_Scatter_EndEye
data.value: Looking at the Sun: what is left

data.name: Sky_Scatter_Note
data.value: Bars: scattering by the air's molecules, as 1/λ⁴. Dashed: the light of the sky (sunlight times scattering), strongest in the blue; the dot is its colour.

data.name: Sky_Scatter_SideEye
data.value: Looking at the sky: the light scattered out

data.name: Sky_Scattering_Fact1
data.value: Nitrogen and oxygen molecules are about a thousand times smaller than a wavelength of light. Things that small scatter short waves far more strongly, as 1/λ⁴: Rayleigh scattering, worked out by Lord Rayleigh in 1871.

data.name: Sky_Scattering_Fact2
data.value: So violet light (400 nm) is scattered about 9 times as much as red (700 nm), and blue (450 nm) about 6 times as much.

data.name: Sky_Scattering_Fact3
data.value: Why not a violet sky? Sunlight has less violet than blue, some violet is absorbed high up, and our eyes are far less sensitive to it: the mix of scattered colours looks sky blue.

data.name: Sky_Scattering_Fact4
data.value: Clouds are white because their droplets are much bigger than a wavelength and scatter every colour almost equally.

data.name: Sky_Scattering_Fact5
data.value: Skylight is polarised, most strongly 90° from the Sun: polarising sunglasses make that part of the sky darker, and bees use the pattern to find their way.

data.name: Sky_Scattering_Note
data.value: The chance of each photon being scattered comes from the real values for air: the box stands for all the air the sunlight crosses at this time of day.

data.name: Sky_Scattering_Subtitle
data.value: The air bounces blue light aside far more than red

data.name: Sky_Sky_Fact1
data.value: Sunlight looks white because it is a mix of every colour. The blue of the sky is that same sunlight, bounced towards you by the air.

data.name: Sky_Sky_Fact2
data.value: After sunset, face east: a dark blue band rising from the horizon is the Earth's own shadow on the air, and the pink band above it, lit by red sunset light, is the belt of Venus.

data.name: Sky_Sky_Fact3
data.value: The sky overhead stays blue after sunset partly thanks to ozone: high up, it absorbs orange and yellow from the sunlight skimming over you.

data.name: Sky_Sky_Fact4
data.value: Dust, smoke and droplets scatter every colour alike, so hazy air makes a paler, whiter sky. Ash from big volcanic eruptions such as Krakatoa (1883) gave vivid red sunsets round the world.

data.name: Sky_Sky_Fact5
data.value: On Mars it is the other way round: fine dust makes the day sky butterscotch, and sunsets are blue, because the dust scatters blue light forward round the Sun.

data.name: Sky_Sky_Note
data.value: The sky is worked out from sunlight scattered by the air and haze, on an equinox day in {0} ({1}), in local solar time. The Sun is drawn about 6 times its real size.

data.name: Sky_Sky_Subtitle
data.value: Why is the sky blue, and the sunset red?

data.name: Sky_Stat_SunDown
data.value: the Sun is below the horizon

data.name: Sky_Sunlight_Note
data.value: Dashed: sunlight before it meets the air. Filled: what of it comes straight through. The lower the Sun, the more blue goes missing; the dot is the colour of what is left.

data.name: SolarSystem_Ariel_Description
data.value: Ariel has the brightest and probably the youngest surface of Uranus's large moons. Long fault valleys cut across it, and some areas look smoothed over by flows that may have been icy lava. Few large craters survive, suggesting it was resurfaced relatively recently.

data.name: SolarSystem_Callisto_Description
data.value: Callisto's dark surface is one of the most heavily cratered in the Solar System and has barely changed in about four billion years. Its largest impact feature, Valhalla, is a bullseye of rings some 3,800 km across. It orbits outside Jupiter's most intense radiation, which makes it a candidate site for a future human base.

data.name: SolarSystem_Deimos_Description
data.value: Deimos is the smaller and more distant of Mars's two moons, only about 12 km across. A thick layer of loose dust fills many of its craters and makes its surface look smooth. Seen from Mars it looks like a bright star and stays above the horizon for about two and a half days at a time. Like Phobos, it may be a captured asteroid or debris from an ancient impact.

data.name: SolarSystem_Dione_Description
data.value: Dione's trailing hemisphere is streaked with bright, wispy lines that turned out to be ice cliffs hundreds of metres high, formed as the crust cracked; its leading side is heavily cratered. Cassini detected a trace of oxygen around it, and studies suggest an ocean may lie deep below the surface.

data.name: SolarSystem_Earth_Description
data.value: Earth is the third planet from the Sun and the only world known to host life. Oceans cover about 71% of its surface, and a nitrogen-oxygen atmosphere together with a magnetic field shields the surface from the solar wind and cosmic rays. Its axis is tilted about 23.4°, which gives us the seasons. Its one large natural satellite, the Moon, raises the ocean tides and helps keep that tilt stable.

data.name: SolarSystem_Enceladus_Description
data.value: Enceladus reflects almost all the sunlight that reaches it, making it the most reflective body in the Solar System. Near its south pole, cracks nicknamed "tiger stripes" vent geysers of water vapour and ice from an ocean beneath the crust. The spray feeds Saturn's E ring, and the Cassini probe found salts and organic molecules in it.

data.name: SolarSystem_Europa_Description
data.value: Europa's smooth, icy crust is criss-crossed by reddish-brown cracks and ridges and has very few craters, a sign that the surface is young. Beneath the ice lies a global salty ocean that may hold about twice as much water as all of Earth's oceans, which makes Europa one of the most promising places to look for life. NASA's Europa Clipper, launched in 2024, is on its way to study it.

data.name: SolarSystem_Ganymede_Description
data.value: Ganymede is the largest moon in the Solar System, bigger than the planet Mercury. It is the only moon known to have its own magnetic field, which produces auroras around its poles. Its surface mixes old, dark, cratered regions with lighter grooved terrain, and a salty ocean is thought to lie deep beneath the ice.

data.name: SolarSystem_Ganymede_Tagline
data.value: The largest moon in the Solar System

data.name: SolarSystem_Hint
data.value: Scroll to zoom (moons appear up close) · drag to pan · click a body for details · double-click to reset

data.name: SolarSystem_Iapetus_Description
data.value: Iapetus is famous for its two-tone colouring: its leading hemisphere is as dark as coal while the trailing one is almost as bright as snow. A ridge up to about 20 km high runs along its equator, giving it a walnut-like shape. It orbits far from Saturn, on an orbit tilted about 15° to the planet's equator.

data.name: SolarSystem_Io_Description
data.value: Io is the most volcanically active body in the Solar System, with hundreds of volcanoes, some throwing plumes of sulfur hundreds of kilometres high. Tidal squeezing by Jupiter and its neighbours Europa and Ganymede keeps its interior hot. Sulfur compounds paint its surface yellow, orange, red and white.

data.name: SolarSystem_Jupiter_Description
data.value: Jupiter is the largest planet: 2.5 times as massive as all the other planets combined, and big enough to hold more than 1,300 Earths. A gas giant made mostly of hydrogen and helium, its clouds are stretched by powerful jet streams into light zones and dark belts. The Great Red Spot in its southern hemisphere is a storm larger than Earth that has been watched for nearly 200 years. Jupiter spins in under 10 hours, faster than any other planet, and its many moons include Ganymede, the largest moon in the Solar System.

data.name: SolarSystem_Mars_Description
data.value: Iron oxide in its dust gives Mars its familiar rusty colour. It hosts the tallest volcano in the Solar System, Olympus Mons — about 22 km high, nearly 2.5 times Everest — and Valles Marineris, a canyon system some 4,000 km long. Its thin atmosphere is mostly carbon dioxide, and caps of water ice and dry ice cover both poles. Ample evidence shows that liquid water once flowed on its surface, and Mars is among the planets most visited by spacecraft.

data.name: SolarSystem_Mercury_Description
data.value: Mercury is the smallest planet and the closest to the Sun, circling it in just 88 days. With almost no atmosphere to hold heat, its surface swings from about 430 °C in daylight to −180 °C at night — the widest range of any planet. Its heavily cratered surface looks much like the Moon's. Mercury spins three times for every two orbits, so one solar day there lasts about 176 Earth days.

data.name: SolarSystem_Mercury_Tagline
data.value: The smallest planet, closest to the Sun

data.name: SolarSystem_Mimas_Description
data.value: Mimas is a small icy moon whose giant crater Herschel, about 140 km across and a third of the moon's width, makes it look like the Death Star from Star Wars. The impact that made it nearly shattered Mimas. Its gravity also clears the Cassini Division, the dark gap in Saturn's rings.

data.name: SolarSystem_Miranda_Description
data.value: Miranda looks as if it were pieced together from different parts: grooved, ridged regions called coronae sit next to old cratered terrain. Its cliff Verona Rupes may be as much as 20 km high, perhaps the tallest cliff in the Solar System. Voyager 2 photographed it during its 1986 flyby.

data.name: SolarSystem_Moon_Description
data.value: The Moon is the fifth-largest moon in the Solar System, a little over a quarter of Earth's diameter. It is tidally locked, so the same face always points at Earth, and its dark plains, the maria, are ancient lava flows. It is drifting away by about 3.8 cm a year. Twelve astronauts walked on it between 1969 and 1972, and in 2019 China's Chang'e 4 made the first soft landing on its far side.

data.name: SolarSystem_Neptune_Description
data.value: Neptune is the farthest planet, about 30 times Earth's distance from the Sun; sunlight takes more than four hours to get there. It was the first planet found by mathematical prediction before anyone saw it, in 1846. Deep blue in colour, it has the fastest winds in the Solar System, reaching about 2,000 km/h. Its largest moon, Triton, orbits backwards and is slowly spiralling inward.

data.name: SolarSystem_Oberon_Description
data.value: Oberon is the outermost of Uranus's large moons and was discovered by Herschel on the same night as Titania in 1787. Its old surface is heavily cratered, and dark material covers some crater floors. Voyager 2 images show a mountain about 11 km high rising at its edge.

data.name: SolarSystem_Oberon_Tagline
data.value: The outermost large moon of Uranus

data.name: SolarSystem_Phobos_Description
data.value: Phobos is a lumpy moon about 22 km across that circles Mars only about 6,000 km above its surface. It goes round faster than Mars spins, so from the ground it rises in the west and sets in the east. Tides are pulling it inward by about 1.8 m per century; in roughly 50 million years it will hit Mars or break up into a ring. Its largest crater, Stickney, is almost 9 km wide.

data.name: SolarSystem_RealScale_Tooltip
data.value: Place the planets at their true distances from the Sun (AU) instead of evenly spaced rings

data.name: SolarSystem_Rhea_Description
data.value: Rhea is Saturn's second-largest moon, a cold, cratered ball of ice and rock. In 2010 Cassini detected a very thin exosphere of oxygen and carbon dioxide around it. In the shade its surface drops to about −220 °C.

data.name: SolarSystem_Saturn_Description
data.value: Saturn, the second-largest planet, is famous for its spectacular rings: countless pieces of ice and rock, from dust grains to house-sized chunks, spread about 280,000 km across yet typically only 10 metres to 1 km thick. Saturn's average density is lower than water's — given a big enough ocean, it would float. It has more known moons than any other planet; Titan has a thick atmosphere, and Enceladus hides a liquid ocean beneath its icy crust.

data.name: SolarSystem_ScaleNote
data.value: Body sizes are not to scale.

data.name: SolarSystem_Sun_Description
data.value: The Sun is a 4.6-billion-year-old yellow dwarf that holds 99.86% of the Solar System's mass. Its core reaches about 15 million °C and fuses roughly 600 million tonnes of hydrogen into helium every second. That energy takes tens of thousands of years to work its way to the surface, then about 8 minutes 20 seconds to reach Earth as sunlight. The Sun's gravity keeps the planets, dwarf planets, asteroids and comets on their paths.

data.name: SolarSystem_Sun_Tagline
data.value: The star at the heart of the Solar System

data.name: SolarSystem_Tethys_Description
data.value: Tethys is made almost entirely of water ice, so its density is barely above that of water. It bears a huge crater, Odysseus, about 450 km wide, and a canyon, Ithaca Chasma, that runs some 2,000 km across its surface.

data.name: SolarSystem_Titan_Description
data.value: Titan is Saturn's largest moon and the only moon with a thick atmosphere, mostly nitrogen, wrapped in orange haze; the pressure at its surface is about 1.5 times Earth's. It is the only world besides Earth known to have stable liquid on its surface: lakes and seas of liquid methane and ethane. The Huygens probe landed there in 2005, and NASA's Dragonfly rotorcraft is due to launch in 2028.

data.name: SolarSystem_Titan_Tagline
data.value: A moon with a thick atmosphere

data.name: SolarSystem_Titania_Description
data.value: Titania is the largest moon of Uranus, discovered by William Herschel in 1787. Fault canyons up to about 1,500 km long scar its surface, signs that its interior once expanded as water froze. A thin layer of liquid water may still lie beneath its crust.

data.name: SolarSystem_Today_Tooltip
data.value: Jump back to today's planet positions

data.name: SolarSystem_Triton_Description
data.value: Triton is Neptune's largest moon and the only large moon that orbits backwards, against its planet's rotation — strong evidence that it is a captured Kuiper Belt object. At about −235 °C it has one of the coldest surfaces known, yet Voyager 2 saw geysers of nitrogen gas rising some 8 km. Tides are slowly drawing it inward, and one day it will be torn apart.

data.name: SolarSystem_Umbriel_Description
data.value: Umbriel is the darkest of Uranus's five large moons, with an ancient, heavily cratered surface. A puzzling bright ring about 130 km across, nicknamed the "fluorescent Cheerio", sits on the crater Wunda near its equator.

data.name: SolarSystem_Umbriel_Tagline
data.value: The darkest of Uranus's large moons

data.name: SolarSystem_Uranus_Description
data.value: Uranus is an ice giant whose methane-rich atmosphere absorbs red light, giving it a pale cyan tint. Its axis is tilted about 98°, so it rolls around the Sun on its side, and each pole gets about 42 years of continuous daylight followed by 42 years of night. It was the first planet discovered with a telescope, by William Herschel in 1781. It has 13 faint, narrow rings, and its cloud tops can drop to −224 °C, the coldest planetary atmosphere in the Solar System.

data.name: SolarSystem_Uranus_Tagline
data.value: The ice giant that rolls on its side

data.name: SolarSystem_Venus_Description
data.value: Venus is close to Earth in size and mass and is often called Earth's twin. A thick carbon-dioxide atmosphere with clouds of sulfuric acid presses down at about 92 times Earth's surface pressure, and a runaway greenhouse effect heats the surface to around 465 °C — hotter than Mercury. Venus spins backwards compared with most planets, and one rotation takes 243 days, longer than its 225-day year. After the Moon, it is the brightest object in the night sky.

data.name: Star_Class_Massive_Lifetime
data.value: Shines for only about 10 to 35 million years

data.name: Star_Class_RedDwarf_Ending
data.value: → fades into a helium white dwarf (none has yet)

data.name: Star_Class_RedDwarf_Lifetime
data.value: Shines for hundreds of billions to trillions of years

data.name: Star_Class_SunLike_Ending
data.value: → red giant → planetary nebula → white dwarf

data.name: Star_Class_SunLike_Lifetime
data.value: Shines for tens of millions to tens of billions of years

data.name: Star_Class_VeryMassive_Lifetime
data.value: Shines for just a few million years

data.name: Star_Core_Agb
data.value: Two burning shells, helium and hydrogen, round a carbon-oxygen core.

data.name: Star_Core_BlackHole
data.value: Nothing inside the event horizon can be seen.

data.name: Star_Core_BlueDwarf
data.value: Hydrogen into helium, nearly all of the star's hydrogen used.

data.name: Star_Core_Caption
data.value: Inside the star (cut open, not to scale)

data.name: Star_Core_HeliumBurning
data.value: Helium into carbon and oxygen in the core, hydrogen in a shell.

data.name: Star_Core_LateBurning
data.value: Each layer burns the ashes of the one outside it, down to an iron core.

data.name: Star_Core_MainSequence
data.value: Hydrogen fuses into helium in the core.

data.name: Star_Core_NeutronStar
data.value: No fusion: neutrons packed as tight as in an atomic nucleus, under a thin iron crust.

data.name: Star_Core_PlanetaryNebula
data.value: The fires are out; the bare carbon-oxygen core lights the gas it has shed.

data.name: Star_Core_Protostar
data.value: No fusion yet: the gas heats up as it falls in.

data.name: Star_Core_RedGiant
data.value: A small, dense helium core, hydrogen burning in a shell, and a huge cool envelope stirred by convection.

data.name: Star_Core_RedSupergiant
data.value: Helium into carbon and oxygen in the core, hydrogen in a shell.

data.name: Star_Core_Subgiant
data.value: The helium core is not burning; hydrogen burns in a shell around it.

data.name: Star_Core_Supergiant
data.value: Hydrogen burning in a shell round a contracting helium core.

data.name: Star_Core_Supernova
data.value: The iron core collapses to neutrons; a shock wave tears the star apart.

data.name: Star_Core_WhiteDwarf
data.value: No fusion: carbon and oxygen (helium, for a red dwarf) pressed so tight that electrons hold it up.

data.name: Star_Diagram_Fact1
data.value: Ejnar Hertzsprung and Henry Norris Russell drew the first versions of the diagram independently, around 1910 to 1913.

data.name: Star_Diagram_Fact2
data.value: About nine in ten stars, the Sun among them, are on the main sequence, because that is where stars spend most of their lives.

data.name: Star_Diagram_Fact3
data.value: Temperature runs backwards, hot on the left, because the first diagrams were drawn by colour, from blue to red.

data.name: Star_Diagram_Fact4
data.value: Stars of one size lie along a diagonal: a cool star can only be very bright by being huge, like Betelgeuse.

data.name: Star_Diagram_Fact5
data.value: Sirius B, the companion of the brightest star in the night sky, is a white dwarf: hotter than Sirius A, but only Earth-sized, so it gives out a twentieth of the Sun's light.

data.name: Star_Diagram_Note
data.value: Temperature across, hot on the left, and brightness up, both on log scales. The dashed line is the star's whole path, the solid one the part it has lived.

data.name: Star_Diagram_Subtitle
data.value: The Hertzsprung–Russell diagram: a star's life is a journey across it

data.name: Star_DragHint_Fates
data.value: Click a row to pick a star of that kind

data.name: Star_DragHint_Strip
data.value: Click or drag along the strip of stages at the bottom to move through the star's life

data.name: Star_Duration_Caption
data.value: How long each stage really lasts

data.name: Star_Duration_Note
data.value: On a log scale: each grid line is a thousand times the last. Almost all of a star's life is spent on the main sequence.

data.name: Star_Fates_Fact1
data.value: The line between Sun-like and massive stars is about 8 Suns; between neutron stars and black holes perhaps 20 to 25, and it is still debated.

data.name: Star_Fates_Fact2
data.value: A white dwarf can weigh at most 1.44 Suns, the Chandrasekhar limit; any heavier and its electrons can no longer hold it up.

data.name: Star_Fates_Fact3
data.value: The Crab Nebula is what is left of a supernova Chinese astronomers recorded in 1054; a pulsar spinning 30 times a second sits at its centre.

data.name: Star_Fates_Fact4
data.value: Betelgeuse, a red supergiant in Orion, will explode some time in the next 100,000 years and shine about as bright as a half Moon.

data.name: Star_Fates_Fact5
data.value: In 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope showed the first picture of a black hole's shadow, in the galaxy M87.

data.name: Star_Fates_Note
data.value: For single stars like the Sun. The mass limits are approximate, the one between neutron stars and black holes especially.

data.name: Star_Fates_Subtitle
data.value: Four ways to end: a white dwarf, a neutron star or a black hole

data.name: Star_Hr_AxisT
data.value: Surface temperature (K), hotter to the left

data.name: Star_Hr_NeutronStar
data.value: Neutron star: too small and faint for the chart

data.name: Star_Hr_Supernova
data.value: Supernova: {0} × the Sun, far off the chart

data.name: Star_Lesson_Diagram_Choice1
data.value: Up and to the right, to the giants

data.name: Star_Lesson_Diagram_Choice2
data.value: Straight down to the white dwarfs

data.name: Star_Lesson_Fates_Choice2
data.value: It becomes a white dwarf, like the Sun

data.name: Star_Lesson_Life_Choice1
data.value: It swells into a red giant

data.name: Star_Life_Fact1
data.value: The Sun is 4.6 billion years old, about halfway through its 10 billion years on the main sequence.

data.name: Star_Life_Fact2
data.value: In about 5 billion years the Sun will become a red giant and swallow Mercury and Venus; whether it reaches Earth is still uncertain.

data.name: Star_Life_Fact3
data.value: Heavier stars burn far faster: a star of 10 Suns is thousands of times as bright and lasts only about 20 million years.

data.name: Star_Life_Fact4
data.value: Every atom of carbon, oxygen and iron in your body was made inside stars and spread by them as they died.

data.name: Star_Life_Fact5
data.value: Red dwarfs are the most common stars, about three in four; Proxima Centauri, the nearest star to the Sun, is one.

data.name: Star_Life_Note
data.value: Not to scale: sizes go by the cube root, so a supergiant a thousand times the Sun and an Earth-sized white dwarf both fit. Playback gives each stage its turn; the real lengths are along the bottom.

data.name: Star_Life_Subtitle
data.value: A star's life is decided by its mass: the heavier, the brighter, and the shorter

data.name: Star_Remnant_Note
data.value: Left, a white dwarf beside Earth; right, a thousand times closer in, a neutron star and a black hole. A teaspoon of white dwarf weighs about 5 tonnes, of neutron star about a billion tonnes.

data.name: Star_Stage_Agb_Description
data.value: The core's helium is used up too. Helium and hydrogen burn in two shells round a carbon-oxygen core; the star swells even bigger, pulses, and blows strong winds that carry off its outer layers.

data.name: Star_Stage_BlackHole_Description
data.value: The core is too heavy even for neutrons to hold it up, and it collapses for ever. Inside the event horizon, a few tens of kilometres across, gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape.

data.name: Star_Stage_BlackHole_Title
data.value: Black hole: not even light gets out

data.name: Star_Stage_BlueDwarf_Description
data.value: A red dwarf stirs all its hydrogen through the whole star, so it burns nearly all of it. At the very end it grows smaller, hotter and bluer. The universe is too young: no star has got this far yet.

data.name: Star_Stage_BlueDwarf_Title
data.value: Blue dwarf: a red dwarf's slow end

data.name: Star_Stage_HeliumBurning_Description
data.value: At 100 million degrees the core ignites helium, fusing it into carbon and oxygen; in a star like the Sun this starts with a flash. The star shrinks back for a while.

data.name: Star_Stage_LateBurning_Description
data.value: Carbon, neon, oxygen and silicon burn one after another, each faster than the last: carbon for centuries, silicon for about a day. The core turns to iron, which gives no energy when it fuses: the fire goes out.

data.name: Star_Stage_LateBurning_Title
data.value: The last fuels, in layers like an onion

data.name: Star_Stage_MainSequence_Description
data.value: In the core, hydrogen fuses into helium at over 10 million degrees. The push of that heat balances gravity, and the star hardly changes for most of its life. The Sun is here now.

data.name: Star_Stage_NeutronStar_Description
data.value: The collapsed core: more mass than the Sun in a ball about 20 km across, made almost entirely of neutrons. It spins many times a second; if its beams sweep over Earth we see a pulsar.

data.name: Star_Stage_NeutronStar_Title
data.value: Neutron star: an atomic nucleus as big as a city

data.name: Star_Stage_PlanetaryNebula_Description
data.value: The star sheds its outer layers. Its bare core, over 100,000 degrees, lights the spreading gas into a glowing shell for some tens of thousands of years. The name is old: it has nothing to do with planets.

data.name: Star_Stage_PlanetaryNebula_Title
data.value: Planetary nebula: the outer layers drift away

data.name: Star_Stage_Protostar_Description
data.value: A cold cloud of gas and dust falls in on itself. Shrinking, it heats up and glows red, fed by a spinning disc and blowing jets from its poles. No fusion yet: the heat comes from the fall.

data.name: Star_Stage_RedGiant_Description
data.value: The burning shell pours out energy and the outside balloons to over a hundred times the Sun's size. The surface cools to orange-red, yet the star is thousands of times as bright.

data.name: Star_Stage_RedSupergiant_Description
data.value: Helium burns in the core. The star is so big that in place of the Sun it would reach past Mars, some past Jupiter. Betelgeuse in Orion is one.

data.name: Star_Stage_RedSupergiant_Title
data.value: Red supergiant: hundreds of times the Sun's size

data.name: Star_Stage_Subgiant_Description
data.value: The core is now helium and stops burning. It shrinks and heats up; hydrogen burns in a shell around it, and the star's outer layers begin to swell.

data.name: Star_Stage_Subgiant_Title
data.value: Subgiant: the core runs out of hydrogen

data.name: Star_Stage_Supergiant_Description
data.value: The core's hydrogen is gone and it contracts while hydrogen burns around it. In thousands of years the star swells from blue to red, crossing the diagram at nearly the same brightness.

data.name: Star_Stage_Supernova_Description
data.value: The iron core collapses in under a second, from Earth's size to a ball of neutrons 20 km across. The infalling layers rebound in a vast explosion, for weeks as bright as billions of Suns, making heavy elements and scattering them into space.

data.name: Star_Stage_WhiteDwarf_Description
data.value: What is left is the core: about half the Sun's mass squeezed to the size of Earth. Nothing burns any more; it just cools, from white-hot to dim red, over billions of years.

data.name: Tides_Bulges_Fact1
data.value: The tidal force is the difference between the Moon's pull on a piece of ocean and its pull on Earth's centre. It weakens with the cube of the distance, so what matters is how near the Moon is, not how big.

data.name: Tides_Bulges_Fact2
data.value: On the far side the Moon pulls the water less than it pulls Earth itself, so Earth is pulled away from that water: it is left behind as the second bulge.

data.name: Tides_Bulges_Fact3
data.value: The Moon's tidal force is only about one ten-millionth of Earth's gravity. On an ocean covering the whole Earth it would lift the water only about half a metre; coasts and bays turn that into metres.

data.name: Tides_Bulges_Fact4
data.value: While Earth turns once, the Moon moves on about 13° the same way, so Earth needs about 50 more minutes to catch up: the tides come about 50 minutes later each day.

data.name: Tides_Bulges_Fact5
data.value: Tidal friction slows Earth's spin: the day grows about 2 milliseconds longer every century, and the Moon moves about 3.8 cm farther away each year.

data.name: Tides_Bulges_Note
data.value: Seen from above the North Pole, sunlight from the left; the Moon's tide alone. Not to scale: the bulges are exaggerated millions of times, and the Moon is really 60 Earth radii away.

data.name: Tides_Bulges_Subtitle
data.value: Why two high tides a day? The Moon stretches the oceans into two bulges

data.name: Tides_Chart_Caption_Moon
data.value: The water where you are (the Moon's tide alone)

data.name: Tides_Chart_Note
data.value: Metres above chart datum; shaded: night. With the Sun added, the time between high tides varies a little around 12 h 25 min.

data.name: Tides_Chart_Note_Moon
data.value: Shaded: night. Two highs and two lows every 24 h 50 min.

data.name: Tides_Coast_Fact1
data.value: Tide tables give heights above chart datum, about the lowest the water ever falls, so the depth shown on a chart is the least to expect.

data.name: Tides_Coast_Fact2
data.value: Rule of twelfths: from low to high water, in each of the six hours the water rises about 1/12, 2/12, 3/12, 3/12, 2/12 and 1/12 of the range, fastest in the middle hours.

data.name: Tides_Coast_Fact3
data.value: On real coasts high water comes hours after the Moon is highest: the oceans cannot keep up with the bulges and the continents get in the way. The delay is nearly the same each day at a given port, which is how tides are predicted.

data.name: Tides_Coast_Fact4
data.value: Some coasts have only one high tide a day, such as the Beibu Gulf off Beihai, where the shape of the gulf strengthens the once-a-day tide.

data.name: Tides_Coast_Fact5
data.value: The Bay of Fundy in Canada has the largest tides in the world, up to about 16 m between high and low water; China's largest are in Hangzhou Bay, up to about 9 m.

data.name: Tides_Coast_Note
data.value: A coast at the latitude of {1} ({0}) where the Moon alone would move the water 1 m above and below the mean. Here high water comes when the Moon is highest or lowest; on real coasts it comes hours later.

data.name: Tides_Coast_Subtitle
data.value: At the coast: the sea comes in and goes out twice a day

data.name: Tides_DragHint_Moon
data.value: Drag the Moon along its orbit

data.name: Tides_DragHint_Time
data.value: Drag sideways to move the time: a day across the view

data.name: Tides_Force_Caption
data.value: Why is there a bulge on the far side too?

data.name: Tides_Force_Note
data.value: Exaggerated: the Moon is drawn 3 Earth radii away instead of 60, so the differences show.

data.name: Tides_Force_Pull
data.value: 1. The Moon's pull: strongest on the near side

data.name: Tides_Force_Tidal
data.value: 2. Take away the pull on the centre: the tidal force

data.name: Tides_Kind_Growing_Description
data.value: Heading for new or full moon: the two pairs of bulges come into line and the range grows day by day.

data.name: Tides_Kind_Neap_Description
data.value: Seen from Earth, the Sun and the Moon are at right angles (first or last quarter): the Sun's bulges fill in the Moon's lows, so the range is smallest.

data.name: Tides_Kind_Shrinking_Description
data.value: Heading for a quarter moon: the two pairs of bulges move apart and the range shrinks day by day.

data.name: Tides_Kind_Spring_Description
data.value: The Sun, Earth and the Moon are nearly in line (new or full moon): the Sun's bulges add to the Moon's, so high water is higher and low water lower.

data.name: Tides_Lesson_Coast_Choice1
data.value: About twelve and a half hours

data.name: Tides_Range_Caption
data.value: Range between high and low water through the month

data.name: Tides_Range_Note
data.value: Dashed: the Moon alone. The Sun makes the range swing between 1.1 m and 2.9 m.

data.name: Tides_SpringNeap_Fact1
data.value: The Sun pulls on Earth about 180 times as hard as the Moon, yet its tidal force is only 46% of the Moon's: it is 389 times as far away, and the tidal force falls with the cube of the distance.

data.name: Tides_SpringNeap_Fact2
data.value: Spring tides have nothing to do with the season (the name means the water springs up): they come twice a month, around new and full moon, the 1st and the 15th of the Chinese lunar month. Neap tides come around the 8th and the 23rd.

data.name: Tides_SpringNeap_Fact3
data.value: Real spring tides usually come one to three days after new or full moon, because the oceans take time to respond to the pull. This delay is called the age of the tide.

data.name: Tides_SpringNeap_Fact4
data.value: When a new or full moon comes with the Moon at its closest to Earth (perigee), its tidal force is nearly 20% stronger than on average and the spring tides are bigger still: perigean spring tides, or king tides.

data.name: Tides_SpringNeap_Fact5
data.value: The Qiantang River bore near Hangzhou is at its grandest around the 18th of the eighth lunar month: an autumn spring tide pushed into a funnel-shaped estuary rises into a wall of water up to a few metres high.

data.name: Tides_SpringNeap_Note
data.value: Dashed outlines: the Moon's and the Sun's bulges on their own; the blue water is the two added together. Not to scale.

data.name: Tides_SpringNeap_Subtitle
data.value: The Sun joins in: big spring tides and small neap tides

data.name: Tides_Stage_Falling_Description
data.value: Earth's turning carries you away from the bulge, and the water goes out.

data.name: Tides_Stage_High_Description
data.value: High water: this place is under one of the two bulges, the one facing the Moon or the one opposite it.

data.name: Tides_Stage_Low_Description
data.value: Low water: you are halfway between the two bulges.

data.name: Tides_Stage_Rising_Description
data.value: You are turning towards the next bulge, and the water comes in.

data.name: Tides_Today_Text
data.value: Today the Moon is {0:0.0} days old · {1}

data.name: Tides_Upcoming_Note
data.value: From the real dates of the new moon, quarters and full moon in your time zone. The biggest tides usually come one to three days later.
