data.name: Trails_Camera_East_Description
data.value: The stars come up out of the horizon in parallel slanting lines. The nearer the equator, the steeper they climb.

data.name: Trails_Camera_East_Title
data.value: Facing east: stars rising at a slant

data.name: Trails_Camera_Equator_Description
data.value: Here the stars rise, arc across the sky and set. Their circles are so big that you only see a gentle curve of each.

data.name: Trails_Camera_Equator_Title
data.value: Away from the pole: wide arcs

data.name: Trails_Camera_Fact1
data.value: Star-trail photos are usually hundreds of 20–30 second shots stacked together, so the sky stays dark and every trail stays sharp.

data.name: Trails_Camera_Fact2
data.value: Polaris is less than a degree from the north celestial pole, so in a northern star-trail photo it draws only a tiny arc near the centre.

data.name: Trails_Camera_Fact3
data.value: The south celestial pole has no bright star near it; the Southern Cross and the two bright Pointers lead the way to it.

data.name: Trails_Camera_Fact4
data.value: The sky turns about 15° an hour: a fist held at arm's length covers about 10°.

data.name: Trails_Camera_Fact5
data.value: Earth's axis slowly wobbles round once in about 26,000 years, so the pole moves among the stars: in about 12,000 years Vega will be close to the north pole.

data.name: Trails_Camera_Note
data.value: A wide-angle camera (120° across) at the latitude chosen on the left page; the shutter opens at 20:00. The bright stars are real, the fainter ones a random fill, and the sky is drawn dark all night.

data.name: Trails_Camera_Pole_Description
data.value: Every trail is an arc round the celestial pole. The longer the exposure, the longer the arcs; stars near the pole draw small circles, stars far from it big ones.

data.name: Trails_Camera_Pole_Title
data.value: Facing the pole: circles round one point

data.name: Trails_Camera_Subtitle
data.value: The sky turns: stars draw circles round the pole

data.name: Trails_Camera_Up_Description
data.value: Overhead the trails are still circles round the pole, which sits as far from the zenith as you are from Earth's pole. Only at a pole are the circles centred right overhead.

data.name: Trails_Camera_Up_Title
data.value: Straight up: circles round the pole, off to one side

data.name: Trails_Camera_West_Description
data.value: The stars go down into the horizon in parallel slanting lines, the mirror image of the east.

data.name: Trails_Camera_West_Title
data.value: Facing west: stars setting at a slant

data.name: Trails_Chart_Hours_Caption
data.value: Hours above the horizon, by declination

data.name: Trails_Chart_Hours_Note
data.value: Declination is a star's latitude on the sky. Gold: never sets; blue: never rises; dots: the stars on the sphere.

data.name: Trails_Chart_Transit_Note
data.value: Each line runs about two hours earlier a month. Shaded: night at this latitude (twilight left out).

data.name: Trails_Hint_Camera
data.value: Drag the picture to turn and tilt the camera.

data.name: Trails_Hint_Sphere
data.value: Drag to turn the sphere; change the latitude on the left page.

data.name: Trails_Hint_Year
data.value: Drag Earth round the Sun, or run the year.

data.name: Trails_Sphere_Equator_Description
data.value: Both celestial poles lie on the horizon. Every star is up for half of each day, and over a year you can see the whole sky.

data.name: Trails_Sphere_Equator_Title
data.value: At the equator: everything rises and sets

data.name: Trails_Sphere_Fact1
data.value: The pole's height above the horizon equals your latitude: sailors measured it to find how far north or south they were.

data.name: Trails_Sphere_Fact2
data.value: From the equator you can see every star in the sky over a year; from a pole, only half of them.

data.name: Trails_Sphere_Fact3
data.value: The celestial equator lies straight above Earth's equator, and the celestial poles straight above Earth's poles.

data.name: Trails_Sphere_Fact4
data.value: Near the horizon, stars look about half a degree higher than they really are: the air bends their light.

data.name: Trails_Sphere_Fact5
data.value: Canopus, the second-brightest star, never rises north of about 37° N; from southern China it is the famous low 'old man star' of winter evenings.

data.name: Trails_Sphere_Middle_Description
data.value: Near the visible pole, stars never set; near the other pole, they never rise; in between, they rise and set, staying up longer the nearer they are to the visible pole.

data.name: Trails_Sphere_Middle_Title
data.value: In between: three kinds of stars

data.name: Trails_Sphere_Note
data.value: The celestial sphere seen from outside, with you at its centre on a disc of ground.

data.name: Trails_Sphere_Pole_Description
data.value: The celestial pole is overhead and every star circles parallel to the horizon. Half the sky is always up; the other half never is.

data.name: Trails_Sphere_Pole_Title
data.value: At a pole: nothing rises or sets

data.name: Trails_Sphere_Subtitle
data.value: Which stars never set, and which never rise

data.name: Trails_Stat_Earlier_Value
data.value: about 4 min a night, 2 h a month

data.name: Trails_Stat_NeverRise_Value
data.value: stars within {0}° of the other pole

data.name: Trails_Year_Description
data.value: On Earth's night side you look away from the Sun. As Earth goes round, that direction sweeps round the sky: each season brings different constellations, and the stars rise about four minutes earlier every night.

data.name: Trails_Year_Exaggerated
data.value: Earth's step along its orbit drawn 15 times too big

data.name: Trails_Year_Fact1
data.value: A sidereal day is 23 h 56 min 4 s, a solar day 24 h. In a year Earth turns once more against the stars than against the Sun: about 366¼ times.

data.name: Trails_Year_Fact2
data.value: Stars rise about 4 minutes earlier each night, so about 2 hours earlier each month.

data.name: Trails_Year_Fact3
data.value: Orion fills the evening sky from about December to March; Scorpius from about June to August.

data.name: Trails_Year_Fact4
data.value: Chinese astronomy divides the sky along the Moon's path into 28 lunar mansions; Antares, 心宿二, is the heart of the Azure Dragon of the east.

data.name: Trails_Year_Fact5
data.value: The zodiac constellations are the ones the Sun passes in front of during the year, Ophiuchus included, though most horoscopes leave it out.

data.name: Trails_Year_Note
data.value: Earth's orbit seen from above the north pole; the constellations really lie far, far beyond it. The evening sky is shown at 21:00 local sun time.

data.name: Trails_Year_StarBack
data.value: 23 h 56 min: the star is back

data.name: Trails_Year_Subtitle
data.value: Why the evening sky changes with the seasons

data.name: Typhoon_Chart_Decay_Note
data.value: As measured (Kaplan and DeMaria 1995): it loses a tenth at the coast, then about 9.5% of what is left above 13.7 m/s each hour.

data.name: Typhoon_Chart_Intensity_Note
data.value: The strongest wind day by day; the red lines are landfalls. It grows over warm sea, weakens over cooler water and dies over land.

data.name: Typhoon_Chart_Potential_Caption
data.value: How strong the sea lets it get

data.name: Typhoon_Chart_Potential_Note
data.value: The strongest wind a storm can reach over sea of this temperature (an empirical fit, DeMaria and Kaplan 1994). Most storms stay below it.

data.name: Typhoon_Chart_Profile_Caption
data.value: Wind and pressure from the centre out

data.name: Typhoon_Chart_Profile_Note
data.value: Gold: the wind, calm in the eye, strongest at the eyewall, slowly falling off outward. Blue: the pressure. The dashed line is the probe.

data.name: Typhoon_Chart_Season_Note
data.value: Named storms a month over the north-west Pacific, averages for 1991–2020 (Japan Meteorological Agency, rounded): about 25 a year.

data.name: Typhoon_Engine_Fact1
data.value: A typhoon needs sea of at least 26.5 °C down to about 50 m, moist air, and winds that change little with height, so the storm is not torn apart.

data.name: Typhoon_Engine_Fact2
data.value: The heat given off by the rain of a typical hurricane is about 6 × 10¹⁴ W, some 200 times the average power of all the world's electricity; only about a four-hundredth of it goes into the wind.

data.name: Typhoon_Engine_Fact3
data.value: The air shoots up the eyewall to 15 km or more, then spreads out at the top as a sheet of cirrus hundreds of kilometres wide: the white disc seen from satellites.

data.name: Typhoon_Engine_Fact4
data.value: In the eye the air sinks and warms as it is squeezed, which is why the eye is clear and the storm's core is warmer than its surroundings.

data.name: Typhoon_Engine_Fact5
data.value: A typhoon cools the sea behind it by stirring up colder water from below, sometimes by several degrees; a slow storm can weaken itself this way.

data.name: Typhoon_Engine_Landfall_Description
data.value: Over land there is no warm sea to evaporate: the air coming in is dry, hills and trees slow it down, and the storm runs down within a day or two. It can still pour down huge amounts of rain.

data.name: Typhoon_Engine_Note
data.value: A slice 600 km wide and 18 km high, heights stretched about 15 times. The storm is 90% as strong as the sea allows (DeMaria and Kaplan 1994); after landfall it fades as measured (Kaplan and DeMaria 1995).

data.name: Typhoon_Engine_Running_Description
data.value: Warm, moist air spirals in over the sea, rises in the eyewall and its water vapour condenses. The heat given off warms the core, the pressure falls further and the wind draws in still more moist air. The warmer the sea, the stronger it can get.

data.name: Typhoon_Engine_Running_Title
data.value: A heat engine on warm sea

data.name: Typhoon_Engine_Subtitle
data.value: A heat engine running on warm sea

data.name: Typhoon_Engine_TooCool_Description
data.value: Below about 26.5 °C the sea cannot give enough heat and moisture: thunderstorms come and go but never organise into a spinning storm.

data.name: Typhoon_Grade_Depression_Description
data.value: 10.8–17.1 m/s, force 6–7: a low whose thunderstorms are starting to circle.

data.name: Typhoon_Grade_None_Description
data.value: Below 10.8 m/s: just a low, not yet a tropical cyclone.

data.name: Typhoon_Grade_SevereTropicalStorm_Description
data.value: 24.5–32.6 m/s, force 10–11: trees are uprooted and the sea runs high.

data.name: Typhoon_Grade_SevereTyphoon_Description
data.value: 41.5–50.9 m/s, force 14–15: a clear eye ringed by violent winds; damage is widespread.

data.name: Typhoon_Grade_SuperTyphoon_Description
data.value: 51 m/s or more, force 16 and above: the most destructive storms, with a sharp, round eye.

data.name: Typhoon_Grade_TropicalStorm_Description
data.value: 17.2–24.4 m/s, force 8–9: the storm gets its name. Showers circle a centre that has no eye yet.

data.name: Typhoon_Grade_Typhoon_Description
data.value: 32.7–41.4 m/s, force 12–13: an eye has usually formed; roofs and signs are torn off.

data.name: Typhoon_Hint_Engine
data.value: Change the sea's temperature, or let the storm come ashore and watch it run down; drag sideways to turn the hours.

data.name: Typhoon_Hint_Storm
data.value: Click or drag the probe anywhere in the storm; switch off the Earth's turn, or go south of the equator, to see why it spins.

data.name: Typhoon_Hint_Track
data.value: Move the subtropical high's west end and change the month; click on the sea to start a storm there; drag sideways to turn the days.

data.name: Typhoon_Lesson_Engine_Choice1
data.value: The heat given off when water vapour condenses

data.name: Typhoon_Lesson_Engine_Choice2
data.value: The spin of the wind itself

data.name: Typhoon_Lesson_Engine_Choice3
data.value: Sunlight warming the tops of the clouds

data.name: Typhoon_Lesson_Storm_Choice1
data.value: The Earth's turn deflects the moving air

data.name: Typhoon_Lesson_Storm_Choice2
data.value: The waves push the air sideways

data.name: Typhoon_Lesson_Storm_Choice3
data.value: The eye blows the air back out

data.name: Typhoon_Lesson_Track_Choice1
data.value: It keeps heading west, into South China

data.name: Typhoon_Lesson_Track_Choice3
data.value: It stops and stays where it is

data.name: Typhoon_Pressure_Note
data.value: The lower the pressure, the stronger the wind (further right is deeper).

data.name: Typhoon_Ridge
data.value: West end of the subtropical high

data.name: Typhoon_Ridge_Note
data.value: Reaching far west, it steers storms into South China; pulled back east, it lets them turn north towards Taiwan, Zhejiang, Japan or out to sea.

data.name: Typhoon_Start_Caption
data.value: Where it forms (or click on the sea)

data.name: Typhoon_Stat_Pass_Far
data.value: {0}: too far away to feel it

data.name: Typhoon_Storm_Anticlockwise
data.value: Northern hemisphere: the air spirals in anticlockwise

data.name: Typhoon_Storm_Clockwise
data.value: Southern hemisphere: the air spirals in clockwise

data.name: Typhoon_Storm_Fact1
data.value: Typhoon, hurricane and cyclone are the same kind of storm: a typhoon in the north-west Pacific, a hurricane in the Atlantic and north-east Pacific, a cyclone in the Indian Ocean and the South Pacific.

data.name: Typhoon_Storm_Fact2
data.value: The eye is calm and often clear, most of them 30–60 km across. The strongest winds and heaviest rain are in the eyewall right around it.

data.name: Typhoon_Storm_Fact3
data.value: Air rushing towards the low is turned aside by the Earth's turn (to the right in the north), so it circles anticlockwise instead of filling the low. Within about 5° of the equator the effect is too weak, and typhoons almost never form there.

data.name: Typhoon_Storm_Fact4
data.value: In the north the right side of the track is the dangerous one: there the storm's forward motion adds to its swirl.

data.name: Typhoon_Storm_Fact5
data.value: The lowest sea-level pressure ever measured was 870 hPa, in Typhoon Tip over the north-west Pacific in October 1979.

data.name: Typhoon_Storm_NoSpin
data.value: Without the Earth's turn the air rushes straight in and fills the low

data.name: Typhoon_Storm_NoSpin_Description
data.value: The air heads straight for the low and fills it within a day. It is the Earth's turn (the Coriolis effect) that bends the air aside, so that it circles round instead of in and the low can deepen.

data.name: Typhoon_Storm_Note
data.value: Seen from above, 1200 km across. Winds from the Holland (1980) profile and the north-west Pacific wind–pressure relation; the cloud is illustrative; time runs about 900 times faster.

data.name: Typhoon_Storm_Subtitle
data.value: A typhoon from above: eye, eyewall and rain bands

data.name: Typhoon_Track_Fact1
data.value: About 25 named storms form over the north-west Pacific each year, more than over any other ocean, most of them in August and September.

data.name: Typhoon_Track_Fact2
data.value: A typhoon hardly moves by itself: it is carried by the winds around it, above all those round the subtropical high. Chinese forecasters watch its edge as the 588 line, where the 500 hPa surface is 5880 m high.

data.name: Typhoon_Track_Fact3
data.value: When the high reaches far west, storms head straight into South China, Hainan or Vietnam; when it pulls back east, they turn north towards Taiwan, Zhejiang, Shanghai, Korea or Japan, or curve away over the sea.

data.name: Typhoon_Track_Fact4
data.value: On average about seven tropical storms or stronger come ashore in China each year, most in Guangdong, Hainan, Taiwan, Fujian and Zhejiang.

data.name: Typhoon_Track_Fact5
data.value: Far inland a weakened typhoon can still bring days of heavy rain, to Hunan, Jiangxi or Guangxi; floods are often the biggest danger there.

data.name: Typhoon_Track_Growing_Description
data.value: Over sea warmer than 26.5 °C the storm draws in more heat and strengthens, carried along by the winds round the subtropical high.

data.name: Typhoon_Track_Land_Description
data.value: Cut off from the warm sea, the storm weakens quickly, but its rain spreads far inland.

data.name: Typhoon_Track_Note
data.value: A simplified steering model: the subtropical high as a ridge, the westerlies north of it and the storm's own drift north-west, with growth over warm sea and decay over land. Real tracks also depend on troughs, other storms and the monsoon.

data.name: Typhoon_Track_Over_Description
data.value: It has died out over land, left the map, or gone north into cold air and become an ordinary low. Click on the sea to start another one.

data.name: Typhoon_Track_Sea_Description
data.value: It goes where the steering winds take it. Over cooler water further north it can no longer grow.

data.name: Typhoon_Track_Subtitle
data.value: Where typhoons go, and where they come ashore

data.name: Water_Chart_Litre_Caption
data.value: If all the water were one litre

data.name: Water_Chart_Litre_Note
data.value: The scale goes up ten times at each line. A drop from a dropper is about 0.05 mL: of the litre, all the world's rivers would be about a thirtieth of a drop.

data.name: Water_Chart_Parcel_Caption
data.value: The parcel's temperature and dew point

data.name: Water_Chart_Parcel_Note
data.value: Below the cloud the two lines close in; they meet at the cloud base and go up together. Dashed: the way down the far side of the mountain.

data.name: Water_Chart_Vapour_Caption
data.value: How much vapour air can hold

data.name: Water_Chart_Vapour_Note
data.value: The curve doubles about every 10 °C. The white dot is the landscape's sea-level air today; the slider warms or cools its world.

data.name: Water_Cloud_Back_Description
data.value: Without rain on the way up, the air arrives as warm and as humid as it set off. Only air that has rained out its water arrives warmer: that is the foehn.

data.name: Water_Cloud_DescendingBack_Description
data.value: No rain fell, so any cloud droplets evaporate again as the air sinks and warms: it comes down just as it went up.

data.name: Water_Cloud_Descending_Description
data.value: Having rained out its water, the air sinks down the far side and warms by about 10 °C per kilometre all the way.

data.name: Water_Cloud_Fact1
data.value: Rising air cools by about 10 °C per kilometre until it reaches its dew point; inside the cloud it cools more slowly, about 4 to 7 °C per km, because condensing vapour gives back heat.

data.name: Water_Cloud_Fact2
data.value: You can estimate the cloud base: about 125 m for every degree between the air's temperature and its dew point. On humid days the clouds are low.

data.name: Water_Cloud_Fact3
data.value: Cloud droplets are tiny, about 0.02 mm across; one raindrop holds about a million of them.

data.name: Water_Cloud_Fact4
data.value: Outside the tropics most rain starts as snow high in the cloud and melts on the way down.

data.name: Water_Cloud_Fact5
data.value: Air that rains out on one side of a mountain comes down the other side warmer and drier: the foehn in the Alps, the chinook in the Rockies. Deserts lie behind many mountain ranges.

data.name: Water_Cloud_Foehn_Description
data.value: The air arrives warmer and drier than it set off: it kept the heat its condensing vapour gave back, but lost the water as rain. This is a foehn wind, and the land here lies in a rain shadow.

data.name: Water_Cloud_Freezing_Description
data.value: Above the 0 °C line the droplets stay liquid at first (supercooled), but ice crystals start to form and grow at their expense.

data.name: Water_Cloud_InCloud_Description
data.value: The air has cooled to its dew point and cannot hold all its vapour: it condenses into droplets. From here it cools more slowly, as the condensing water gives back heat.

data.name: Water_Cloud_NoCloud_Description
data.value: The air never cooled to its dew point: it was too dry for the height it was lifted to. Raise the humidity to bring the cloud base down.

data.name: Water_Cloud_Note
data.value: Heights are to scale; the land is squeezed sideways. The parcel is one lump of air followed as it rises, not mixing with the air around it.

data.name: Water_Cloud_Raining_Description
data.value: The cloud is deep enough for droplets to grow into raindrops, or into snowflakes that melt on the way down. Water that evaporated far away falls back.

data.name: Water_Cloud_Rising_Description
data.value: The air rises into lower pressure, expands and cools by about 10 °C every kilometre. Its dew point falls only about 2 °C per km, so the two close in.

data.name: Water_Cloud_Snowing_Description
data.value: The air near the ground is cold enough that the snowflakes do not melt before they land.

data.name: Water_Cloud_Subtitle
data.value: Air that rises cools, until its vapour condenses into a cloud

data.name: Water_Cloud_ThinCloud_Description
data.value: The cloud is too thin for its droplets to grow big enough to fall. Lift the air higher, or make it more humid.

data.name: Water_Cycle_Fact1
data.value: Every year about 500,000 km³ of water evaporates, as much as a metre of water over the whole Earth, and the same amount falls back as rain and snow.

data.name: Water_Cycle_Fact2
data.value: About 90 % of the water that evaporates from the sea falls straight back onto the sea; the rest is blown over land and comes back by rivers and groundwater.

data.name: Water_Cycle_Fact3
data.value: A water molecule stays in the air for about 9 days on average, in a river a couple of weeks, in the ocean about 3,000 years, and in deep groundwater or Antarctic ice for up to hundreds of thousands of years.

data.name: Water_Cycle_Fact4
data.value: Plants move a great deal of water: a big tree can give off over a hundred litres on a summer day, and transpiration is more than half of all the water rising from land.

data.name: Water_Cycle_Fact5
data.value: Warmer air holds about 7 % more water vapour for every degree, so a warmer world has heavier downpours, more of its snow falls as rain, and the snow line moves up the mountains.

data.name: Water_Cycle_Note
data.value: Heights are real but the land is squeezed sideways: the picture is a few hundred kilometres across. Trees and the river are drawn much bigger than real.

data.name: Water_Cycle_Subtitle
data.value: Water goes round: from the sea into the air, onto the land, and back

data.name: Water_Flow_OceanPrecipitation
data.value: Rain and snow on the sea

data.name: Water_Hint_Cloud
data.value: Change the air's temperature and humidity on the left page and watch the cloud base move.

data.name: Water_Hint_Cycle
data.value: Click a label to light up that part of the cycle, or follow one drop all the way round.

data.name: Water_Hint_Stores_Flows
data.value: The dots run along each flow; the wider the band, the more water each year.

data.name: Water_Hint_Stores_Spheres
data.value: Switch the picture to the yearly flows to see how water moves between sea, air and land.

data.name: Water_Leg_Condensation_Description
data.value: The air carrying it rises and cools to its dew point; the drop condenses onto a speck of dust and becomes a cloud droplet.

data.name: Water_Leg_Evaporation_Description
data.value: Warmed by the Sun at the surface, the drop escapes into the air as vapour: invisible, and leaving its salt behind.

data.name: Water_Leg_Groundwater_Description
data.value: Now groundwater, the drop creeps through the rock toward the sea, perhaps only metres a year. Shallow groundwater takes years to centuries; deep groundwater thousands of years.

data.name: Water_Leg_Infiltration_Description
data.value: The drop soaks into the soil and trickles down through cracks and gaps until it reaches the water table.

data.name: Water_Leg_Ocean_Description
data.value: The drop is one of some 1.3 billion km³ of sea water. On average water stays in the ocean for over 3,000 years before it evaporates.

data.name: Water_Leg_Rain_Description
data.value: About a million cloud droplets have merged into one raindrop, heavy enough to fall. From a cloud a couple of kilometres up it lands in a few minutes.

data.name: Water_Leg_River_Description
data.value: Streams join into a river that carries the drop back to the sea. A river holds its water only a couple of weeks on average.

data.name: Water_Leg_Snowfall_Description
data.value: Above the 0 °C line the water freezes onto an ice crystal and falls slowly as a snowflake onto the mountain.

data.name: Water_Leg_Snowmelt_Description
data.value: In spring the Sun melts the snow, and the drop trickles down the slope toward a stream.

data.name: Water_Leg_Snowpack_Description
data.value: The drop waits in the snow through the winter. In a glacier it could wait for centuries; deep in Antarctic ice, for hundreds of thousands of years.

data.name: Water_Leg_Transpiration_Description
data.value: Through a tiny pore in the leaf the drop escapes as vapour. Over land, plants send more water into the air than the soil and lakes do.

data.name: Water_Leg_Transport_Description
data.value: As vapour, the drop travels with the wind, often hundreds or thousands of kilometres. Water stays in the air about 9 days on average.

data.name: Water_Leg_Uptake_Description
data.value: Roots take the drop up from the soil; it rises through the trunk to a leaf within days.

data.name: Water_Lesson_Cloud_Choice1
data.value: The vapour condenses into a cloud

data.name: Water_Lesson_Cycle_Choice1
data.value: It cools, and rain or snow falls

data.name: Water_Lesson_Cycle_Choice2
data.value: It warms up, and the clouds vanish

data.name: Water_Process_Condensation_Description
data.value: Rising air expands and cools. Once it cools to its dew point, vapour condenses onto tiny specks of dust, salt or smoke as cloud droplets about 0.02 mm across, giving back the heat the Sun put in when the water evaporated.

data.name: Water_Process_Evaporation_Amount
data.value: about 413,000 km³ from the sea, 73,000 km³ from land and plants

data.name: Water_Process_Evaporation_Description
data.value: Sunlight gives water molecules at the surface enough energy to escape into the air as invisible vapour. The salt stays behind, so rain is fresh water. Most evaporation, about 85 %, is from the oceans.

data.name: Water_Process_Groundwater_Amount
data.value: most of it feeds rivers and lakes; a few percent seeps straight into the sea

data.name: Water_Process_Groundwater_Description
data.value: Below the water table, water creeps through the rock, often only metres a year, toward rivers, lakes and the sea. Wells and springs tap it. It is the largest store of liquid fresh water by far.

data.name: Water_Process_Infiltration_Amount
data.value: about 13,000 km³ refills groundwater, a tenth of the rain on land

data.name: Water_Process_Infiltration_Description
data.value: Rain soaks into the soil. Some stays there for plants; some trickles on down through gaps in the soil and rock to the water table, below which every gap is full of water.

data.name: Water_Process_Overview_Description
data.value: The Sun warms the sea and water evaporates as invisible vapour. The wind carries it; rising air cools and the vapour condenses into clouds; rain and snow fall; water runs back to the sea in rivers or slowly through the ground. Nothing is lost: the same water has gone round for billions of years.

data.name: Water_Process_Precipitation_Amount
data.value: about 373,000 km³ on the sea, 113,000 km³ on land

data.name: Water_Process_Precipitation_Description
data.value: Cloud droplets merge, or ice crystals grow at their expense, until they are heavy enough to fall. Below the 0 °C line it reaches the ground as rain, above it as snow. Air pushed up a mountain rains on the near side and leaves the far side dry.

data.name: Water_Process_Runoff_Amount
data.value: about 40,000 km³ back to the sea, with groundwater

data.name: Water_Process_Runoff_Description
data.value: Water that does not soak in or evaporate runs downhill in streams that join into rivers and flow to the sea. A drop spends on average only a couple of weeks in a river.

data.name: Water_Process_Snowmelt_Amount
data.value: the main water supply of about a sixth of the world's people

data.name: Water_Process_Snowmelt_Description
data.value: Snow and glaciers store water through the winter and let it go in spring and summer. Rivers such as the Yangtze, the Ganges and the Indus get much of their summer water from snow and ice far upstream.

data.name: Water_Process_Sublimation_Amount
data.value: a small share worldwide; on dry high mountains a fifth of the snow or more

data.name: Water_Process_Sublimation_Description
data.value: In dry, sunny, windy air, snow and ice can turn straight into vapour without melting first. It takes much more energy than melting, but high on dry mountains it removes a good part of the snow.

data.name: Water_Process_Transpiration_Amount
data.value: about 45,000 km³, some 60 % of what evaporates from land

data.name: Water_Process_Transpiration_Description
data.value: Plants draw water up from the soil through their roots and stems and give it off as vapour through tiny pores in their leaves. It cools them, like sweating, and pulls more water up behind it.

data.name: Water_Process_Transport_Amount
data.value: about 40,000 km³ from over the sea to over land

data.name: Water_Process_Transport_Description
data.value: Water vapour is invisible. Winds carry it far from where it evaporated, much of it inland from the sea. Without this, rain would fall only over the sea and the land would be desert.

data.name: Water_Stat_RainDepth_Value
data.value: about a metre of rain and snow a year

data.name: Water_Store_Land
data.value: Land: ice, groundwater, lakes, soil, rivers

data.name: Water_Stores_Flows_Description
data.value: The bands show how much water moves each year. The air gains as much as it loses, and so do the sea and the land: the vapour carried over land each year comes back by rivers and groundwater.

data.name: Water_Stores_Flows_Fact1
data.value: Each year about 413,000 km³ evaporates from the sea and 73,000 km³ from land and plants; 373,000 km³ falls back on the sea and 113,000 km³ on land.

data.name: Water_Stores_Flows_Fact2
data.value: The 40,000 km³ of vapour blown from sea to land each year comes back down rivers and through the ground; the Amazon alone carries about a sixth of it.

data.name: Water_Stores_Flows_Fact3
data.value: On land almost two thirds of the rain and snow goes back into the air from soil, lakes and plants; only about a third runs off to the sea.

data.name: Water_Stores_Flows_Fact4
data.value: The air's water is replaced about every 9 days: 12,900 km³ in the air, against about 500,000 km³ falling out of it each year.

data.name: Water_Stores_Flows_Fact5
data.value: The Sun drives it all: evaporating water uses about half the sunlight the ground and sea absorb, and the heat comes back out where the vapour condenses into clouds.

data.name: Water_Stores_Flows_Note
data.value: Band widths are to scale with the yearly amounts (Trenberth and others, 2007); the stores are from the USGS.

data.name: Water_Stores_Flows_Subtitle
data.value: Each year about a metre of water rises from the whole Earth, and falls again

data.name: Water_Stores_Flows_Title
data.value: Where the water goes each year

data.name: Water_Stores_Spheres_Description
data.value: The big ball is all of Earth's water: oceans, ice, groundwater, lakes, air, everything. The middle one is the liquid fresh water: groundwater, lakes, swamps and rivers. The tiny one is the fresh water in lakes and rivers, the water we can use most easily.

data.name: Water_Stores_Spheres_Fact1
data.value: Gathered into one ball, all of Earth's water would be only about 1,380 km across, about a ninth of Earth's diameter.

data.name: Water_Stores_Spheres_Fact2
data.value: Over 96 % of it is salty sea water. Of the 2.5 % that is fresh, about 69 % is frozen in ice caps and glaciers and about 30 % is underground.

data.name: Water_Stores_Spheres_Fact3
data.value: All the fresh water in the world's lakes and rivers would fit in a ball 56 km across. Lake Baikal alone holds about a fifth of the unfrozen fresh water on the surface.

data.name: Water_Stores_Spheres_Fact4
data.value: The air holds only about 13,000 km³ of water: if it all fell at once, it would cover Earth about 2.5 cm deep.

data.name: Water_Stores_Spheres_Fact5
data.value: The Antarctic ice sheet holds about 90 % of the world's ice; if it all melted the sea would rise by about 58 m.

data.name: Water_Stores_Spheres_Note
data.value: Earth and the balls on it are to the same scale; on the right the same balls are enlarged.

data.name: Water_Stores_Spheres_Subtitle
data.value: All of Earth's water would make a surprisingly small ball

data.name: Water_Stores_Spheres_Title
data.value: All the water in three balls
